teile.einleitung: Earwigs are a group of insects that can be recognised by the striking pincers at the rear end. Worldwide there are almost 2000 species, and in Switzerland the common earwig is the most frequent. Despite their uncanny name they are completely harmless to people.
wichtigste: Earwigs are insects and have six legs.
Their body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
Their hard outer covering consists of chitin.
On the head they carry two antennae for touching and smelling.
Their pincers serve for defence, for holding on and for folding the wings.
They develop through larval stages without a pupa.
The name probably comes from the old belief that they crawled into ears at night.

abschnitte.text: Like all **insects**, earwigs have six legs and a body made of head, thorax and abdomen. A hard outer covering of **chitin** protects the body like armour. On the head sit two long antennae with which they touch and smell. With their biting and chewing mouthparts they break up plants and small animals.

At the end of the abdomen earwigs carry pincers, which have developed from two modified appendages, the **cerci**. With them they defend themselves and hold on to prey or partners. In males the pincers are usually more strongly curved than in females. If you touch an earwig, it can nip briefly, but this is harmless.

The front wings of earwigs are short and hard. Beneath them lie large, membranous hind wings that are folded many times like a fan. In folding them the pincers help, pushing the wings under the wing cases. This **folding** is among the most complicated in the whole animal kingdom, yet many earwigs fly only rarely.

From the egg hatches a **larva** that already looks almost like a small earwig. It moults several times and grows larger. There is no pupal stage as in butterflies or beetles. Experts call this development incomplete metamorphosis.

Earwigs live on all continents except Antarctica, most species in warm regions. They are mostly **nocturnal** and hide by day in narrow, damp crevices. Many species eat parts of plants, small insects and dead matter. The females look after eggs and young, which is rare in insects.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name come from?
abschnitte.text: In the past many people believed that earwigs crawled into the ears of sleepers at night. This is a **superstition** that is not true. Perhaps it arose because the animals like to slip into narrow openings. Another explanation says that dried earwigs used to be used as a remedy for earaches.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm substance of which the outer covering of insects is made.
Two appendages on the abdomen that have become pincers in the earwig.
The young form of an insect.
A development from the egg via larvae to the adult animal without a pupa.

gewusst: The hind wings of an earwig are about ten times as large unfolded as folded.
Researchers have studied the wing folding of earwigs in order to develop foldable solar sails and tents.
The mother earwig turns and cleans her eggs again and again so that they do not go mouldy.

teile.einleitung: A pony is a small horse. A horse counts as a pony if it is smaller than 148 centimetres at the withers. Ponies are tough, clever and very popular with children as riding animals.
wichtigste: Ponies belong to the same species as the large horses.
A horse under 148 centimetres at the withers counts as a pony.
Height is measured at the withers, the highest point of the back between the shoulders.
Well-known pony breeds are the Shetland pony, the Welsh pony and the Connemara pony.
Ponies often come from barren regions and are very undemanding.
They often live to over 30 years old.
Ponies are ridden, harnessed to carriages and in the past were also used as working animals.

abschnitte.text: Ponies and large horses both belong to the species **domestic horse**. The difference lies mainly in size. The **height at the withers** is measured, which is the height from the ground to the withers. If it is under 148 centimetres, it is called a pony. Some breeds such as the Icelandic horse are as small as ponies, but are still called horses.

Ponies usually have a strong build, short legs and a rather short neck. Their mane and tail are often especially dense. In winter they grow a thick, shaggy **winter coat** that protects them from cold and wet. Their hooves are hard and tough, which is why many ponies do not need horseshoes.

The **Shetland pony** comes from the Shetland Islands in the north of Scotland and is one of the smallest breeds, often only about a metre tall. The Welsh pony comes from Wales, the Connemara pony from Ireland. The Fjord horse from Norway and the Haflinger from South Tyrol are also often counted as ponies. There are also tiny miniature horses such as the Falabella from Argentina.

In the past, ponies were important working animals. In England, Shetland ponies worked as so-called **pit ponies** in coal mines, because they fitted into the low tunnels. On farms, ponies pulled small carts and ploughs. Today they are used mainly for riding, carriage driving and in riding therapy.

Because of their size, ponies are well suited to children learning to ride. In Switzerland too there are many riding schools, pony farms and pony clubs. Ponies are clever and sometimes also a little stubborn. They need plenty of exercise, the company of other horses and above all hay, because too much juicy grass and concentrated feed quickly makes them too fat and ill.

begriffe.erklaerung: The raised spot between the neck and back of a horse, where height is measured.
The height of a horse from the ground to the withers.
A pony that in the past pulled carts underground in mines.
Treatment in which working with horses is meant to make people healthy or support them.

gewusst: In proportion to its size, a Shetland pony can pull more than a large horse.
Some ponies have lived to over 40 years old, older than most large horses.
Foals of large horses are not ponies, even if they are still small.

teile.einleitung: The pupa is the stage between caterpillar and butterfly. In this seemingly resting case, the insect's body is completely rebuilt. Pupae exist in all insects with complete metamorphosis, so also in beetles, bees and flies.
wichtigste: The pupa is the stage between larva and adult insect.
In a butterfly, the pupa lies between the caterpillar and the adult.
In the pupa, the body of the larva is almost completely rebuilt.
Pupae are often green or brown like their surroundings and so well camouflaged.
Shortly before hatching, the pupal case becomes transparent in the butterfly.
Development with a pupal stage is called complete metamorphosis.
Some pupae overwinter and hatch only the following spring.

abschnitte.text: Butterflies go through four stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa and adult. This development is called **complete metamorphosis**. The caterpillar eats and grows, moults several times and finally turns into a pupa. From the pupa the adult butterfly then emerges, which experts call the **imago**.

From the outside a pupa looks calm, but inside something astonishing happens. A large part of the caterpillar's body is dissolved. From small groups of cells that were already laid down in the caterpillar, wings, legs, antennae and compound eyes form anew. Depending on the species, this rebuilding takes a few days to several weeks.

Many pupae are green or brown and look like a leaf or a piece of bark, so they are well **camouflaged**. Some butterfly pupae hang head down from a thread, and these are called **suspended pupae**, for example in the peacock butterfly. Others are fastened upright with a silk girdle, and these are girdled pupae such as in the swallowtail. Some caterpillars spin a protective cocoon of silk around themselves, like the silk moth.

Beetles, bees, wasps, ants, flies and mosquitoes also have a pupal stage. Beetles and bees usually form a free pupa, in which the legs and wings already lie free against the body. Flies pupate in a hard, brown case, the **puparium**. The so-called ant eggs that you see in anthills are in reality often ant pupae.

Shortly before a butterfly hatches, the pupal case becomes transparent, and you can make out the colours of the wings. Then the case splits open and the butterfly crawls out. Its wings are at first soft and crumpled. It pumps body fluid into the wing veins until they unfold and, after a while, are hard and ready for flight.

begriffe.erklaerung: The transformation of an animal from the larva to the adult form.
The fully developed adult insect.
A protective case of silk that some caterpillars spin around themselves.
A pupa that hangs head down from a thread.

gewusst: Some pupae can wriggle or make noises to scare off enemies.
For thousands of years, people have obtained silk from the cocoons of the silk moth.
The German word Puppe for the insect stage comes from the fact that the case is reminiscent of a wrapped-up doll.

teile.einleitung: The olive ridley turtle is a small sea turtle with an olive-green shell. It is famous for its mass arrivals, in which tens of thousands of females come to one beach at the same time to lay eggs. It is the most common sea turtle in the world.
wichtigste: The olive ridley turtle sometimes lays its eggs on the beach by day, in huge groups.
These mass arrivals are called ‘arribadas’, Spanish for ‘arrival’.
Its shell is olive green and about 60 to 70 centimetres long.
It lives in the warm seas of the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic.
It is the most common sea turtle, but nevertheless a threatened one.
Whether males or females hatch depends on the temperature in the sand.

abschnitte.text: The olive ridley turtle is among the smallest **sea turtles**. Its almost round shell is about 60 to 70 centimetres long and coloured olive green to grey. Adult animals usually weigh 35 to 45 kilograms. Instead of legs it has flat **flippers**, with which it glides elegantly through the water.

It lives in tropical and warm seas around the world. It is especially common in the Pacific off Central America and in the Indian Ocean. The animals migrate long distances through the open sea. To lay eggs the females return to beaches, often those where they hatched themselves.

The olive ridley turtle is an **omnivore**. It eats crabs, shrimps, snails, jellyfish, fish and algae. With its strong jaw it can crack hard shells. Sometimes it dives over 100 metres deep to look for food.

What is special about this species is the **arribada**, the mass arrival to lay eggs. In it tens of thousands of females come to the same beach within a few days, sometimes also by day. Famous arribada beaches lie in Costa Rica, Mexico and in the Indian state of Odisha. Each female digs a hole in the sand and lays about 100 eggs in it.

After about 45 to 60 days the little turtles hatch. If the sand is warmer, more females hatch, and if it is cooler, more males. The young usually crawl to the sea at night and orient themselves by the brighter horizon. Many are eaten on the way by birds, crabs and fish.

The olive ridley turtle is regarded as **vulnerable**. Many animals die as bycatch in fishing nets, and in addition eggs and meat are collected. Plastic waste and artificial light on beaches threaten them further. On some beaches protection programmes watch over the nests, and in Costa Rica local people may collect eggs only under control.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mass arrival of sea turtles to lay eggs, Spanish for ‘arrival’.
Animals that are caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
A turtle that lives in the sea and comes onto land only to lay eggs.
An animal that eats both plant and animal food.

gewusst: In an arribada so many females can come that, while digging, they accidentally dig up the eggs of other turtles.
The temperature in the nest decides the sex of the young, not the genes.
Where the German name ‘Bastardschildkröte’ (‘bastard turtle’) comes from is still not clearly established.

teile.einleitung: Oviparous means egg-laying. This is what animals are called that lay eggs from which the young hatch only outside the mother’s body. They include, for example, all birds, most fish and insects, and also the sand lizard.
wichtigste: Oviparous means egg-laying.
Oviparous animals lay eggs, and the young develop outside the mother’s body.
All birds are oviparous.
Most reptiles, amphibians, fish and insects also lay eggs.
The sand lizard is an egg-laying reptile that also occurs in Switzerland.
Only two groups of mammals lay eggs, the platypus and the echidnas.
The opposite of oviparous is viviparous, that is, giving birth to live young.

abschnitte.text: The word **oviparous** comes from Latin: ovum means egg and parere means to give birth. Oviparous animals lay eggs in which the embryo grows. It is fed in the process by the **yolk**, a store of nutrients in the egg. When development is complete, the young hatches from the egg.

The **sand lizard** also lives in Switzerland, for instance on sunny banks, railway embankments and woodland edges. In early summer the female digs a small hollow in loose soil and lays about 5 to 15 eggs in it. The sun warms the ground and with it the eggs, and the mother no longer looks after them. After a few weeks the little lizards hatch and are independent at once.

All birds lay eggs with a hard **shell**. Most birds incubate their eggs, that is, they warm them with their own body. The largest egg is laid by the ostrich, and it weighs about as much as 20 to 25 hen’s eggs. Hummingbirds lay very small eggs, some hardly bigger than a pea.

Most fish and frogs lay many soft eggs in the water, which are called **spawn**. A common frog, for example, lays over a thousand eggs in one clump of spawn. Insects such as butterflies or ladybirds are also oviparous and often stick their eggs to leaves. Because many eggs are eaten, such animals usually lay very many of them.

Almost all mammals give birth to live young. An exception are the **monotremes** in Australia and New Guinea, namely the platypus and the echidnas. They lay eggs with a leathery shell. After hatching, the young nevertheless drink milk, as in other mammals.

Laying eggs has advantages for the mother, because she does not have to carry the young for long inside her and stays mobile. On the other hand, the eggs are often unprotected and are easily eaten by predators. Besides oviparous, a distinction is made between **viviparous**, that is, live-bearing, and ovoviviparous, when the eggs stay in the mother’s body until the young hatch. In Switzerland the common lizard shows that even related species can differ, because it usually gives birth to live young.

begriffe.erklaerung: Egg-laying, the young hatch from eggs outside the mother.
Live-bearing, the young develop inside the mother’s body.
A store of nutrients in the egg on which the embryo feeds.
The soft eggs of fish or amphibians, usually laid in water.

gewusst: Many chicks have a small egg tooth on the beak with which they break open the eggshell and which they lose later.
In proportion to her body, a female kiwi lays one of the largest eggs of any bird.
The platypus is a mammal, but lays eggs like a reptile.

teile.einleitung: The Arctic fox, also called the polar fox, is a small fox that lives in the icy regions around the North Pole. Its dense fur keeps it warm even in extreme cold. In winter, in many animals it is snow white, so that it becomes almost invisible in the snow.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the Arctic fox is Vulpes lagopus.
In the past it was often placed in a genus of its own, Alopex.
The species name “lagopus” literally means “hare's foot”.
It belongs to the dog family (Canidae) and is also called the polar fox.
There is a white and a blue colour form.
Worldwide it is not threatened, but in Fennoscandia it is seriously endangered.
In Iceland it is the only originally native land mammal.

abschnitte.text: The Arctic fox is smaller than our red fox and usually weighs only about 3 to 5 kilograms. Its ears and its muzzle are short and round, so it loses little heat. The soles of its feet are also densely covered in hair, which is where the species name **lagopus** comes from, literally meaning “hare's foot”. There are two colour forms: the **white form** is snow white in winter and brownish-grey in summer, and the blue form is dark bluish-grey all year round.

The Arctic fox lives in the **tundra** and on the pack ice around the North Pole, in North America, Greenland, northern Europe and Siberia. Its winter coat is so dense that it can withstand temperatures below minus 40 degrees. In Iceland it is the only originally native land mammal. It migrated there over the frozen sea at the end of the Ice Age.

Arctic foxes eat mainly **lemmings** and other small rodents. They hear the animals under the snow and then leap in with a bound to seize them. They also eat birds, eggs, berries and fish. In winter, some Arctic foxes follow polar bears across the pack ice and eat the remains of their seal prey.

Arctic fox pairs often stay together for several years and raise their young together. They live in a **den** with many entrances, which is sometimes used by generations for centuries. In years with many lemmings, a female has a great many young, often more than ten. When there is little food, the litter is much smaller.

The Arctic fox belongs to the **dog family** (Canidae), like the wolf, the dog and the red fox. Today its scientific name is Vulpes lagopus, so it is in the same genus as the red fox. In the past it was often placed in a genus of its own called Alopex. In German it is also called **Eisfuchs**, meaning ice fox.

Worldwide the Arctic fox is listed as not threatened on the IUCN Red List. In Fennoscandia, that is, in Norway, Sweden and Finland, however, it is very rare and seriously endangered. At the start of the 20th century it was hunted heavily there for its valuable **fur**, until the populations collapsed. Finland placed it under protection in 1940, but despite a hunting ban lasting decades, the populations are recovering only slowly because of a lack of lemmings and competition from the red fox.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treeless, cold landscape in the far north with mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.
A small, hamster-like rodent of the north, the Arctic fox's most important prey.
A colour form of an animal species, like the white and the blue form of the Arctic fox.
The underground living burrow of a fox with several entrances.

gewusst: The Arctic fox only starts to freeze in extreme cold, and its fur is among the warmest of all mammals.
Arctic foxes can wander thousands of kilometres in search of food.
In summer, Arctic foxes hide food in the ground as a store for the winter.

teile.einleitung: The Salamandridae, or true salamanders, are a family of the tailed amphibians. They include salamanders and newts such as the fire salamander and the alpine newt. All of these animals have a long tail and live, at least part of the time, in or beside water.
wichtigste: Salamandridae is the scientific name of the family of true salamanders.
The family includes salamanders and newts, for example the alpine newt.
They are amphibians from the order of the tailed amphibians.
The family includes over 100 species in Europe, Asia, North Africa and North America.
Many species have poisonous skin glands and warning colours.
In Switzerland live, among others, the fire salamander, the alpine salamander, the alpine newt and the great crested newt.
All native amphibians are protected in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **Salamandridae** are a family of the **tailed amphibians**. They look like lizards, but are amphibians with moist, scaleless skin. The family includes the salamanders proper, which mostly live on land, and the **newts**, which go into the water to mate. Their relatives are frogs and toads.

True salamanders live in the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. You find them in Europe, North Africa, Asia as far as Japan and in North America. Many species live in forests with streams, pools and ponds. In the mountains some occur up to over 2,000 metres.

Newts migrate in spring into ponds, where the males wear a splendid **breeding dress**. The females wrap their eggs one by one in leaves of water plants. From the eggs hatch larvae with external gills, which later change into land animals. The fire salamander, by contrast, puts live larvae into the water, and the alpine salamander even gives birth to fully formed young on land.

Many true salamanders have **skin glands** that secrete a poison. It protects them from enemies and from fungi and bacteria. Bright colours such as the yellow of the fire salamander or the orange belly of the alpine newt warn enemies. For people the poison is harmless, but you should wash your hands after touching them.

In Switzerland live fire salamanders, **alpine salamanders**, alpine newts, palmate newts, smooth newts and great crested newts, and in Ticino also the Italian crested newt. The alpine newt is the most common newt in the country. Many species are endangered because pools and wetlands are disappearing. A new danger is an introduced skin fungus that can kill salamanders.

begriffe.erklaerung: Amphibians with a long tail, such as salamanders and newts.
A tailed amphibian that lives in the water for a longer time in order to reproduce.
The young form of an animal that looks different from the adult animal.
Animals that live in water and on land.

gewusst: Newts can regrow lost legs and even parts of the heart.
An alpine salamander can be pregnant for up to four years, depending on altitude.

teile.einleitung: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest octopus in the world. It lives in the cold water of the northern Pacific and can measure several metres from arm tip to arm tip. It is regarded as very intelligent and can change its colour in a flash.
wichtigste: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest octopus in the world.
From arm to arm it can grow several metres across.
It lives in the northern Pacific, for example off Japan, Alaska and Canada.
It has eight arms with many suckers.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
It usually lives only three to five years.
The female guards her eggs for months and dies afterwards.

abschnitte.text: The giant Pacific octopus has the scientific name **Enteroctopus dofleini**. It is mostly reddish brown, but can change colour and pattern in a flash. For this it has colour cells in the skin, which it can open and close at will. Its eight **arms** each carry two rows of strong suckers. Adult animals often weigh about 20 to 40 kilograms, and some much more.

From arm tip to arm tip, a large giant Pacific octopus measures several metres. In especially large animals it is over 4 metres. Even so, it has no bones and can squeeze through astonishingly narrow gaps. Only its hard **beak** decides how small a hole may be. In this way it is among the most flexible animals in the sea.

It lives in the cool water of the **North Pacific**, from Japan and Korea via Russia and Alaska to California. It is found from shallow coasts to depths of several hundred metres. By day it hides in caves and rock crevices. In front of its den there are often empty shells of mussels and crabs. At night it goes hunting.

The giant Pacific octopus eats crabs, mussels, snails and fish. With its suckers it can also pull open tightly closed mussels. Sometimes it drills a hole in the shell and squirts a paralysing poison into it. With its parrot-like **beak** it cuts up its prey. When in danger it expels a cloud of ink and escapes by jet propulsion.

Octopuses live only a short time, and the giant Pacific octopus usually lives three to five years. The female lays tens of thousands of eggs in a den. For months she guards the eggs, fans fresh water over them and keeps them clean. During this time she eats nothing. Shortly after the young have hatched, the mother dies.

Octopuses are regarded as the most **intelligent** invertebrates. In aquariums, giant Pacific octopuses learn to open screw lids on jars. Some recognise individual keepers. A large part of their nerve cells sits in the arms, so that the arms partly “think” for themselves. The three hearts pump a blood that is coloured **blue** by a substance containing copper.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cephalopod with eight arms and no inner shell.
A round adhesive disc on the arms with which the octopus holds on and grabs prey.
Animals without a backbone, for example insects, snails and octopuses.
A dark liquid that octopuses expel to hide their escape.

gewusst: A giant Pacific octopus has over 2,000 suckers, with which it can also taste.
Octopuses can slip through an opening that is hardly larger than their beak.
An octopus can regrow a lost arm.

teile.einleitung: Orangutans are large apes with reddish-brown fur that live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Their name comes from Malay and means ‘person of the forest’. They are the largest animals in the world that live mainly in trees.
wichtigste: Today three orangutan species are distinguished.
Orangutans live only on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra.
The fur of most orangutans is reddish-brown.
Their arms are very long and reach to the ankles when standing.
Adult males are bigger than females and often have cheek pads.
A young orangutan often stays with its mother for seven to nine years.
All three species are critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: A distinction is made between the **Bornean orangutan**, the Sumatran orangutan and the Tapanuli orangutan. The Tapanuli orangutan lives in a small area in the north of Sumatra and was described as a separate species only in 2017. It is the rarest great ape species in the world. Like gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos, all orangutans belong to the **great apes**.

Orangutans have long, mostly reddish-brown fur. Their arms are very long, and the arm span of adult males is over two metres. Adult males are about twice as heavy as females and often have broad **cheek pads** on the face. Hands and feet are built for grasping, so they can hold on with all four.

Orangutans climb and swing carefully through the treetops. Every evening they build themselves a new **sleeping nest** from branches and leaves. When they sense danger, they usually withdraw into the trees. In rain they sometimes hold large leaves over their heads like an umbrella.

Orangutans eat mainly ripe fruit such as figs and durian. In addition there are leaves, bark, flowers, insects and honey. With their skilful hands they peel fruit and crack nuts. Some orangutans use sticks as a **tool** to get at seeds or insects.

Pregnancy lasts about nine months, as in humans. A young orangutan stays with its mother for several years, often until the age of seven to nine. Because females have young so rarely, numbers grow only very slowly. Adult males give a loud **long call**, a long cry with which they announce their territory.

All three species are regarded as **critically endangered**. The main reason is the clearing of the rainforest, above all for oil palm and timber plantations. In addition there are forest fires, poaching and the illegal trade in young animals. In Switzerland Sumatran orangutans can be seen, for example, at Zurich Zoo, where the enclosures are designed with climbing trees and ropes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The closest relatives of humans: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos.
Broad pads on the cheeks of adult male orangutans.
A long, loud cry of male orangutans.
A bed of branches and leaves that orangutans build in the trees every evening.

gewusst: Orangutans help to spread seeds and are therefore also called ‘gardeners of the rainforest’.
In orangutans there are often six to nine years between two births, as long as in hardly any other mammal.
Young orangutans learn from their mother which of the hundreds of plants in the forest are edible.

teile.einleitung: The Red List of threatened species is a large register that shows how strongly animals, plants and fungi are threatened with extinction. The best-known list is kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the IUCN, which has its seat in Switzerland. It helps experts to decide which species most urgently need protection.
wichtigste: The Red List shows how strongly species are threatened with extinction.
The worldwide Red List is kept by the IUCN, based in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
There are categories from “not threatened” to “extinct”.
“Critically endangered” means that there are only very few animals left.
“Vulnerable” means that the species could die out in the future.
The chimpanzee, too, is on the Red List as an endangered species.
Switzerland also has its own Red Lists for its animals and plants.

abschnitte.text: The Red List is a collection of assessments for a very large number of species. For each species, experts check how many animals are still left, how fast the population is shrinking and how large its habitat is. The worldwide list is kept by the **IUCN**, the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The IUCN was founded in 1948 and has its headquarters in Gland on Lake Geneva.

The list divides species into **categories**, rather like a traffic light. “Least concern” means that the species is doing well, and “near threatened” is an early warning. After that come “vulnerable”, “endangered” and “critically endangered”. At the very end come “extinct in the wild” and “extinct”.

The **chimpanzee** is regarded as endangered because its forest is being cleared and it is hunted. The Sumatran orangutan and the Amur leopard are even critically endangered. Many frogs, sharks and corals are also in danger. In total, by about 2024 over 160,000 species had been assessed, and more than a quarter of them count as threatened.

The most important reason is the **destruction of habitats**, for example when forests are cleared or wetlands are drained. Added to this are poaching, overfishing, environmental poisons and introduced alien species. Climate change, too, changes habitats faster than many species can adapt. Mostly several causes work together.

The Federal Office for the Environment, **FOEN**, publishes its own Red Lists for Switzerland. They show that about a third of the species studied in Switzerland are threatened or have already disappeared. Especially affected are animals and plants of wetlands, moors and dry meadows. The lists help cantons and municipalities to plan protected areas.

Protection can work: the **Alpine ibex** had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1911. Today many thousands of ibex live in the Alps again. The bearded vulture, too, has circled over the Swiss mountains again since its reintroduction from 1991. Such successes show how important the Red List is as a warning system.

begriffe.erklaerung: The International Union for Conservation of Nature, which keeps the worldwide Red List.
A group of living things that can reproduce with one another.
A place where an animal or a plant finds everything it needs to live.
There is not a single living thing of this species left on Earth.

gewusst: The colour red was chosen because, as with a traffic light, it means danger.
The headquarters of the worldwide Red List, the IUCN, is in Switzerland on Lake Geneva.
Some species that were thought to be extinct were later rediscovered.

teile.einleitung: The common redshank, in German Rotschenkel, is a slender wader that you recognise at once by its bright red legs. It lives mainly on coasts, in the Wadden Sea and in damp meadows. With its loud alarm calls it often alerts all the other birds in the area.
wichtigste: You recognise the redshank by its red legs.
The base of its beak is also red.
It belongs to the sandpipers and snipes, a family of waders.
It lives on coasts, in the Wadden Sea and in damp meadows.
It eats worms, crustaceans, snails and insects.
In Switzerland you see it mainly on migration.

abschnitte.text: The redshank is about 27 to 29 centimetres long, so roughly as big as a blackbird with long legs. Its plumage is grey-brown and finely spotted. Most striking are the **orange-red legs** and the red base of the beak. In flight you see a white wedge on the back and broad white stripes on the rear edges of the wings.

The redshank is a **wader** and lives where it is wet and open. You find it on sea coasts, in the **Wadden Sea** of the North Sea, in salt marshes and in damp meadows inland. It occurs in large parts of Europe and Asia. In winter many redshanks move to the coasts of western Europe, to the Mediterranean or to Africa.

With its long, straight beak, the redshank probes the soft mud for food. It eats worms, small **crustaceans**, mussels, snails and insects. In doing so it often runs hectically back and forth and pecks quickly. At low tide, when the mudflats dry out, it finds especially much food.

The redshank is very alert and calls loudly and shrilly when in danger. Its calls also warn other birds, which is why it is sometimes called the **sentinel** of the salt marsh. In the breeding season it likes to sit on posts or fence posts and watch the surroundings. In its display flight the male climbs high and sings as he does so.

The nest is a simple hollow in the grass, often hidden by stalks bent over it. The female usually lays four spotted eggs. Both parents incubate, and the chicks can run and look for food themselves soon after hatching. Because damp meadows are being drained, the redshank as a breeding bird has become **rarer** in many countries.

In Switzerland the redshank does not breed regularly. But you can watch it in spring and autumn as a **passage migrant** on lake shores and in wetlands, for example on Lake Neuchâtel. Similar in appearance is the spotted redshank, which also has red legs, but is longer and slimmer. Its close relative, the greenshank, by contrast, has greenish legs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with long legs that looks for food in shallow water.
A coastal area that dries out at low tide and is flooded at high tide.
A migratory bird that crosses an area only on its journey.
A bird family with many waders, to which the redshank also belongs.

gewusst: The German name Rotschenkel refers to the legs, called Schenkel, which are coloured red in the redshank.
Redshank chicks leave the nest only a few hours after hatching.

teile.einleitung: The Saanen goat is a Swiss goat breed with mostly pure white fur. It comes from the Saanenland in the Bernese Oberland and is today the best-known dairy goat in the world. Hardly any other goat gives so much milk.
wichtigste: The Saanen goat comes from the Saanenland around Saanen and Gstaad in the canton of Bern.
Its coat is short and mostly entirely white.
It is a pure dairy goat and gives a great deal of milk.
Saanen goats are mostly hornless, have upright ears and are large and strong.
The breed has been exported to many countries of the world.
Cheese, yoghurt and drinking milk are made from its milk.

abschnitte.text: The Saanen goat is one of the largest goat breeds. A buck can weigh over 80 kilograms, and a doe about 50 to 70 kilograms. Typical are the short, **white coat**, the ears that stand forward or sideways and a calm, friendly nature. Many animals have no horns, and some carry two small growths of skin on the neck, which are called **wattles**.

The breed arose in the **Saanenland**, a mountain region in the Bernese Oberland on the border with Vaud. There farming families had kept goats for centuries that coped well on steep pastures. Through selective breeding, white animals with especially much milk were chosen. In the 19th century the Saanen goat became known as a breed of its own.

A good Saanen goat gives, in one lactation, that is, the time in which she gives milk, often 800 litres or more. That is several litres a day on good days. The milk is somewhat lower in fat than that of some other goat breeds, but plentiful. It is processed into **goat cheese**, yoghurt or fresh cheese.

From about 1890, Saanen goats were sold to many countries, for example to Germany, France, the USA and Australia. From them came further breeds such as the **White German Improved goat**. Today the Saanen goat is the most widespread dairy goat breed in the world. In hot countries, however, it suffers more easily from sunburn because of its pale skin.

In Switzerland the Saanen goat counts among the most common goat breeds. You see it on farms, in petting zoos and on Alpine pastures. Breeders are organised in the **Swiss Goat Breeding Association** and present their animals at shows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species with the same inherited features.
A goat that is kept mainly for its milk.
The time in which an animal gives milk after giving birth.
The Swiss word for a female goat.

gewusst: The Saanen goat is found on all continents except Antarctica.
The two flaps of skin on the neck of many goats have no known function.

teile.einleitung: Horseshoe crabs look like armoured helmets with a long spike as a tail. Despite their name they are not crabs at all, but are more closely related to spiders and scorpions. They have existed for hundreds of millions of years, and today their blue blood even helps medicine.
wichtigste: Horseshoe crabs belong to the chelicerates (Chelicerata), not to the crabs.
They form the order Xiphosura, and only four species are alive today.
Limulus polyphemus lives on the Atlantic coast of North America.
Their blood is blue because it contains copper-bearing haemocyanin.
The LAL test is made from the blood and detects endotoxins from bacteria.
The US authority FDA approved the LAL test in 1977.
The genetically engineered recombinant Factor C can replace the test.

abschnitte.text: A horseshoe crab has a horseshoe-shaped, hard **shell**, with its legs hidden underneath. At the back it has a long, pointed tail spine, which it uses to turn itself over when it is lying on its back. Females grow to about 60 centimetres including the spine and are larger than the males. On the shell sit two large **compound eyes** and several small eyes.

Although they are called crabs, horseshoe crabs belong to the **chelicerates** (Chelicerata) and are therefore related to spiders, scorpions and mites. They form the order Xiphosura. Their ancestors lived over 400 million years ago, which is why they are often called **living fossils**. Today only four species remain, one in North America and three in Asia.

The best-known species, **Limulus polyphemus**, lives on the Atlantic coast of North America and in the Gulf of Mexico. The three other species live on coasts of South and East Asia. Horseshoe crabs root around on the sea floor for worms, mussels and other small animals. In spring, at high tide, they come in their thousands to sandy beaches to lay their eggs, and Delaware Bay in the USA is especially well known.

The blood of horseshoe crabs is blue because it contains the copper-bearing pigment **haemocyanin**, whereas our blood is red because of iron-bearing haemoglobin. In the 1950s the researcher Frederik Bang discovered at Woods Hole that their blood clots when bacteria are present. From this came the **LAL test**, the abbreviation standing for Limulus amoebocyte lysate. The test detects endotoxins of gram-negative bacteria, that is, poisonous substances that can cause fever.

The LAL test is used to check whether vaccines, syringes and medicines are free of dangerous bacterial toxins. The US medicines authority FDA approved it in 1977, and it largely replaced the pyrogen test on **rabbits**. For the test, blood is taken from captured animals, and afterwards they are returned to the sea, but some of them do not survive. At the National University of Singapore, the researcher Jeak Ling Ding developed **recombinant Factor C**, a genetically engineered alternative that uses no animal blood.

Horseshoe crabs have come under pressure from blood collection, fishing for use as bait and the loss of beaches. Their eggs are important food for migratory birds such as the **red knot**, which stops off at Delaware Bay on its long flight to the Arctic. If the crabs decline, the birds therefore suffer too. Today there are catch rules and protected areas, and more and more companies are relying on the artificial substitute test.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals including spiders, scorpions and mites, whose first mouthparts are small claws.
A blue, copper-bearing blood pigment that carries oxygen.
A poisonous substance from the wall of certain bacteria that can cause fever.
A living thing that has hardly changed for a very long time.

gewusst: Horseshoe crabs existed long before the dinosaurs.
A litre of horseshoe crab blood is very valuable and can cost thousands of dollars.
Almost everyone who has had a vaccination was probably protected by a test using horseshoe crab blood.

teile.einleitung: An ecosystem is a habitat together with all the plants, animals and other living things that live in it. All parts depend closely on one another, like the cogwheels of a watch. A rainforest, a lake or an Alpine pasture are examples of ecosystems.
wichtigste: An ecosystem consists of a habitat and all the living things in it.
The whole of the plants and animals of a rainforest in which gibbons live is an ecosystem.
In every ecosystem there are producers, consumers and decomposers.
Living things are linked by food chains and food webs.
Predators such as the jaguar keep the numbers of their prey in balance.
The term was introduced in 1935 by the British researcher Arthur Tansley.
Healthy ecosystems provide people with clean water, air and food.

abschnitte.text: An ecosystem is made up of two parts: the **biotope** and the **biocoenosis**. The biotope is the lifeless habitat with soil, water, light and climate. The biocoenosis is the community of all plants, animals, fungi and bacteria there. The two constantly influence each other.

Plants are the **producers**, because they make food with sunlight. Animals are consumers, eating plants or other animals. Fungi, bacteria and worms are decomposers, which turn dead matter back into nutrients. In this way the substances stay in a constant cycle.

At the top of many food webs stand large predators such as the **jaguar** in the rainforest. They hunt plant eaters and so prevent them from becoming too numerous. Without hunters some animals would eat the plants bare. When wolves were reintroduced in 1995 in Yellowstone National Park in the USA, many plants recovered there.

The tropical rainforest is the ecosystem with the most species on land, and there live, for example, gibbons, jaguars and countless insects. Lakes, seas, deserts, bogs and meadows are also ecosystems. Even a small **garden pond** or a dead tree trunk can be regarded as an ecosystem. Large and small ecosystems are often linked to each other.

Thanks to mountains, lakes and valleys Switzerland has very varied ecosystems. They include mountain forests, Alpine pastures, glacier forelands, bogs and river floodplains. The **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps. There nature may develop without human intervention.

Clearing, pollution, introduced species and **climate change** can throw ecosystems out of balance. If an important species disappears, this can affect many other species. Healthy ecosystems clean water and air, protect against floods and supply food. That is why protecting them is vital for people too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lifeless habitat with soil, water, light and climate.
The community of all living things in a habitat.
Many linked food chains that show who eats whom.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals.

gewusst: In a handful of forest soil live more living things than there are people on Earth.
Tropical rainforests cover only a small part of the Earth, but are home to about half of all animal and plant species on land.
Beavers change whole ecosystems, because their dams create new ponds and wetlands.

teile.einleitung: Osmoregulation means that a living thing regulates the water and salt balance in its body. This is especially fascinating in fish, because fresh water and salt water make quite different demands. Our kidneys, too, carry out osmoregulation every day.
wichtigste: Osmoregulation is the regulation of the water and salt balance in the body.
Its basis is osmosis, in which water moves through thin membranes.
Freshwater fish constantly take in water and excrete a lot of dilute urine.
Marine fish lose water, so they drink sea water and give off salt through the gills.
Salmon and eels move between fresh water and salt water and have to adjust.
In humans it is mainly the kidneys that carry out osmoregulation.

abschnitte.text: **Osmosis** is the name for the movement of water through a thin membrane that lets water through but hardly any dissolved salts. The water always flows to where more salt is dissolved. Such a membrane is called **semipermeable**. You can observe this yourself: if you put a slice of cucumber in salt water, it goes limp because water is drawn out of it.

In the body of a freshwater fish more salt is dissolved than in the water of a lake or river. That is why water constantly seeps in through the gills and the skin. So the fish hardly drink and excrete a lot of very dilute **urine** through the kidneys. They take up important salts actively through the gills and with their food, as, for example, trout and perch do in Swiss waters.

Sea water contains about 3.5 per cent salt, more than the blood of a marine fish. That is why the fish loses water through the gills, much like the slice of cucumber. It therefore drinks sea water constantly and gives off the excess salt again through special **salt cells** in the gills. Its urine is therefore only very scanty.

Salmon hatch in fresh water, grow up in the sea and return to their rivers to spawn. Eels do the opposite and migrate to the sea to spawn. Such fish have to switch their osmoregulation completely when they change, and they are called **migratory fish**. Sharks solve the problem in another way: they store a lot of urea in the blood and so match their salt content to the sea.

Humans, too, have to keep their water and salt balance in equilibrium. This task is carried out mainly by the **kidneys**, controlled by hormones. Anyone who drinks little makes little, dark urine, and anyone who drinks a lot makes a lot of pale urine. That is why a person cannot drink sea water, because the kidneys would have to give off more water than had been taken in.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of water through a thin membrane towards the saltier side.
A membrane that lets only certain substances, such as water, through.
The breathing organs of fish, through which water and salts are also exchanged.
A mixture of fresh water and salt water, for example in river mouths.

gewusst: A freshwater fish would dry out in the sea, even though it is surrounded by water.
Shipwrecked people are told not to drink sea water, because the body then loses even more water.
Osmosis was already observed in the 18th century with a pig’s bladder.

teile.einleitung: Salonga National Park is a huge protected area in the tropical rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is the largest rainforest national park in Africa. The rare bonobos live here, the closest relatives of humans besides the chimpanzee.
wichtigste: Salonga National Park lies in the centre of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It was founded in 1970 and is about 36,000 square kilometres in size.
That makes it almost as big as the whole of Switzerland.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.
Bonobos, forest elephants, Congo peafowl and many other rare animals live in the park.
The park can only be reached by boat or small aircraft.

abschnitte.text: The park lies in the **Congo Basin**, in the middle of the second largest rainforest on Earth. It consists of two large parts, a northern and a southern block. Between them lies an area where people live. There are no roads, and people travel on rivers such as the Salonga or the Lomela.

The park is almost completely covered by dense **rainforest**. Many parts are flooded regularly, and there are swamp forests and broad rivers. It is warm and damp all year round. Because the forest is so remote, it has still been little explored.

The park is one of the most important protected areas for the **bonobo**, a species of great ape that occurs only south of the Congo River. Bonobos live in groups and are known for often settling quarrels peacefully. **Forest elephants**, the rare Congo peafowl, leopards, dwarf crocodiles and many species of monkey also live here. Numerous species of birds and fish occur as well.

For a long time the park suffered from **poaching**, above all of elephants and for bushmeat. That is why it was on the List of World Heritage in Danger from 1999 to 2021. Thanks to more rangers and cooperation with the local people, the situation has improved. Organisations such as the WWF support its protection.

Large rainforests such as Salonga store a great deal of **carbon** and are therefore important for the climate. They are home to thousands of species of plants and animals. People in the surrounding area also live from fishing, hunting and small fields. The protection of the park is meant to help nature and people alike.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large area in which nature is especially protected.
Places that UNESCO honours as especially valuable for the whole of humanity.
The illegal hunting of animals.
A great ape from the Congo, closely related to the chimpanzee.

gewusst: In the wild, bonobos exist only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The Congo peafowl was not scientifically described until 1936, after at first only a single feather had been found.

teile.einleitung: The burbot, in German called Quappe, Aalquappe or in Switzerland Trüsche, is a freshwater fish with a long body and a barbel on its chin. Despite the German name Aalquappe, it is not related to the eel, but belongs to the cod-like fishes. It is the only relative of the cod that lives in fresh water.
wichtigste: The burbot is a fish of its own and is not related to the eel.
In Switzerland it is mostly called Trüsche.
It belongs to the cod-like fishes and is related to the cod.
Its scientific name is Lota lota.
It has a single barbel on its chin.
It loves cold, oxygen-rich water and spawns in the middle of winter.
The burbot is active mainly at night.

abschnitte.text: The burbot has a long, rounded body that is flattened from the side towards the back. Its skin is slimy, with very small scales, and mottled brown, yellowish and olive green. Typical is a single **barbel** in the middle of the lower jaw. It usually grows 30 to 60 centimetres long, and large animals can reach over a metre.

abschnitte.titel: Not an eel, but a cod fish
abschnitte.text: Because of its long body, the burbot reminds people of an eel, hence the German name Aalquappe, meaning eel burbot. In reality it belongs to the **cod-like fishes**, like cod and haddock. It is the only member of this large group of fishes that lives permanently in fresh water. Its scientific name is **Lota lota**.

The burbot lives in cool rivers and lakes in Europe, Asia and North America. It needs cold, oxygen-rich water and likes to stay in the depths, under stones or among roots. In Switzerland it occurs, for example, in **Lake Constance**, Lake Geneva and other large lakes of the Central Plateau. By day it hides, and at night it goes hunting.

Young burbot eat small crustaceans, insect larvae and worms. Adult animals are **predatory fish** and hunt mainly other fish, such as bullheads, perch and whitefish. They also eat fish eggs. They use their barbel and their good sense of smell to track down prey in the dark.

The burbot is one of the few native fish species that spawn in the middle of winter, mostly between December and March. Then many animals gather at their spawning grounds at water temperatures of only a few degrees. A female lays hundreds of thousands of tiny eggs. Because rivers have been straightened and built over by power stations, their **spawning grounds** have become rare in many places.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thread-like growth at a fish's mouth with which it can feel and taste.
A group of fishes that includes cod, haddock and the burbot.
When fish release their eggs into the water.
A fish that feeds mainly on other fish.

gewusst: The burbot's liver is very large in proportion to its body and was once regarded as a special delicacy.
The burbot is most active when the water is cold, and in warm summers it often hardly eats.

teile.einleitung: Renaturation, in German Renaturierung, means making a landscape that has been changed by humans closer to nature again. Very often it concerns streams and rivers that were once straightened and forced into concrete channels. When a stream is renaturated, many animals such as the lake trout return.
wichtigste: Renaturation makes changed habitats closer to nature again.
Many streams and rivers were once straightened and built over.
Near-natural streams offer the lake trout gravel for spawning and hiding places.
Moors, floodplains and lake shores can also be renaturated.
Fish ladders help fish to get past obstacles such as weirs.
Switzerland wants to restore about 4,000 kilometres of waters in the coming decades.
Renaturated rivers often also protect better against flooding.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from “nature” and means something like “back to nature”. Over time, people have straightened rivers, drained marshes and reinforced banks with concrete. In a **renaturation**, such interventions are partly undone. For waters, people in Switzerland often also speak of **revitalisation**. The aim is that plants and animals find a good habitat again.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, many rivers were put into straight channels. People wanted to gain land for fields, settlements and roads and to let the water run off faster. A well-known example is the correction of the Rhone in Valais or the Linth correction. As a result, however, gravel banks, oxbows and shallow bank zones disappeared. For many fish, birds and insects, the **habitat** was lost in this way.

The **lake trout** lives in large lakes, but swims up into rivers and streams to spawn. There the female lays her eggs in clean, loose **gravel**. In a concrete channel she finds no such gravel and no hiding places. A near-natural stream with stones, roots and deep spots offers the young fish protection from enemies. That is why a renaturation directly helps the lake trout to survive.

Diggers remove concrete walls and give the stream more room. The course is allowed to form bends again, and shallow and deep spots appear. High sills and weirs are rebuilt or supplemented with a **fish ladder**. On the bank, willows, alders and other native plants are planted. After that, nature is given time to go on shaping the stream itself.

Since 2011, the Swiss Water Protection Act has required that built-over waters be restored. The plan is to revitalise about 4,000 kilometres of rivers and streams by about 2090. There are well-known projects, for example, on the Thur, the Aare and the Rhone. Moors are also being re-wetted so that rare plants and animals return. In this way species such as the **kingfisher** or the beaver come back to some places.

A wide, near-natural river can take up more water in heavy rain. This lowers the risk of floods in villages further downstream. Renaturated banks are also lovely places for walking, playing and watching. Clean gravel banks even clean the water a little. A renaturation costs a lot of money, but brings great benefit in the long term.

begriffe.erklaerung: A changed habitat is made closer to nature again.
Another word for the restoration of a built-over water.
A kind of staircase of pools by which fish can get past a weir.
Laying fish eggs in the water.

gewusst: Beavers themselves help with renaturation, because with their dams they dam up streams and create new habitats.
Just a few years after a renaturation, a stream often has clearly more animal species than before.
In Switzerland, many kilometres of rivers and streams count as heavily built over or culverted, that is, laid underground.

teile.einleitung: The moon jellyfish is one of the best-known jellyfish in Europe. You recognise it by the four ring-shaped structures in its transparent bell, which look like little ears. For people it is usually harmless.
wichtigste: The moon jellyfish is common in European seas and usually harmless to people.
It gets its German name, Ohrenqualle (‘ear jellyfish’), from four ear-shaped rings in the bell.
Its body consists of about 98 per cent water.
It has no brain, no heart and no bones.
Moon jellyfish eat tiny plankton.
In the course of its life it alternates between polyp and jellyfish.

abschnitte.text: The moon jellyfish has a flat, transparent **bell**, which usually grows 10 to 25 centimetres, sometimes up to 40 centimetres across. In the middle four ring-shaped organs shimmer, which are whitish, pink or violet depending on the animal. These are the **reproductive organs**, which look like ears. Along the edge hang many short, fine tentacles.

Moon jellyfish live in almost all the seas of the world, in Europe for example in the North Sea, the Baltic and the Mediterranean. They mostly drift in the water near the coast. In summer they sometimes appear in huge swarms. They can hardly swim against strong currents, because they belong to the **plankton**.

The moon jellyfish eats small crustaceans, fish larvae and other plankton. With its **stinging cells** it paralyses the tiny prey. Mucus on the bell carries the food to the oral arms. Its sting is so weak that it hardly penetrates human skin.

From the eggs hatch tiny larvae that settle on the sea floor. There they grow into small **polyps**, which look like mini flowers. In winter the polyps bud off little discs, which swim away as young jellyfish. These then grow by summer into large moon jellyfish.

Moon jellyfish are eaten by leatherback turtles, ocean sunfish and some seabirds. When there are very many jellyfish, they can clog fishing nets. Mass multiplication is often linked with warm water and **overfishing**. In many zoos and aquariums you can watch moon jellyfish in round tanks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bell-shaped body of a jellyfish.
A cell that fires a tiny venomous dart on touch.
A sessile life form of cnidarians that looks like a small flower.
Tiny living things that drift in the water.

gewusst: A moon jellyfish has no brain, yet it can tell light from dark with sensory bodies at the edge of the bell.
Moon jellyfish washed up on the beach dry out until almost nothing is left of them.
In 1991 moon jellyfish flew into space on a space shuttle so that researchers could study their development in weightlessness.

teile.einleitung: Pill woodlice, in German Rollasseln, are small grey animals that roll up in a flash into a hard ball when in danger. Although they live on land, they belong to the crustaceans and so are related to crabs and lobsters. You find them almost everywhere that it is damp and dark.
wichtigste: Pill woodlice are land isopods and belong to the crustaceans.
When in danger they roll up into a ball.
They have seven pairs of legs, so 14 legs.
Pill woodlice eat mainly dead parts of plants.
They need moisture, because otherwise they dry out.
They are often mistaken for the pill millipede, which also rolls up.
The females carry their eggs in a brood pouch on the underside.

abschnitte.text: The best-known species is the **common pill woodlouse**, which grows up to about 18 millimetres long. Its body is domed and covered with hard, overlapping plates that look like a knight's armour. Most animals are slate grey, and some have pale spots. On the head there are two antennae with which the woodlouse feels and smells.

When a pill woodlouse is touched, it rolls up into an almost perfect **ball**. Head, legs and belly are then safely hidden under the shell. In this way it protects itself from enemies such as spiders, shrews, toads and birds. The ball also helps against drying out, because less of the body surface is exposed to the air.

The **pill millipede** looks very similar to the pill woodlouse and also rolls up. But it is not a crustacean, but a millipede. You can recognise it by its much more numerous legs and by its glossy, often darker shell. Pill woodlice, by contrast, have only 14 legs and two small outgrowths at the back.

Pill woodlice live under stones, wood, leaves and in compost heaps. They eat wilted leaves, rotten wood and other plant remains. In doing so they break up the material, and bacteria and fungi can then more easily turn it into **humus**. For their shell they need lime, which is why they are especially common on limy soils.

The female carries her eggs in a **brood pouch**, a fluid-filled pocket on the underside. There the young also hatch and stay protected for a while. The small woodlice already look like their parents, but are pale and soft. As they grow they moult several times, first the rear and then the front half of the body.

In Switzerland, pill woodlice occur in almost every garden. If you lift a flower pot or a board in spring, you often find several at once. They are harmless and do hardly any damage. On the contrary: as small waste recyclers, they are very useful for healthy soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with a shell that includes crabs, lobsters and also woodlice.
A millipede that can roll up like a pill woodlouse.
A pocket on the female's underside in which eggs and young are protected.
Fertile dark soil that is formed from decomposed plant remains.

gewusst: Pill woodlice breathe with small organs on the rear legs, which in some species look like white spots.
Pill woodlice moult in two halves, which is why you sometimes see animals that are pale at the back and dark at the front.
Some people keep pill woodlice in terrariums, where they eat up leftovers as a small cleaning crew.

teile.einleitung: The orca, also called the killer whale, is a black and white marine mammal found in all the oceans of the world. Although it is called a killer whale, it is really the largest dolphin. As an apex predator it has no natural enemies in the sea.
wichtigste: The orca belongs to the dolphin family and is its largest member.
Typical is its black and white colouring with a light grey saddle patch behind the dorsal fin.
The dorsal fin of the males is very tall and can measure up to 1.8 metres.
Orcas live in fixed family groups led by the oldest females.
Females often live for over 50 years, sometimes even 80 to 90 years.
In murky water orcas find their way by echolocation using clicking sounds.
Orcas sleep with only one half of the brain so that they can keep breathing.

abschnitte.text: Orcas have a black back, a white belly and a white patch above each eye. Behind the dorsal fin lies a light grey **saddle patch**, by whose shape researchers can recognise individual animals. Males are usually 6 to 8 metres long and weigh several tonnes, while females stay clearly smaller. The **dorsal fin** of the males is tall and triangular and can measure up to 1.8 metres, while in females it is smaller and slightly curved.

Orcas live in all the world’s oceans, from the icy polar seas to warm waters. They are most common in cold seas rich in food, for example off Norway, Alaska, Canada or in the Antarctic. Some groups are **resident orcas**, which always stay in the same area. Other groups wander far and roam huge areas of sea.

The orca is an **apex predator** and stands at the very top of the food chain. Resident orcas eat mainly fish, for example salmon or herring. Other groups hunt seals, sea lions, penguins or even large whales. Orcas hunt as a team and have clever methods, for instance creating a wave that washes a seal off an ice floe.

Orcas live in family groups called **pods**, which are led by an old mother or grandmother. Each group has its own calls, a kind of **dialect**, which the young learn from the adults. A female is pregnant for about 15 to 18 months and then has a single calf. When an orca leaps completely out of the water and splashes down again, this is called **breaching**.

Orcas breathe air and so have to come to the surface. That is why they sleep with only one half of the brain, while the other stays awake and controls breathing. To find their way they give out **clicking sounds** and listen for the echo that comes back from fish or rocks. This **echolocation** also works in murky or dark water.

As apex predators, orcas keep the ecosystem in the sea in balance. Dangerous for them are environmental toxins that build up in their bodies and the noise of ships, which disturbs their echolocation. Some groups also find too little food, because there are fewer salmon. Of course no orcas live in Switzerland, but Swiss organisations work for **marine conservation**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A light grey patch behind the dorsal fin of an orca.
Finding one’s way with sounds whose echo shows the animal what is around it.
A leap in which a whale shoots wholly or almost wholly out of the water.
A predator at the very top of the food chain that has hardly any enemies itself.
The word for a family group of whales or dolphins.

gewusst: Female orcas are among the few animals that live on for many years after their own babies and help their family as experienced leaders.
Every orca family has its own language of calls, much as people in different regions speak different dialects.
A newborn orca is already about 2 metres long.

teile.einleitung: A nest box is an artificial nesting hole for birds, usually a small wooden house. Many birds such as the great tit breed in tree holes, which hardly exist any more in gardens and towns. With a nest box you can help them very easily.
wichtigste: A nest box for great tits is a small wooden house for breeding.
The entrance hole for great tits should be about 3 centimetres across.
The size of the hole determines which bird species moves in.
It is best to hang nest boxes at a height of 2 to 3 metres.
The entrance hole should not face west, because rain often comes from there.
You should clean nest boxes every year in autumn.
There are also boxes for swifts, owls and bats.

abschnitte.text: A nest box replaces a natural **nesting hole**, such as woodpeckers hack into old trees. It usually consists of untreated wood or wood concrete. At the front it has a round entrance hole, and at the top a roof that protects against rain. Inside, the bird builds its nest from moss, stalks and feathers.

How big the **entrance hole** is decides who moves in. For blue tits about 2.7 centimetres is enough, and for great tits about 3 centimetres is needed. Bigger holes suit starlings. A hole that is too big is dangerous, because then enemies such as magpies can reach in.

Besides hole boxes there are **open-fronted boxes** with a broad opening at the front. They are gladly used by black redstarts, robins or pied wagtails. For swifts you hang flat boxes directly under the roof of a house. Bats and owls such as the barn owl also have their own box shapes.

A nest box is best hung at a height of 2 to 3 metres on a tree or a house wall. The hole ideally faces east or south-east, away from the weather. Cats and martens should not be able to reach the box. In autumn you remove the old nest, because **parasites** such as fleas and mites often overwinter in it.

abschnitte.titel: The great tit as a tenant
abschnitte.text: The great tit is one of the most frequent occupants of nest boxes in Switzerland. In spring it usually lays 6 to 12 eggs and incubates them for about two weeks. The parents feed their young with thousands of caterpillars and insects. This makes tits important **beneficial animals** in the garden.

In Switzerland the **Swiss Ornithological Institute** at Sempach and BirdLife Switzerland publish building instructions and tips. Many school classes build their own nest boxes in craft lessons. In municipalities and forests, nature conservation societies often hang up hundreds of boxes. In this way they help birds that find hardly any nesting sites because of a lack of old trees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sheltered cavity in which a bird builds its nest and breeds.
The round opening through which the bird slips into the nest box.
A nest box with a large, half-open front.
A bird that breeds in holes instead of open nests.

gewusst: In winter nest boxes are often used by birds as a warm sleeping place.
A pair of tits brings food to its young several hundred times in one day.
A nest box needs no perch in front of the hole, because it mainly helps enemies to break in.

teile.einleitung: Even-toed ungulates are a large group of mammals whose feet end in an even number of toes, usually two or four. They include cows, sheep, goats, pigs, deer and also the African Cape buffalo. Their cloven hooves are called claws.
wichtigste: Even-toed ungulates are an order of mammals.
Their weight rests mainly on two toes, the third and the fourth.
The cloven hooves are called claws.
Even-toed ungulates include cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, deer, camels and giraffes.
The Cape buffalo, too, is an even-toed ungulate with cloven hooves.
Many even-toed ungulates are ruminants with a stomach of several chambers.
According to recent research, whales are close relatives of hippopotamuses.

abschnitte.text: Even-toed ungulates form an **order** of mammals with over 200 species worldwide. Their foot ends in an even number of toes, and the body weight is carried mainly by the third and fourth toes. These are covered with horn and form the **claws**, that is, a cloven hoof. In many species there are two smaller toes further back, the dewclaws.

Even-toed ungulates include important farm animals such as **cattle**, sheep, goats and pigs. Wild animals such as red deer, roe deer, wild boar, chamois and ibex also belong to them. In Africa the giraffe, hippopotamus, antelopes and Cape buffalo belong to this group. Camels are also even-toed ungulates, but have a soft sole pad under their two toes.

Many even-toed ungulates are **ruminants**, for example cows, sheep and deer. Their stomach consists of four chambers: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. They first swallow the grass hardly chewed, bring it up again later and chew it once more in peace. In this way they can digest tough plants well.

Many even-toed ungulates carry head ornaments that serve them in fighting and for defence. **Horns** as in cow, goat or ibex grow for a lifetime and are not shed. An **antler** made of bone as in the stag or roe deer, by contrast, falls off every year and grows anew. The giraffe has small bony knobs covered with skin on its head.

Horses, donkeys, rhinoceroses and tapirs do not belong to the even-toed ungulates. In them it is mainly the middle toe that carries the weight, so they are called **odd-toed ungulates**. A horse therefore stands, so to speak, on a single large toenail. Researchers have also discovered that whales descend from even-toed land animals and are closely related to hippopotamuses.

In Switzerland live wild even-toed ungulates such as roe deer, red deer, wild boar, **chamois** and ibex. The ibex was exterminated in Switzerland in the 19th century and was reintroduced from 1911. Today there are again many thousands of ibex in the Alps. On Swiss farms cows, sheep, goats and pigs are the most important even-toed ungulates.

begriffe.erklaerung: The cloven hooves of even-toed ungulates.
A plant eater that brings its food up and chews it a second time.
A hoofed animal such as the horse or rhinoceros in which the middle toe carries the weight.
The bony head ornament of deer, which falls off every year and grows back.

gewusst: The hippopotamus is more closely related to whales than to the horse.
A cow spends many hours every day chewing the cud.
The pig is an even-toed ungulate, but not a ruminant.

teile.einleitung: The puma is a large, slender big cat from the Americas, and its scientific name is Puma concolor. It is also called the mountain lion or silver lion, although it cannot roar like a lion. It lives as a loner and is a skilful hunter with a long, strong tail.
wichtigste: The puma is called Puma concolor in science.
It lives in North, Central and South America, from Canada to Patagonia.
The puma is a pure meat eater, and a typical prey in North America is deer.
It usually lives alone as a loner and not in a pride.
Pumas cannot roar, but they hiss, spit and purr.
The pregnancy lasts about three months.
Dangers for pumas are loss of habitat and hunting by humans.

abschnitte.text: The puma has a single-coloured coat, yellowish-brown to grey, which is where the name concolor comes from, meaning one colour. Males usually weigh about 50 to 70 kilograms, and females are smaller. Striking is the **long, strong tail**, which helps to keep its balance when jumping and climbing. With its sharp, retractable claws it can climb well and hold on to prey.

No other wild land mammal in the Americas is as widespread as the puma. It lives from the Yukon in Canada to **Patagonia** in the south of South America. It is found in mountains, forests, deserts and swamps. In Florida lives a small, endangered subspecies, the **Florida panther**.

The puma is a pure **carnivore**. In North America it hunts mainly deer, but it also eats wild sheep, hares, raccoons and other animals. It sneaks up silently and overpowers its prey with a powerful leap. What it does not eat at once it covers with leaves and earth and returns to later.

Pumas are **loners** and normally do not live in prides. Each animal has a large territory, which it marks with scratch marks on trees and scent marks. Males and females meet briefly only to mate. Unlike lions, pumas cannot roar, but they hiss, spit, whistle and purr.

After a pregnancy of about three months, the female usually gives birth to two to four young. The birth mostly takes place in a sheltered den or rock crevice. The young at first have a **spotted coat** and blue eyes, and the spots disappear in the first year of life. They stay with their mother for about one and a half to two years and learn hunting from her.

Overall the puma is not threatened with extinction, but in many areas it has become rare. Loss of habitat, road traffic and hunting by humans cause it problems. In the east of North America it was almost completely wiped out except for the Florida panther. Attacks on humans are very rare, because pumas usually keep out of the way of people.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that lives mainly alone.
An area that an animal regards as its own and defends against others of its species.
The time in which a young animal grows up in its mother's belly.
A group within a species that lives in a particular area and looks slightly different.

gewusst: The puma holds a world record: no other mammal has so many different names in English.
Although it is so large, the puma counts among the small cats and is more closely related to the house cat than to the lion.
A puma can jump several metres high from a standing start.

teile.einleitung: A savanna is a wide grassland in warm regions in which single trees and shrubs grow. There is a rainy season and a long dry season. In the savannas of Africa live large herds of zebras, wildebeest and elephants, but also lions and spotted hyenas.
wichtigste: Savannas are areas with grass and single trees in the tropics and subtropics.
Typical is the alternation of rainy season and dry season.
The largest savannas lie in Africa, such as the Serengeti.
There are also savannas in South America, India and Australia.
Well-known trees are the umbrella thorn acacia and the baobab.
In savannas live spotted hyenas, lions, giraffes and huge herds of plant eaters.

abschnitte.text: A savanna is a **grassland** with scattered trees and bushes. It lies between the rainforests and the deserts. It rains only for part of the year, and that is not enough for a dense forest. The more rain falls, the more trees grow.

In the **rainy season** the savanna turns green, and the grass grows tall quickly. In the dry season it turns yellow and parched, and many trees drop their leaves. Often there are then bush fires. The fires burn the old grass, and many plants quickly sprout again afterwards.

The largest savannas lie in Africa, for example the **Serengeti** in Tanzania and the Masai Mara in Kenya. In South America there are the Llanos in Venezuela and the Cerrado in Brazil. Northern Australia and parts of India also have savannas. In all, they cover about a fifth of the land surface of the Earth.

Huge herds of wildebeest, zebras and antelopes roam the Serengeti every year in search of fresh grass. This **animal migration** is one of the largest in the world. It is followed by predators such as lions, cheetahs and **spotted hyenas**. Giraffes eat the leaves of tall acacias, and elephants knock over trees and so keep the landscape open.

Typical are the flat **umbrella thorn acacias** with thorns and the thick baobab tree. The baobab stores a lot of water in its trunk for the dry season. Grasses have deep roots and survive fire and drought. Many plants have thorns that protect them from animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the year in which it hardly rains or does not rain at all.
An African tree with a thick trunk that stores water.
The warm regions around the equator.
A fire that spreads through dry grass and shrubs.

gewusst: Termite mounds in the savanna can grow several metres high.
In the Serengeti, over a million wildebeest travel in a great circle every year.

teile.einleitung: Sooty mould is a black, soot-like coating on leaves that is formed by fungi. These sooty mould fungi grow on the sticky honeydew that aphids and other sap-sucking insects excrete. Where you see sooty mould, then, many small insects are usually not far away.
wichtigste: Sooty mould is a black fungal coating on leaves.
Sooty mould fungi grow on the honeydew of aphids.
Scale insects and whiteflies also excrete honeydew.
The fungi do not penetrate the plant, but only sit on top.
The coating takes light away from the leaves.
Anyone who wants to fight sooty mould must above all fight the insects.

abschnitte.text: **Sooty mould** looks as if someone had sprinkled soot or ash over the leaves. In reality it is a thin network of dark **fungi**. These fungi belong to various species that are together called sooty mould fungi. You find the coating on leaves, twigs and sometimes also on fruits.

Aphids, scale insects and **whiteflies** pierce plants and suck their sugary sap. Because they take up much more sugar than they need, they excrete the rest as sticky **honeydew**. This drips onto leaves below and forms a sweet layer there. On this layer the sooty mould fungi grow, because they feed on the sugar.

Ants love honeydew and collect it directly from the aphids. In return they protect the aphids from enemies such as ladybirds. The more ants there are on a plant, the more aphids there often are. And the more aphids there are, the more honeydew and sooty mould is produced.

Sooty mould fungi are not **parasites**, because they do not penetrate the plant. Even so they harm it, because the black layer keeps out the sunlight. Without enough light, the plant can carry out less **photosynthesis** and grows worse. The greatest damage, however, is usually done by the sucking insects themselves.
