On houseplants, sooty mould can be wiped off with a damp cloth or lukewarm water. To stop it coming back, you have to fight the **aphids**, for example by spraying them off with water. In the garden, natural enemies such as ladybirds, lacewings and birds help. That is why it is worth encouraging such beneficial insects in the garden.

In summer, sticky honeydew drips from many **lime trees** and maples onto cars and garden furniture. After some time it often turns dark there, because sooty mould fungi settle on it. In Switzerland this is especially familiar from cities with avenue trees. Bees, by the way, also collect the honeydew and make forest honey from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sweet, sticky excretion of aphids and other sap-sucking insects.
A living thing that is neither plant nor animal and feeds on nutrients from its surroundings.
The process by which plants make sugar using sunlight.
An animal that eats pests and so helps the gardener.

gewusst: Without aphids there would be no dark forest honey, because it is made from honeydew.
Sooty mould can often simply be rubbed off with a finger, because it sits only loosely on the leaf.

teile.einleitung: The Rhine is one of the largest and most important rivers in Europe. It rises in the Swiss Alps and flows through Germany and the Netherlands into the North Sea. For fish such as eel and salmon it is an important migration route between the sea and Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Rhine is about 1,233 kilometres long.
It rises in Graubünden and flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands.
The Rhine links Switzerland with the North Sea, and eels can migrate up and down it.
It flows through Lake Constance and forms the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen.
Large ships travel on the Rhine as far as Basel.
In the past the Rhine was heavily polluted, and today the water is much cleaner again.
Salmon are meant to be able to return as far as Switzerland again.

abschnitte.text: The Rhine has two source rivers, the **Vorderrhein** and the **Hinterrhein**. The traditional source is Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass in Graubünden. At Reichenau both join together, and the river flows towards Lake Constance. After that it forms the border between Switzerland and Germany and flows to Basel. From there it goes through Germany and the Netherlands to the North Sea.

Near Schaffhausen the Rhine plunges about 23 metres down over the **Rhine Falls**. It is one of the waterfalls with the most water in Europe. Before that, the Rhine flows through Lake Constance, which borders on Switzerland, Germany and Austria. The lake acts like a huge basin in which mud and rubble settle. After that the water is clearer.

Many fish species live in the Rhine, such as barbel, grayling, trout and pike. The European **eel** migrates up the Rhine from the Atlantic as a young animal. Adult eels later swim back down in order to spawn in the sea. The **salmon** also used to live far into Switzerland, but disappeared in the 20th century. Power stations and weirs are great obstacles for migrating fish.

In the 20th century the Rhine was heavily polluted by sewage from cities and factories. In 1986, a warehouse of a chemical company burned down at Schweizerhalle near Basel. With the fire-fighting water, poisons got into the Rhine, and countless fish died. After that the countries on the Rhine worked together more closely and built more **sewage treatment plants**. Today the water is much cleaner, and in many places you can even swim in the Rhine.

The Rhine is one of the busiest **waterways** in the world. Large cargo ships bring goods from Rotterdam as far as the Rhine ports near Basel. In this way Switzerland gets a route to the sea. On the Rhine lie large cities such as Basel, Strasbourg, Cologne and Düsseldorf. In addition, power stations on the Rhine supply electricity.

The countries on the Rhine want to bring the **salmon** back. For this, fish ladders are being built at power stations and spawning grounds are being restored. Individual salmon have already got back as far as the area near Basel. So that they can swim further into Switzerland, a few more obstacles on the High Rhine still have to be made passable. The aim is that salmon spawn in Swiss rivers again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where a river rises.
The place where a river flows into a sea, a lake or another river.
A river or canal on which ships transport goods.
A plant that cleans dirty waste water.

gewusst: For a long time books said that the Rhine was 1,320 kilometres long, until around 2010 an old transposed-digits error was discovered.
An eel from the Rhine swims as far as the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic to spawn, thousands of kilometres away.
By the amount of water, the Rhine Falls is one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The orchid mantis is a tropical praying mantis that looks like a white or pink orchid flower. With this perfect camouflage it lures insects and catches them in a flash. It is regarded as one of the most beautiful insects in the world.
wichtigste: The orchid mantis is a praying mantis from the rainforests of South-East Asia.
Its body looks like an orchid flower.
Its legs carry broad lobes that look like petals.
It lies in wait motionless and catches insects with its grasping forelegs.
The females are much larger than the males.
Young orchid mantises are at first coloured red and black.

abschnitte.text: The orchid mantis has the scientific name **Hymenopus coronatus**. It is coloured white to delicate pink and can change its colour slightly depending on its surroundings. On its walking legs it has broad, flat **lobes** that look like petals. Females grow to about 6 to 7 centimetres long, males only about half as big or even smaller.

The orchid mantis lives in the humid, warm **rainforests** of South-East Asia. It can be found, for example, in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. There it sits on the leaves and flowers of plants. It does not occur wild in Switzerland, but it can sometimes be seen in zoos or insect exhibitions.

The orchid mantis is an **ambush hunter**. It hardly moves and waits until an insect comes close enough. Then its **grasping forelegs** with their small spines shoot forward and seize the prey. Researchers have found that bees and flies often even visit it more often than real flowers.

The female lays her eggs in a foamy package, the **ootheca**, which hangs on a twig. From it hatch tiny larvae called nymphs. The youngest nymphs are red and black and look like inedible bugs, which protects them from enemies. Only after several moults do they become white and pink like a flower.

The orchid mantis belongs to the **mantises**, to which over 2000 species worldwide belong. Its best-known relative in Europe is the European mantis. It also lives in warm parts of Switzerland, for example in the Valais and in Ticino. All mantises have a movable head and typical grasping forelegs.

begriffe.erklaerung: When an animal imitates something else in order to protect itself or deceive prey.
Front legs with spines with which praying mantises seize prey.
A foamy egg case in which praying mantises lay their eggs.
A young insect that already looks like the adult animal.

gewusst: The orchid mantis does not imitate a particular species of flower, but simply looks like an especially tempting blossom.
A male orchid mantis is often less than half as long as the female.
The lobes on the legs are so thin that in the light they look almost transparent.

teile.einleitung: The Saint Helena giant earwig, in German Riesenohrwurm, was the largest earwig in the world. It lived only on the small island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic and grew up to 8.4 centimetres long. Today it is regarded as extinct, because no living animal has been found since 1967.
wichtigste: The giant earwig lived only on the island of Saint Helena.
At up to 8.4 centimetres long, it was the largest earwig in the world.
Its scientific name is Labidura herculeana.
It was scientifically described in 1798.
The last living animal was found in 1967.
Since 2014 it has officially been regarded as extinct.
Introduced animals and the destruction of its habitat led to its disappearance.

abschnitte.text: The **Saint Helena giant earwig** was an insect from the group of the earwigs. It bears the scientific name Labidura herculeana, after the strong hero Hercules. It was described in 1798 by the Danish insect researcher Johann Christian Fabricius. It was glossy black and had reddish legs. Like all earwigs, it carried a large **pair of pincers** on its abdomen.

The giant earwig grew up to 84 millimetres long. Of this, about 50 millimetres were body and a good 30 millimetres were the pincers. By comparison, the common earwig in Swiss gardens is only about 1 to 1.5 centimetres long. The giant earwig had no wings and could not fly. It was probably active at night and lived in burrows in the earth.

**Saint Helena** is a small volcanic island in the middle of the South Atlantic, far away from any continent. It is well known because the French emperor Napoleon lived there in exile and died there in 1821. On remote islands, animal species often develop that exist nowhere else. Such species are called **endemic**. The giant earwig lived mainly in a dry area in the north-east of the island.

People brought mice, rats and predatory centipedes to the island, which hunted the earwigs. In addition, many large stones under which the animals lived were taken away as building material. As a result, their habitat disappeared. The last living animal was found in 1967, and later searches were unsuccessful. In 2014 the International Union for Conservation of Nature officially declared the species **extinct**.

The giant earwig shows how sensitive animals are on small islands. They often have no way of moving away when their habitat changes. Introduced species are one of the greatest dangers for island animals worldwide. Today only specimens in museums are a reminder of the giant earwig. On Saint Helena there are now protection programmes for other rare animals and plants of the island.

begriffe.erklaerung: An insect with a pair of pincers on its abdomen.
A species that occurs only in one particular place in the world.
A species of which not a single animal is still alive.
Brought by humans to a new area in which the species did not live before.

gewusst: Altogether only about 40 giant earwigs were ever collected, and they now lie in museums.
Earwigs do not crawl into people's ears, even if their name suggests it.
The giant earwig was almost six times as long as a common earwig.

teile.einleitung: Panthera is the scientific name of the genus of big cats. It includes the lion, the tiger, the leopard, the jaguar and the snow leopard. They are the largest and strongest cats in the world, and most of them can roar.
wichtigste: Panthera is the genus of big cats.
It includes the lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard.
Lions, tigers and leopards live in Africa and Asia, the jaguar in the Americas.
Most Panthera species can roar.
The tiger is the largest cat in the world.
All five species are considered threatened or near threatened.

abschnitte.text: **Panthera** is a genus within the cat family. These animals are called **big cats** together. Today the genus includes five species: lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard. All of them are predators that can hunt large prey such as deer, antelopes or wild boar.

The **lion** lives mainly in the savannas of Africa, with a small group also in India. The tiger is found only in Asia, from India to the east of Russia. The leopard is the most widespread and lives in Africa and Asia. The **jaguar** is the only Panthera species in the Americas, and the snow leopard lives in the high mountains of Central Asia.

Big cats have a powerful body, strong jaws and long canine teeth. Most of them can **roar** loudly because their larynx is built in a special way. In return, unlike house cats, they cannot purr continuously. The snow leopard is an exception: it cannot roar.

The **tiger** is the largest cat in the world, and large male Siberian tigers can weigh over 250 kilograms. The lion is hardly smaller and is the only cat that lives in prides. In proportion to its size, the jaguar has the strongest bite of all cats. The snow leopard uses its very long tail as a balancing aid and as a scarf against the cold.

The ancestors of the big cats appeared several million years ago, probably in Asia. During the ice ages the **cave lion**, a close relative of today's lion, lived in Europe. Remains of such animals have also been found in caves in Europe, and people of the Stone Age painted them on cave walls. Today there are no wild big cats left in Europe.

All big cats are threatened by **poaching**, the destruction of their habitat and conflicts with people. Only a few thousand tigers are left in the wild. Many protected areas and programmes aim to save the big cats. In Swiss zoos such as Zurich and Basel you can see big cats that take part in breeding programmes to protect their species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related animal species.
Another name for the large cats of the genus Panthera.
The organ in the throat that produces sounds.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.

gewusst: The clouded leopard looks like a big cat but belongs to a genus of its own.
A lion's roar can be heard several kilometres away.
Black panthers are not a separate species either, but dark leopards or jaguars.

teile.einleitung: Poikilothermy means being cold-blooded: an animal has no fixed body temperature but adapts to its surroundings. Reptiles such as the European pond turtle, amphibians, fish and insects live this way. This strategy saves a great deal of energy, but makes the animals dependent on the weather.
wichtigste: Poikilothermy means being cold-blooded.
In the pond turtle, body temperature depends on the surroundings.
Most animals on Earth are cold-blooded.
Warm-blooded animals such as birds and mammals keep their temperature constant themselves.
Cold-blooded animals regulate their heat mainly through their behaviour.
In some reptiles, temperature even decides the sex of the young.

abschnitte.text: **Poikilothermy** is the technical term for an animal being cold-blooded. Its body produces only little heat of its own, so its body temperature follows the air or the water. The opposite is **homeothermy**, the warm-bloodedness of birds and mammals. The vast majority of animal species on Earth, from insects to fish, are cold-blooded.

The **European pond turtle** is the only turtle species that occurs naturally in central Europe. In Switzerland it has become very rare and is being reintroduced in some places. Because it is cold-blooded, its body temperature depends on the surroundings. That is why it often lies on tree trunks in the water and takes a **sunbath** before it hunts worms, snails or insect larvae.

Cold-blooded animals are not helpless, as they control their temperature through clever **behaviour**. Lizards lie flat in the sun in the morning and hide in the shade at midday when it gets too hot. Some dark-coloured animals take up the sun's warmth especially quickly. In summer, fish seek out cooler, deeper layers of water.

In many turtles and crocodiles, the temperature in the nest decides whether a male or a female hatches from an egg. In the pond turtle, a warm nest produces mainly **females** and a cooler one rather more males. How quickly eggs and larvae develop also depends strongly on warmth in cold-blooded animals. Tadpoles in a warm pond, for example, turn into frogs more quickly.

Cold-blooded animals save a lot of energy because they do not have to heat their bodies all the time. They get by on little food and can go hungry for a long time. In the cold, however, they fall into a **cold torpor** and are then easy prey or cannot feed. That is why cold-blooded land animals are much more common in warm countries than in cold mountains.

Because their body temperature depends on the surroundings, cold-blooded animals react strongly to **climate change**. If the water in rivers gets too warm, fish such as the brown trout suffer, as has also been seen in hot summers in Switzerland. Some insects and reptiles, by contrast, are spreading further north or to higher elevations. In turtles, warmer sand can mean that almost only females hatch.

begriffe.erklaerung: Being cold-blooded: body temperature adapts to the surroundings.
Being warm-blooded: body temperature always stays about the same.
When an animal lies in the sun to warm up.
The almost motionless state of a cold-blooded animal in the cold.

gewusst: The European pond turtle can live to over 50 years old.
Some frogs in North America even survive the winter partly frozen.
For its size, a crocodile needs only a small part of the food that a lion of the same weight needs.

teile.einleitung: The okapi is a shy forest animal from the Congo that looks like a mixture of horse, zebra and giraffe. In fact it is the giraffe’s closest relative. For Europe it was discovered only around 1901.
wichtigste: The okapi is most closely related to the giraffe.
In the wild it lives only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The stripes on its legs probably camouflage it in the dim light of the forest.
Its long tongue is bluish dark.
The explorer Harry Johnston made the okapi known in Europe.
Its natural enemy is mainly the leopard.
Deforestation and poaching threaten the okapi especially.

abschnitte.text: The okapi has a dark brown, velvety body and legs striped white and black. The stripes probably serve as **camouflage** in the dim light of the rainforest. It grows about 1.5 metres tall and weighs 200 to 350 kilograms. The males carry short, fur-covered bony knobs on the head, like the giraffe.

Although the stripes recall a zebra, the okapi belongs to the **giraffe family**. The genus is called Okapia, and the okapi is its only species. The British explorer Harry Johnston sent pieces of skin to London around 1900 and in this way made the animal known in Europe. That is why the scientific name is Okapia johnstoni.

Okapis live only in the dense rainforests of the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**, especially in the Ituri Forest in the north-east. They are loners and usually move at a calm pace through the forest. Because they are so shy, you hardly ever see them in the wild. Their most important natural enemy is the **leopard**.

Okapis eat leaves, buds, fruit, ferns and fungi from over a hundred plant species. With their long, bluish dark tongue they pluck leaves from the twigs. The tongue is so long that they can even clean their eyes and ears with it. To take in important **minerals** they also eat clay and charcoal from burnt trees.

A female okapi is pregnant for about 14 to 15 months and has a single **calf**. The young one hides in the first weeks in a nest in the undergrowth. During this time it hardly passes dung, so that enemies cannot smell it. The mother comes by regularly to suckle.

The okapi is regarded as **endangered**. Deforestation, mining, poaching and wars in the Congo threaten the animals. For protection the Okapi Wildlife Reserve was founded in the Ituri Forest. Zoos such as Basel Zoo also keep okapis and support protection projects in the Congo.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that mostly lives alone.
Colours or patterns with which an animal hardly stands out in its surroundings.
Substances such as salt or calcium that the body needs to live.
A dense forest in warm regions in which it rains a great deal.

gewusst: The okapi is the national animal of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Okapis can communicate with very low sounds that humans can hardly hear.
For a long time European researchers took the okapi for a kind of forest zebra.

teile.einleitung: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer is an invented reindeer with a bright red nose who pulls Santa Claus's sleigh. The character comes from the USA and became famous all over the world through a Christmas song. Behind the story there is a real animal, the reindeer.
wichtigste: Rudolph is the famous reindeer with the red nose.
The character was invented in 1939 in the USA.
Rudolph is first laughed at because of his nose and then becomes a hero.
With his glowing nose he leads Santa Claus's sleigh through the fog.
The Christmas song about Rudolph became a worldwide hit in 1949.
Real reindeer live in the far north and all carry antlers.

abschnitte.text: Rudolph is a young **reindeer** who has a glowing red nose. The other reindeer laugh at him because of it and do not let him join in their games. On a foggy Christmas night, Santa Claus cannot find the way. So he asks Rudolph to lead the sleigh at the front with his bright nose, and Rudolph becomes a celebrated hero.

Rudolph was invented in 1939 by the advertising copywriter **Robert L. May**. He wrote the story for a little colouring book that a department store in Chicago gave to children at Christmas. The booklet was handed out in its millions. Santa Claus already had reindeer before that, whose names come from an American poem of 1823, and Rudolph was added as a new reindeer.

Robert May's brother-in-law, **Johnny Marks**, wrote a song about Rudolph in 1949. Sung by the cowboy singer Gene Autry, it was a huge success and is still among the best-known Christmas songs today. In 1964 a television film with moving puppets was made, which is shown in the USA every year at Christmas. In this way Rudolph became a fixed character of the American **Christmas tradition**.

Reindeer, in German also called Ren, belong to the deer family. They live in the tundra and the forests in the north of Europe, Asia and North America. They are the only species of deer in which the females also carry **antlers**. With their broad hooves they walk well on snow and use them to scrape lichens out from under the snow.

No real reindeer has a truly glowing nose. Researchers have found, however, that the nose of reindeer is crossed by very many fine **blood vessels**. These warm the cold air that is breathed in and protect the nose from frost. On thermal images the reindeer's nose therefore really does look bright.

The story of Rudolph shows that something that makes you different can be a special strength. It also tells how hurtful **exclusion** is and how important it is to let everybody join in. In Switzerland, by the way, the Samichlaus traditionally comes not with reindeer, but often with a donkey. Rudolph and his colleagues belong to the American Santa Claus.

begriffe.erklaerung: A species of deer from the far north in which both sexes have antlers.
When someone is not taken along by a group or is shut out.
A cold, treeless landscape in the far north.
Living things made of a fungus and an alga that reindeer eat in winter.

gewusst: Robert May first considered other names for his reindeer before he decided on Rudolph.
In Lapland, reindeer have been kept as domestic animals by the Sami for centuries.

teile.einleitung: Pro Natura is the oldest and one of the largest nature conservation organisations in Switzerland. It works for rare animals such as the fire salamander, looks after hundreds of protected areas and once helped to found the Swiss National Park. Many children know it from the Schoggitaler or from the youth groups.
wichtigste: Pro Natura is a Swiss nature conservation organisation.
It was founded in 1909 as the Swiss League for Nature Conservation.
Since 1997 it has been called Pro Natura.
Pro Natura helped to found the Swiss National Park in 1914.
It looks after hundreds of nature reserves all over Switzerland.
Among other things, it works to protect amphibians such as the fire salamander.
Pro Natura is financed mainly by its members.

abschnitte.text: Pro Natura was founded in 1909 as the **Swiss League for Nature Conservation**. One of its main aims at that time was to raise money for a national park in the Engadine. In 1914 the **Swiss National Park** was created, the first national park in the Alps. In 1997 the organisation got its present name, which is Latin and means for nature.

Pro Natura works for threatened animals and plants and their habitats. These include amphibians such as the **fire salamander**, frogs and toads, which depend on damp forests and ponds. Every year Pro Natura chooses an Animal of the Year to draw attention to a particular animal and its problems. Beavers, wild bees and floodplain forests have also been at the centre of its campaigns.

Pro Natura owns or looks after over 700 **nature reserves** in all the cantons. These include bogs, dry meadows, woods and the shores of lakes and rivers. Experts and volunteers mow meadows there, create ponds and remove bushes so that rare species have room. Well-known visitor centres are the Pro Natura Aletsch Centre in the Villa Cassel and the Champ-Pittet Centre on Lake Neuchâtel.

Every year, schoolchildren all over Switzerland sell the **Schoggitaler**, a medal made of chocolate. Pro Natura and the Swiss Heritage Society share the proceeds for projects in nature and culture. For children and young people there are Pro Natura youth groups, which watch animals outdoors, build nest boxes or plant hedges. In this way young people get to know the nature on their own doorstep.

Pro Natura also works for nature in politics, for example with popular initiatives and statements on laws. As a recognised environmental organisation it has the **right of associations to appeal**. With this it can have large building projects checked to see whether nature conservation laws are being observed. The head office is in Basel, and there are branches in all the cantons.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area in which animals and plants are especially protected.
A chocolate medal whose sale finances nature and heritage conservation projects.
The right of environmental organisations to have building projects checked for compliance with the law.
Animals such as frogs, toads and salamanders that live on land and in water.

gewusst: The Schoggitaler has been sold since 1946 and is therefore older than most grandparents of today's schoolchildren.
The Swiss National Park is still the most strictly protected natural area in Switzerland.
Pro Natura belongs to the international network Friends of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Smoked salmon is salmon that has been salted and then preserved with smoke. It is usually served in wafer-thin slices, for example on bread or with an apéro. In Switzerland, for many families it simply belongs to Christmas and New Year.
wichtigste: Smoked salmon in thin slices is called Räucherlachs in German.
The fish is first salted and then smoked over wood smoke.
Smoked salmon is mostly cold smoked, at temperatures below about 30 degrees.
Most smoked salmon comes from Atlantic salmon from fish farms, for example in Norway.
The orange-red colour comes from a natural pigment that salmon take in with their food.
Smoked salmon must always be kept chilled.
Pregnant women should avoid raw smoked salmon because of possible germs.

abschnitte.text: Smoked salmon is mostly made from the **Atlantic salmon**, a large fish that lives in the sea and migrates into rivers to spawn. For smoked salmon, the side pieces of the fish, the fillets, are used. They are salted, smoked and then cut into thin slices. The result is soft, slightly salty and tastes of smoke.

First the fillet is rubbed with salt or put in brine, so that it loses water and keeps longer. Then it is hung in a smokehouse in which wood such as beech or alder smoulders slowly. In **cold smoking**, the temperature stays below about 30 degrees, so the fish is not cooked and stays tender. In **hot smoking** it is much hotter, and the salmon becomes cooked and firmer, like fried fish.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the salmon come from?
abschnitte.text: Wild salmon have become rare in many regions today. That is why most salmon comes from **aquaculture**, that is, from fish farms in sea inlets in Norway, Scotland or Chile. Wild salmon from the Pacific, such as the sockeye, often has darker, stronger flesh. In Switzerland there is even a salmon farm in a hall on land in Lostallo in the canton of Graubünden.

The colour comes from the pigment **astaxanthin**, which wild salmon take in by eating small crustaceans such as krill. Farmed salmon get this pigment in their feed, otherwise their flesh would be a pale grey-pink. The same substance also makes flamingos pink. Depending on feed and species, salmon flesh can be light orange to deep red.

Smoked salmon is a delicate food and always belongs in the **fridge**. Because it is not heated, germs such as **listeria** can multiply in it, which are dangerous for pregnant women. It contains a lot of protein and healthy omega-3 fatty acids, but also a lot of salt. It is typically served on toast, with horseradish, lemon and dill, or on a blini.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smoking at a low temperature, in which the food stays raw.
The farming of fish and other water animals in tanks or net pens.
A red pigment that gives salmon flesh and flamingos their colour.
Bacteria that occur in raw foods and can make people ill.

gewusst: Gravlax looks similar to smoked salmon, but is not smoked, being cured with salt, sugar and dill instead.
In the past, salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland, and in the 20th century they disappeared there.
Norway is the country that produces the most farmed salmon in the world.

teile.einleitung: Reynard the Fox, in German Reineke Fuchs, is a famous character from old animal stories: a clever, cunning fox who tricks all the other animals. The stories came into being in the Middle Ages and were later retold by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. Behind the animals lies a witty criticism of people and their society.
wichtigste: Reynard the Fox is a well-known medieval story character, a cunning fox with a name of his own.
The stories belong to the genre of the animal epic, a long tale with animals as characters.
The king of the animals is the lion Nobel, and the wolf is called Isegrim.
The famous badger character is called Grimbart and is Reynard's nephew.
In 1498 the Low German version “Reynke de vos” appeared in Lübeck.
Goethe published his version “Reineke Fuchs” in 1794.
In the story, Reynard gets away again and again with lies and tricks.

abschnitte.text: Reynard is a **fox** who lives in a world in which animals speak and act like people. He is clever, cheeky and without scruples, and he lies and cheats to help himself. The name comes from the old name Reinhart, which means roughly “good adviser”. Because he became so famous, in German the fox was often simply called “Master Reineke”.

Stories about a clever fox have existed since antiquity, for example in the fables of the Greek poet Aesop. In the 12th century, the tales of the fox Renart came into being in France, the **Roman de Renart**. From these came versions in Dutch, German and other languages. Especially successful was the Low German book **Reynke de vos**, which was printed in Lübeck in 1498.

At the centre stands the court of the lion **Nobel**, the king of the animals. Reynard's enemies include the wolf **Isegrim**, the bear Braun, the tomcat Hinze and the cock Henning. The badger **Grimbart** is Reynard's nephew and is the only one who defends him before the king. The hare Lampe also appears and is treated badly by Reynard.

At a great court day, many animals complain to the king about Reynard's misdeeds. Nobel first sends Braun and then Hinze to fetch the fox, but both are tricked by him and badly hurt. Only Grimbart brings Reynard to court, where he is sentenced to death on the gallows. With an invented story about a hidden **treasure** he saves himself, and in the end he even becomes a powerful adviser to the king.

**Johann Wolfgang von Goethe** wrote the story anew and published it in 1794 as “Reineke Fuchs” in twelve cantos. For this he used a verse form from antiquity, the **hexameter**. Later the work was illustrated with famous pictures by the painter Wilhelm von Kaulbach. To this day there are many retellings for children, radio plays and cartoon films.

Reynard the Fox is a **satire**: the animals stand for people at the court of a king. The story shows how the powerful let themselves be deceived by flattery and lies, and how the cunning profit from it. Many readers found in it a mirror of their own time. Names such as Isegrim for a grumpy person are therefore known to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long tale in verse or prose in which animals play the main roles.
A short story with talking animals that contains a lesson.
A text that presents abuses in an exaggerated and mocking way.
An old verse form from Greece with six stressed syllables per line.

gewusst: The real red fox is the most common wild predator in Switzerland and even lives in the middle of cities such as Zurich.
Grimbart is still a popular name for badgers in children's books today.
The stories of Reynard were retold and translated again and again for over 500 years.

teile.einleitung: The Okapi Wildlife Reserve is a large protected area in the rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was founded mainly to protect the rare okapi. Since 1996 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Okapi Wildlife Reserve is the best-known protected area for okapis in the Congo.
It lies in the Ituri rainforest in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The reserve was founded in 1992.
It covers about 13,700 square kilometres, around a third of the area of Switzerland.
Since 1996 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Poaching, mining and armed groups threaten the area.

abschnitte.text: The Okapi Wildlife Reserve lies in the north-east of the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**. It covers about a fifth of the huge Ituri rainforest. At about 13,700 square kilometres it is about a third as large as Switzerland. Through the area flows the Epulu River, on which the reserve’s most important station also lies.

The reserve is covered by dense, tropical **rainforest**. Here live an estimated several thousand okapis, as many as nowhere else. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, leopards and many species of monkeys and birds also occur. That is why the area is regarded as especially valuable for **biodiversity**.

The Okapi Wildlife Reserve was founded in 1992. In 1996 UNESCO added it to the list of **World Heritage** sites. Only a year later it was put on the list of World Heritage in Danger, because war and poaching threatened the area. At Epulu okapis were also kept and studied.

In the Ituri Forest live peoples such as the **Mbuti** and the Efe, and have done for a very long time. They traditionally live from hunting and gathering in the forest. In the reserve they may continue their way of life. Farmers from other areas have also moved into the Ituri, which puts additional pressure on the forest.

Illegal gold mining, logging and **poaching** endanger the reserve. In 2012 armed poachers attacked the Epulu station and killed people and several okapis kept there. Rangers repeatedly risk their lives in their work. International protection projects, which are also supported by zoos, help to protect the area.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protected area in which wild animals are especially protected.
An award for natural areas that are valuable for all humanity.
The large number of different animal and plant species in an area.
A person who watches over a protected area and protects animals from poachers.

gewusst: More okapis live in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve than anywhere else in the world.
The Mbuti are among the smallest people in the world and know the rainforest better than any researcher.
Besides the Okapi Wildlife Reserve, other natural areas in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are also on the World Heritage list, for example Virunga National Park.

teile.einleitung: A riding helmet is a special protective helmet that you wear when riding and when handling horses. It protects the head if you fall off the horse or are hit by a hoof. For children especially, it is an absolute must when riding.
wichtigste: A riding helmet protects the head in a fall from a horse.
Children should always wear a helmet when riding.
A good riding helmet has a hard outer shell and a cushioning inner layer.
A chin strap makes sure that the helmet does not slip in a fall.
The helmet must fit exactly and must not wobble.
After a hard fall, you should replace the helmet.
In Europe, riding helmets must meet a safety standard.

abschnitte.text: A horse is much larger and stronger than a person. Anyone sitting in the saddle is often more than two metres above the ground. If the horse takes fright and leaps, you can easily fall off. On impact the **head** is especially at risk, because injuries to the brain can have serious consequences. A helmet can absorb a large part of the force.

On the outside, a riding helmet has a hard **shell** made of plastic. Underneath lies a layer of rigid foam, which is compressed on impact and so swallows the energy. On the inside, a soft pad provides a good hold and comfort. A short peak at the front protects the face and keeps off the sun. Ventilation openings prevent you from sweating too much underneath.

A helmet protects only if it fits well. It sits level on the head and covers the forehead to just above the eyebrows. The **chin strap** is adjusted so that about one finger still fits in between. Many helmets have a dial at the back of the head with which the size can be fine-tuned. Because children grow, you have to check regularly whether the helmet still fits.

In Europe, riding helmets are tested to a fixed **safety standard**. A test mark in the helmet shows that it has passed these tests. In the tests, for example, how well the helmet cushions a blow is measured. At competitions in equestrian sport, too, a tested helmet is now compulsory. A bicycle helmet is no substitute, because it is built for other kinds of accidents.

After a violent fall, the foam layer inside can be damaged even if you see nothing on the outside. That is why you should then **replace** the helmet. Sun, heat and age also make the material brittle over time. Many manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet after a few years. It is best kept dry and not in a hot car.

In Switzerland, many children and young people ride at riding stables, pony farms or riding clubs. There the helmet is of course part of the equipment. Safe clothing also includes sturdy shoes with a heel, so that the foot does not slip through the **stirrup**. Some riders also wear a protective vest for the back. When leading and grooming a horse, too, care is important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protective helmet that protects the head when riding.
A strap under the chin that holds the helmet in place.
A loop on the saddle in which you put your feet when riding.
A padded vest that protects the back and upper body in a fall.

gewusst: In the past, riders often wore velvet-covered caps that hardly protected at all, and today helmets are much safer.
A riding helmet usually weighs only about half a kilogram.
Even experienced professionals in show jumping wear a helmet on every ride.

teile.einleitung: Salmonids, or fishes of the salmon family, are a family of fishes that includes salmon, trout, char, grayling and whitefish. They love cold, oxygen-rich water. A good mark of recognition is the small adipose fin on the back.
wichtigste: The trout belongs to the salmon family, scientifically Salmonidae.
Typical is the adipose fin, a small extra fin on the back without fin rays.
Salmonids need cool, clean and oxygen-rich water.
Many species migrate into rivers and streams to spawn.
In Switzerland live brown trout, lake trout, grayling, Arctic char and many species of whitefish.
Salmonids are important food fish and are often kept in fish farms.

abschnitte.text: Salmonids have a slim, streamlined body and small scales. Between the dorsal fin and the tail sits the **adipose fin**, a small fin without supporting rays. Many species have spots on the skin, such as the red dots of the brown trout. At spawning time, some males get strong colours and a hooked lower jaw.

The family includes the **salmon**, the trout, the char, the huchen, the grayling and the whitefish. Worldwide, over 200 species are known. The largest is the taimen from Siberia and Mongolia, which can grow over 1.5 metres long. The rainbow trout originally comes from North America and was introduced to Europe.

Salmonids live in streams, rivers, lakes and partly in the sea of the Northern Hemisphere. The Atlantic salmon grows up in the sea and returns to spawn in the river of its birth. To do so it even leaps up waterfalls. Trout lay their eggs in hollows in the **gravel**, which the female beats out with her tail.

Salmon and trout are among the most popular food fish. A large part comes from **aquaculture**, that is, from fish farming, for example from Norway. In many Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Lucerne, whitefish are the most important catch of professional fishermen. Many anglers fish for trout in streams.

In Swiss waters, the **brown trout** and the whitefish are especially important, and in some lakes there live species of whitefish of their own that exist nowhere else. The salmon used to be common in the Rhine as far as Basel and in the Aare, but disappeared in the 20th century because of power stations and pollution. With fish ladders and releases, people are trying to bring it back. Warm summers are hard on trout and grayling, because water above about 25 degrees becomes dangerous for them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small fin without rays between the dorsal fin and the tail.
The laying and fertilising of fish eggs.
The farming of fish and other water animals.
Silvery salmonids that live in many Swiss lakes.

gewusst: Salmon probably find their river of birth again with the help of their sense of smell.
In fish farms the adipose fin was often cut off, in order to recognise released fish later.

teile.einleitung: Radial symmetry means that a body is built around a centre, like the spokes of a wheel. A starfish, a jellyfish or a sea urchin looks similar from all sides. Such animals are called radially symmetrical, and they have neither a front nor a back.
wichtigste: Radially symmetrical bodies are built around a central axis.
Animals such as the starfish are called radially symmetrical.
They can be divided into equal halves by several cuts.
Typical examples are jellyfish, sea anemones, starfish and sea urchins.
The opposite is bilateral symmetry with a left and a right half, as in humans.
Many flowers are also radially symmetrical, for example the tulip.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “radius”, which means ray or spoke. In a **radially symmetrical** body, equal parts repeat around a **central axis**. So you can cut it, like a cake, in several ways into mirror-image halves. A starfish with five arms, for example, has five such mirror planes.

Radially symmetrical animals are mostly sea animals. They include the **cnidarians** such as jellyfish, sea anemones and coral polyps. **Echinoderms** such as starfish, sea urchins and sea cucumbers also have a ray-shaped body, usually based on the number five. The larvae of echinoderms, however, are still built with two sides, and only later do they become five-rayed.

Most animals, including humans, dogs, fish and insects, are **bilaterally symmetrical**. They have a single mirror plane that divides the body into a left and a right half. They have a head at the front and mostly move purposefully in one direction. Radially symmetrical animals, by contrast, have no head and no front or back.

Many radially symmetrical animals sit fixed to the ground or drift in the water. For them, food or danger can come from **all directions**. With tentacles all around its mouth, a sea anemone can grab prey from any side. A jellyfish can contract its bell evenly and so pulse forwards.

abschnitte.titel: Symmetry in plants and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many **flowers** are also radially symmetrical, such as tulips, wild roses or daisies. Other flowers, such as the snapdragon or orchids, have only one mirror plane. In everyday life you meet radial symmetry in wheels, pizzas, stars or snowflakes, which have six equal arms. Even an orange shows a ray-shaped structure in cross-section.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regular structure in which parts mirror or repeat one another.
An imaginary surface that divides something into two mirror-image halves.
A body plan with a left and a right half of the body.
Sea animals with a chalky skeleton and often spines, such as starfish and sea urchins.

gewusst: Starfish have no head and no brain, but at the tip of each arm a simple light-sensing organ.
There are starfish with more than 20 arms, for example the sun stars.
The larva of a starfish swims freely and has two sides, quite unlike the finished animal.

teile.einleitung: The Nile crocodile is the largest aquatic predator in Africa. It belongs to the family of true crocodiles and can weigh up to 1000 kilograms. The ancient Egyptians already revered and feared this reptile.
wichtigste: The Nile crocodile belongs to the family of true crocodiles (Crocodylidae).
Josephus Nicolaus Laurenti described it in 1768 as Crocodylus niloticus.
The species name ‘niloticus’ means ‘from the Nile’.
Adult males usually grow to about 3.3 to 5 metres long and weigh up to about 1000 kilograms.
Females are about 30 per cent smaller than males.
A Nile crocodile has about 64 to 68 teeth.
Among today’s reptiles only the saltwater crocodile grows even larger.

abschnitte.text: The Nile crocodile belongs to the family of **true crocodiles**. The naturalist Josephus Nicolaus Laurenti gave it in 1768 the name Crocodylus niloticus, which means ‘from the Nile’. The word ‘crocodile’ comes from Greek and means roughly ‘pebble worm’. Presumably the Greeks were thinking of lizards basking on warm stones.

For a long time the crocodiles of West Africa were also counted as Nile crocodiles. In 2011 researchers even examined **DNA** from ancient Egyptian crocodile mummies. This showed that two species were hidden in the ‘Nile crocodile’. The West African crocodile (Crocodylus suchus) is now regarded as a species of its own, and the Nile crocodile is even more closely related to American species such as the American crocodile.

Adult males typically grow to 3.3 to 5 metres long and can weigh up to about 1000 kilograms. Females are about 30 per cent smaller. The body is covered with hard **horny scales**, and there are bony plates on the back. In the mouth are 64 to 68 cone-shaped teeth, with which it can grip but not chew.

Nile crocodiles live in large parts of Africa south of the Sahara and on Madagascar. They are found in rivers, lakes and swamps, for example in the Nile, the Zambezi and the Okavango. Eyes, ears and nostrils sit on top of the head, so the crocodile can lie in wait almost invisible in the water. As a **cold-blooded** animal it warms up on the bank in the sun.

Young crocodiles eat insects, frogs and small fish. Large animals hunt fish, birds and even zebras or wildebeest that drink at rivers or cross the river. The crocodile seizes the prey in a flash and drags it under water. With the **death roll**, a fast spin around its own axis, it tears off large pieces.

The female digs a nest in the sand and usually lays 25 to 80 eggs in it. Whether males or females hatch depends on the **incubation temperature**. The mother guards the nest and afterwards carries the young carefully in her mouth to the water. In ancient Egypt the crocodile-headed god Sobek was worshipped, and many crocodiles were even mummified.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cold-blooded vertebrate with scales, for example a crocodile, snake or lizard.
The body temperature depends on the surroundings, so the animal has to warm up in the sun.
A fast spin with which crocodiles tear pieces from their prey.
The blueprint of life in every cell, with which relationships can be investigated.

gewusst: Nile crocodiles can stay under water for over an hour if they keep calm.
Crocodiles often lie in the sun with their mouth open in order to give off surplus heat.
A crocodile changes its teeth many times in its life, and lost teeth simply grow back.

teile.einleitung: A fish trap, in German Reuse, is a trap for catching fish and other water animals. It works with a funnel: swimming in is easy, but the way out is hard to find. With a special form, the eel trap, fishermen catch mainly eels.
wichtigste: A fish trap is a trap with a funnel-shaped entrance.
Fish find it easy to get in, but hardly ever get out again.
The eel trap is a fish trap with which people mainly catch eels.
In the past, fish traps were woven from willow rods.
Today fish traps usually consist of nets or wire over rings.
Fish traps are among the oldest fishing gear of humankind.
The animals caught mostly stay alive in the trap.

abschnitte.text: A **fish trap** is a piece of fishing gear that looks like a basket or a tube. It is put into the water and often stays there overnight or for several days. The fisherman does not have to be there while the animals swim in. Later he pulls the trap out and empties it. Fish traps are used in lakes, rivers and on sea coasts.

The secret of the fish trap is the **funnel** at the entrance. It is wide on the outside and becomes narrower and narrower towards the inside. A fish swims in through the wide opening, for example looking for food or a hiding place. From inside it can hardly find the small opening again. Many fish traps have several funnels one behind the other, so that the fish get in even deeper.

Eels are active at night and like to creep into narrow, dark tubes. The **eel trap** makes use of this behaviour. It is long and narrow and is often fitted with bait. Fishermen set it on the bed of rivers, lakes or coastal waters. Because the European eel is now heavily endangered, catching it is strictly regulated in many countries.

Fish traps are among the oldest fishing gear of humans. Archaeologists have found remains of woven fish traps that are several thousand years old. In the past, fish traps were made of **willow rods** or other flexible twigs. Today people mostly use nets of plastic or wire mesh stretched over rings. The basic idea, however, has stayed the same.

Not only fish are caught with fish traps. In the sea, lobsters, crabs and spiny lobsters are caught with similar baskets. In Switzerland, traps are also used to remove introduced **crayfish** such as the signal crayfish from waters. Researchers catch fish or newts with small traps in order to count them and release them again. In this way the fish trap also helps with nature conservation.

Anyone who wants to fish in Switzerland needs a **licence** or a permit. For fish traps, special rules apply, and they may often be used only by professional fishermen or with permission. One advantage of the fish trap is that the animals are mostly caught alive. In this way fish that are too small or protected can be released again. Lost fish traps can, however, become a danger to animals if they go on catching.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish trap with a funnel-shaped entrance.
A long, narrow fish trap for catching eels.
Food that lures animals into a trap or onto the hook.
Someone who earns their living by fishing.

gewusst: The German word “Reuse” is very old and was already known in German in the Middle Ages.
Fish traps and nets that are lost at sea can go on catching animals for years, and these are called ghost nets.
With similar funnel traps, people in Africa and Asia still catch fish in rivers and rice fields today.

teile.einleitung: Primates are an order of mammals that includes monkeys, lemurs such as the ring-tailed lemur and also us humans. Typical of them are hands that can grasp, forward-facing eyes and a large brain. Worldwide there are several hundred species of primate today.
wichtigste: Primates are an order of mammals.
Primates include lemurs, lorises, tarsiers, monkeys, apes and humans.
The ring-tailed lemur from Madagascar is a well-known primate.
In many primates the thumb can be placed opposite the other fingers.
Most primates have nails instead of claws.
In proportion to the body, primates have a large brain.
Many primate species are threatened today.

abschnitte.text: Primates have hands, and often feet too, with which they can grasp. The thumb can be placed opposite the other fingers, and it is said to be **opposable**. In this way they can clasp branches and skilfully hold small things. Their eyes are at the front of the face, so they see in three dimensions and can judge distances well. Instead of claws, most have flat nails.

Primates are divided into two groups. The **wet-nosed primates** include the lemurs of Madagascar, such as the ring-tailed lemur, as well as the lorises and galagos in Africa and Asia. The dry-nosed primates include the tarsiers, the New World monkeys in the Americas, the Old World monkeys in Africa and Asia and the **great apes**. The great apes include orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and also humans.

Almost all primates live in warm regions, mainly in the tropical rainforests of Africa, Asia and South America. A few species, such as the Japanese macaques, also live in snowy mountain forests. The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur from Madagascar, which weighs only about 30 grams. The largest is the **gorilla**, and a fully grown male can weigh around 200 kilograms.

Many primates live in groups with clear relationships and pecking orders. They groom each other's fur, which strengthens friendships in the group. Chimpanzees use **tools**, for example little sticks for fishing out termites or stones for cracking nuts. The researcher Jane Goodall made this behaviour famous in Tanzania from 1960.

Around 60 per cent of all primate species are considered threatened. The greatest dangers are the clearing of forests, hunting and the illegal animal trade. Zoos take part in breeding programmes and support conservation projects. In Switzerland you can watch primates, for example, at **Zurich Zoo** and at Basel Zoo.

begriffe.erklaerung: An order of mammals with monkeys, lemurs, tarsiers and humans.
A thumb that can be placed opposite the other fingers in order to grasp.
A group of large, tailless primates such as the gorilla, chimpanzee and orangutan.
Primates that live only on Madagascar, for example the ring-tailed lemur.

gewusst: The word primates comes from the Latin primus and means something like the first ones.
Ring-tailed lemurs sunbathe in the morning with their arms spread out, as if meditating.
Humans and chimpanzees match in about 98 per cent of their genetic material.

teile.einleitung: The rainbow trout is a fish of the salmon family with a shimmering pink-red stripe on its side. It originally comes from North America, but was brought to Europe over a hundred years ago. Today it is the most important food trout in fish farms, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The rainbow trout originally comes from North America.
Typical is a pink-red, shimmering stripe on the side of the body.
It belongs to the salmon family.
It was introduced to Europe at the end of the 19th century.
Most trout from fish farms are rainbow trout.
In Switzerland it counts as a non-native species that may be released into waters only with a permit.
It differs from the native brown trout, among other things, by the many black spots on the tail fin.

abschnitte.text: The rainbow trout has a slim, strong body and usually grows 30 to 50 centimetres long, large animals considerably more. On its side it carries a **pink-red stripe** that shimmers like a rainbow. Back and fins, including the tail fin, are covered with many small **black spots**. The native **brown trout**, by contrast, has red spots with a pale edge and no rainbow stripe.

The rainbow trout originally lives in rivers and lakes on the Pacific coast of **North America**, from Mexico to Alaska. At the end of the 19th century it was brought to Europe because it grows fast and is easy to breed. Today it occurs on all continents except Antarctica. A form that migrates to the sea and grows very large is called **steelhead** in America.

Rainbow trout eat insect larvae, freshwater shrimps, snails and food that arrives from above, such as flies that fall onto the water. Large animals also hunt smaller fish. They like cool, oxygen-rich water, but tolerate warmer water better than the brown trout. To spawn, they seek out gravelly places in streams and rivers.

The rainbow trout is one of the most important farmed fish in the world. In **fish farms** it grows up in ponds or tanks with fresh spring water. In Switzerland too, most trout in shops and restaurants come from farms. It is popular fried, as “trout au bleu”, hot smoked or in butter “à la meunière”.

In the past, rainbow trout were released into many Swiss streams and lakes so that anglers could catch more. Today people know that it can **compete** with native fish such as the brown trout for food and spawning grounds. That is why it counts in Switzerland as a **non-native** species, and releasing it into open waters requires a permit. In some waters it nevertheless reproduces on its own.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish family that includes salmon, trout, char and graylings.
A species that was originally not native to an area.
Laying eggs, in fish.
The farming of fish and other water animals.

gewusst: The scientific name of the rainbow trout is Oncorhynchus mykiss, so it is more closely related to the Pacific salmon than to the brown trout.
In trout au bleu, the skin turns bluish when cooked in vinegar water, because the layer of slime stays undamaged.
The sea form, the steelhead, can migrate back from the sea to its home river like a salmon.

teile.einleitung: “Peter and the Wolf” is a famous musical fairy tale for children by the Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev. A narrator tells the story, and each character is played by an instrument of its own. In this exciting way, children get to know the instruments of an orchestra.
wichtigste: “Peter and the Wolf” was composed in 1936 by Sergei Prokofiev.
It is a fairy tale for narrator and orchestra.
Each character has its own instrument and its own melody.
The wolf is represented by three horns.
Peter catches the wolf with a rope, and the hunters take it to the zoo.
The piece lasts about half an hour.
It is still performed all over the world today.

abschnitte.text: The Russian composer **Sergei Prokofiev** lived from 1891 to 1953. He wrote “Peter and the Wolf” in 1936 in Moscow for a children's theatre. He wrote not only the music but also the text of the story himself. The aim was to bring the instruments of the orchestra closer to children.

The boy Peter lives with his grandfather at the edge of a forest. One day a wolf slinks out of the forest and swallows the duck. Peter bravely climbs a tree and, with the help of the little bird and a **rope**, catches the wolf by the tail. The hunters arrive, and everyone takes the wolf to the zoo in a triumphal procession.

Each character has its own instrument and its own **theme**, that is, a melody you can recognise. Peter is played by the string instruments, the bird by the flute and the duck by the **oboe**. The cat creeps along with the clarinet, and the grandfather grumbles with the bassoon. The wolf is played by three horns, and the hunters' shots can be heard on the timpani.

At the start, the narrator introduces each character with its instrument. In this way, as you listen, you can tell who is currently appearing in the story. When the wolf appears, the music sounds dark and threatening. At the end you can even hear the duck quacking softly in the wolf's belly, because in his haste the wolf swallowed it whole.

“Peter and the Wolf” is one of the best-known works of **classical music** for children. Many famous people have taken on the narrator's role, in the German-speaking world for example the humorist Loriot. There are animated films, for example one by Walt Disney from 1946. A puppet animation from 2006 even won an **Oscar**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who invents and writes down music.
A large group of musicians with many different instruments.
A short melody that you can recognise again and again.
The person who reads out the story between the pieces of music.

gewusst: Prokofiev is said to have written the music for “Peter and the Wolf” in just a few days.
Prokofiev died on the same day as the Soviet ruler Joseph Stalin.
In many Swiss schools and concert halls there are family concerts with “Peter and the Wolf”.

teile.einleitung: Phoresy means that one animal lets itself be transported by another animal without harming it. It is like hitchhiking in the animal world. Small animals such as mites in particular use this trick to reach new habitats.
wichtigste: Phoresy is the transport of one animal by another without harming it.
The word comes from Greek and means “carrying”.
It is usually small, slow animals that let themselves be carried.
Some mites let dung beetles carry them to fresh dung.
Pseudoscorpions also often travel on flies or beetles.
The transporting animal is not eaten and not sucked dry.

abschnitte.text: In **phoresy**, one animal clings to another and lets itself be taken along. The word comes from the Greek “phoresis”, which means “carrying”. The passenger uses the transporting animal only as a vehicle and does not feed on it. This is what distinguishes phoresy from **parasitism**, in which one animal harms another.

A well-known example is **mites** on dung beetles and burying beetles. Dung and animal carcasses are only there for a short time and lie far apart. The tiny mites could hardly reach these food sources on foot. So they climb onto a beetle and get off again at the next pile of dung or carcass.

**Pseudoscorpions** are tiny arachnids with pincers that often live under bark or in leaf litter. To get further away, they grab the leg of a fly or beetle with their pincers and fly along. Some roundworms also travel on insects to new habitats. In oil beetles, the young larvae climb onto wild bees and let themselves be carried into their nests.

The **remora** is a fish that attaches itself with a sucker on its head to sharks, whales or turtles. In this way it saves energy and eats scraps from its carrier's prey. Because it also feeds, this relationship is usually counted as **commensalism**, a related form of living together. The boundaries between phoresy and other forms are not always sharp.

Phoresy helps small animals to spread far and to settle new habitats. Sometimes even the carrier gains an advantage: mites on burying beetles, for example, eat fly eggs on the carcass and so protect the food of the beetle larvae. In a similar way, plants spread seeds with hooks in the fur of animals, as the burdock does. Researchers study phoresy to understand better how living things are connected.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal lets itself be transported by another without harming it.
A way of living together in which one animal exploits and harms another.
A way of living together in which one gains and the other has neither benefit nor harm.
A tiny arachnid with pincers but without a venomous sting.

gewusst: Some mites wait motionless on flowers until a hummingbird comes by, and then dash into its bill to fly along to the next flower.
Pseudoscorpions are often only a few millimetres in size and completely harmless to people.
Dozens of mites can ride along on a single burying beetle at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The paw is the foot of many mammals such as dogs, cats, foxes or bears. Under the paw lie soft pads, the paw pads, which work like shock absorbers. Paws also have claws, with which the animals dig, climb or hunt.
wichtigste: Paws are the feet of many mammals, for example dogs and cats.
The soft cushions under the paws are called pads.
Dogs sweat mainly through the pads of their paws.
Cats can draw in their claws, dogs cannot.
Dogs and cats walk on their toes, so they are digitigrade.
In hunters' language, the print of a paw is called a track.

abschnitte.text: A paw consists of the toes with their **claws** and several soft cushions, the **pads**. In dogs and cats there is a small toe pad under each toe and, behind them, a large main pad. The pads have thick, rough skin and a layer of fat underneath. In this way they cushion the shocks when running and jumping.

Dogs and cats are **digitigrade**: they walk only on their toes, and the heel does not touch the ground. This makes them fast and quiet. Bears, by contrast, are **plantigrade** and put the whole sole of the foot down, much as we humans do. Dogs and cats usually have five toes at the front and four at the back, with the inner front toe sitting higher up and not touching the ground.

Cats can draw their pointed claws into sheaths of skin, so that they stay sharp and the cat creeps along silently. When climbing or hunting, it extends the claws in a flash. Dogs cannot draw in their claws, which is why you can hear them clicking on hard floors. They use their claws mainly for **digging** and for a good grip when running.

Dogs and cats have hardly any sweat glands in their skin. They sweat mainly through the **paw pads**, which is why on hot days they sometimes leave damp prints. To cool down, dogs mostly pant. The pads are also very sensitive and feel the ground, warmth and vibrations.

Animals from cold regions have special paws: the polar bear and the Arctic fox have fur on their soles, which keeps them warm and stops them slipping. The lynx has broad, hairy paws that work like **snowshoes** in deep snow. For dogs in Switzerland, road salt in winter and hot asphalt in summer are a danger to the pads. Dog owners therefore care for the paws with grease or rinse them off after a walk.

In hunters' language, the print of a paw is called a **track**. From the tracks in snow or mud you can tell which animal has passed by. In a dog's print you can usually see the claws, but not in a cat's, because it draws its claws in. A fox track is narrower than a dog track, and the fox often places its paws in a dead straight line one behind the other.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft, thick cushion under the paw.
A hard, pointed nail on an animal's toe.
An animal that walks only on its toes, like a dog and a cat.
The print of a paw in the ground.

gewusst: The paw pads of some dogs smell slightly of popcorn, because of bacteria on the skin.
Cats have scent glands in their paws and mark their territory when scratching.
Many dogs and cats prefer one paw, much as people are right-handed or left-handed.

teile.einleitung: Polydactyly means that a living thing has more fingers or toes than usual. In cats, a gene variant means that some animals have extra toes on their paws. Such cats look as if they were wearing little mittens.
wichtigste: Polydactyly means having many fingers and refers to extra fingers or toes.
In cats it arises from a gene variant that is inherited.
A normal house cat has 18 toes, five on each front paw and four on each hind paw.
Polydactyl cats usually have extra toes on the front paws.
The feature is usually harmless for the animal.
Humans, chickens and dogs can also have extra fingers or toes.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek: **poly** means many and daktylos means finger. In polydactyly, an extra finger or toe forms during the development of the embryo. Often it sits next to the thumb or next to the little finger. The cause is a change in the genetic material, that is, a **mutation**.

An ordinary house cat has five toes on each front paw and four on each hind paw. Polydactyl cats can have six, seven or even more toes on one paw. Usually the front paws are affected, less often the hind paws too. The gene variant is **dominant**, so it is enough for one parent to pass it on for kittens to get it.

The American writer Ernest Hemingway was given a six-toed cat by a ship's captain. Many descendants of this cat still live today on his former property in Key West in Florida. That is why polydactyl cats are often called **Hemingway cats**. In the past such cats were regarded by sailors as lucky charms and good mouse hunters on ships.

Polydactyly also occurs in other animals. Some chicken breeds such as the **Silkie** quite regularly have five toes instead of four. The Norwegian Lundehund even has at least six toes on each paw, which help it to climb rock cliffs. In humans, a sixth finger occurs in about one in a thousand births.

For most cats, polydactyly is no problem, and they run, climb and play quite normally. Sometimes, however, an extra claw grows crooked and can grow into the toe. That is why you should check the claws of such cats now and then. In humans, an extra finger is sometimes removed by surgery in childhood if it gets in the way.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a living thing has more fingers or toes than usual.
A change in the genetic material of a living thing.
A gene that shows itself even if it comes from only one parent.
A living thing in its earliest development before birth.

gewusst: The cat with the most toes in the Guinness book had 28 toes, that is, seven on each paw.
In the original Maine Coon cat in the USA, polydactyl animals used to be especially common.

teile.einleitung: Little Red Riding Hood, in German Rotkäppchen, is one of the best-known fairy tales in the world, in which a girl with a red hood meets a wolf in the forest. The wolf is the dangerous villain in it, who wants to eat the grandmother and the girl. The fairy tale has shaped the image of the “big bad wolf” for centuries.
wichtigste: Little Red Riding Hood is a fairy tale that became especially well known through the Brothers Grimm.
In the fairy tale the wolf is the dangerous villain.
Little Red Riding Hood is supposed to bring cake and wine to her sick grandmother.
The wolf eats the grandmother and then Little Red Riding Hood too.
In the Grimms' version, a huntsman rescues the two from the wolf's belly.
An older version was written by the Frenchman Charles Perrault in 1697.
Real wolves are shy and attack people only very rarely.

abschnitte.text: A little girl always wears a red hood and is therefore called **Little Red Riding Hood**. Her mother sends her with cake and wine to the sick grandmother, who lives alone in the forest. She warns her not to stray from the path. In the forest, however, Little Red Riding Hood meets the wolf and innocently tells him where she is going.

In the fairy tale the **wolf** is clever and sly. He lures Little Red Riding Hood off the path so that she picks flowers, and hurries to the grandmother's house himself. There he eats the grandmother, lies down in her bed and disguises himself with her cap. When Little Red Riding Hood arrives and wonders at the big ears, eyes and the big mouth, he eats her too.

In the version of the **Brothers Grimm**, a huntsman hears the wolf snoring loudly. He cuts open his belly and frees Little Red Riding Hood and the grandmother alive. Then they fill the wolf's belly with heavy stones, so that he dies. The message is: listen to your parents and trust no strangers.

The fairy tale was told orally for a long time before it was written down. The Frenchman **Charles Perrault** published a version in 1697 in which the wolf wins in the end and nobody is rescued. The brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm included their version with the happy ending in 1812 in the **Children's and Household Tales**. Today the fairy tale exists in many languages, as a picture book, a play and a film.

Fairy tales such as Little Red Riding Hood made the wolf a symbol of danger. In reality, wolves are **shy animals** that mostly avoid people. In Switzerland the wolf was wiped out for a long time and has been migrating back from Italy since 1995. It causes conflicts today mainly because it sometimes kills sheep and goats.

Little Red Riding Hood is one of the fairy tales that almost every child knows. The sentence about the grandmother's big eyes and ears has become proverbial. Many books and films play with the story and retell it, sometimes even from the wolf's point of view. The fairy tale shows how strongly stories influence the image that people have of an **animal**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invented story, often with magic, talking animals and good against evil.
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, who collected fairy tales in the 19th century.
A character in a story who wants to harm others.
A particular form of a story.

gewusst: In the oldest known version by Perrault, there is no huntsman, and the fairy tale ends sadly.
The “Children's and Household Tales” of the Brothers Grimm are part of the UNESCO Memory of the World.

teile.einleitung: Rays are cartilaginous fishes with a flat, disc-shaped body and are close relatives of the sharks. Many lie well camouflaged on the sea floor, while others glide through the water with wing-like fins. They include the huge manta ray, the stingray and the electric ray.
wichtigste: Rays are close relatives of the sharks.
First and foremost, rays differ from sharks by their flattened body.
Like sharks, rays have a skeleton of cartilage instead of bone.
Many rays lie on the sea floor and are well camouflaged.
Their gill slits lie on the underside.
There are over 600 species of ray worldwide.
The giant manta reaches a wingspan of about 7 metres.

abschnitte.text: Like the sharks, rays belong to the **cartilaginous fishes**. So their skeleton consists of flexible cartilage and not of bone. Their body is flat, and the pectoral fins are fused with the head into a broad disc. The gill slits lie on the underside, the eyes and **spiracles** on the upperside. Through the spiracles they draw in water for breathing, even when they are lying in the sand.

Rays live in all the world's oceans, from shallow coasts to the deep sea. Some species even live in rivers of South America, Africa and Asia. Many rays lie half buried in the sand on the **sea floor** by day. Their colour often matches the ground, so they are well camouflaged. In the North Sea and the Mediterranean live, for example, the thornback ray and the common stingray.

Most rays eat animals from the sea floor such as mussels, crabs, worms and small fish. With flat, paving-like teeth they crack hard shells. They track down their prey with fine sense organs that pick up the **electrical signals** of living things. Manta rays, by contrast, are filter feeders and eat plankton. To do so they swim through the water with their mouth wide open.

The **giant manta** is the largest ray and reaches a wingspan of about 7 metres. It can even leap completely out of the water. Stingrays carry a poisonous spine on the tail, with which they defend themselves. Electric rays can produce **electric shocks** in order to paralyse prey or ward off enemies. Sawfishes have a long snout with teeth on both sides.

Some rays lay eggs in tough, leathery egg cases. These cases have tendrils at the corners and are often found on beaches as **mermaid's purses**. Other rays such as stingrays and mantas give birth to live young. At birth the young are already small, finished rays. Many rays have only a few young.

Many ray species are endangered today. They get caught as **bycatch** in fishing nets or are caught for meat and gill plates. Because they reproduce only slowly, their populations recover badly. For divers, encounters with mantas are a special experience. In Swiss zoos and aquariums you can also watch rays.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish whose skeleton consists of cartilage instead of bone, for example sharks and rays.
An opening behind the eyes through which rays take in water for breathing.
The empty egg case of a ray or shark that you find on the beach.
A pointed, often poisonous barb on the tail of the stingrays.

gewusst: The funny “face” that you think you see on the underside of a ray is in truth made of nostrils and a mouth.
The ancient Greeks and Romans already used electric rays to treat headaches with their electric shocks.
In proportion to their body size, manta rays have one of the largest brains of all fish.

teile.einleitung: Przewalski's horse is a wild horse from the steppes of Central Asia and a close relative of our domestic horses. In the wild it had died out by around 1970, but thanks to zoos it now lives free again in Mongolia. Its stocky body and upright mane make it look like a horse from the Stone Age.
wichtigste: Przewalski's horse is a wild horse and a close relative of the domestic horse.
It is named after the Russian explorer Nikolai Przewalski.
It originally lives in the steppes of Mongolia and northern China.
In the wild it was considered extinct from about 1969.
All animals alive today descend from a few zoo animals.
Since 1992 it has been reintroduced into the wild in Mongolia.
It has a short, upright mane and no forelock.

abschnitte.text: Przewalski's horse, at around 1.3 metres at the shoulder, is rather small and strongly built. Its coat is sandy brown to yellowish, the muzzle is pale, and it has a dark **dorsal stripe** along the back. The dark mane stands upright like a brush and is changed every year. Unlike domestic horses, it lacks the forelock between the ears.

The Russian officer and explorer **Nikolai Przewalski** brought back a skull and skin of such a horse from Central Asia around 1879. In 1881 it was described scientifically and named after him. The Mongols call it **takhi**, which means roughly sacred or worthy. Around 1900 a few foals were caught and taken to European zoos.

Hunting, competition with grazing livestock and hard winters caused the wild populations to shrink. In 1969 the last Przewalski's horse was seen in the wild in Mongolia. After that, the survival of the species depended only on animals in zoos. All Przewalski's horses today descend from only about a dozen founder animals, which is why zoos plan breeding very carefully using a **studbook**.

From 1992, zoos and conservation organisations brought Przewalski's horses back to Mongolia, for example to the **Khustain Nuruu** National Park and to the Takhin Tal area. There they now live again in herds with a stallion, several mares and their foals. By now there are again several hundred free-living animals. Reintroduction projects are also under way in China and Kazakhstan.

Przewalski's horses and domestic horses are closely related and can have foals together. Even so there are differences: Przewalski's horse has 66 **chromosomes**, the domestic horse only 64. Genetic studies suggest that the ancestors of Przewalski's horses were once kept by humans over 5,000 years ago. In Switzerland you can watch Przewalski's horses, for example, in the Langenberg Wildlife Park near Zurich.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horse that has not been bred by humans and lives in nature.
A dark stripe along the middle of the back in some horses and donkeys.
When animals bred in captivity are brought back into nature.
A record of all animals of a species in zoos, to avoid inbreeding.

gewusst: In the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power station, free-roaming Przewalski's horses live today.
Przewalski's horse is one of the few animals that had died out in the wild and was successfully brought back.

teile.einleitung: Sawfishes are large rays with a long, flat saw on the snout. With this saw they track down prey and strike with it. Unfortunately they are today among the most heavily threatened sea fishes in the world.
wichtigste: Sawfishes belong to the rays and not to the sharks.
