They share the order Rhinopristiformes with the guitarfishes.
Today people usually distinguish five living species in the genera Pristis and Anoxypristis.
The saw makes up about a quarter to a third of the body length.
Depending on the species, the saw carries about 14 to 37 teeth on each side.
Lost saw teeth do not grow back.
All species are regarded as heavily threatened.

abschnitte.text: Sawfishes have a long, shark-like body, but are **rays**. Their gill slits lie on the underside, whereas in the similar sawshark they lie at the sides. The largest species such as the green sawfish can grow over 7 metres long. In this way they are among the largest fishes of all.

The saw is called the **rostrum** and is an elongated snout made of cartilage. The teeth at the sides developed from modified **skin teeth** and are about equal in size. If a tooth falls out, it is not replaced. The sawshark, by contrast, has teeth of unequal size and a pair of long barbels on the saw, which the sawfish lacks.

On the saw sit thousands of **ampullae of Lorenzini**. These sense organs pick up the weak electric fields that every living thing produces. In this way the sawfish also finds animals that are hidden in the mud. It strikes sideways with the saw into shoals of fish and stuns or spears prey.

Sawfishes live in warm, shallow coastal waters of the tropics and subtropics. Some species also swim far into river mouths and rivers, for example in Australia or in the Amazon region. Young animals often grow up in **mangroves**, where they find protection. They give birth to live young whose saw at birth is still covered by a sheath.

Sawfishes have almost or completely disappeared from many seas. Their saw easily gets caught in **fishing nets**, and saws and fins are traded. The destruction of mangroves also harms them. Today international trade in sawfishes is banned, and in some countries such as Australia and the USA there are protection programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long, saw-like snout of the sawfish.
Sense organs with which sharks and rays pick up electric fields.
Fishes with a skeleton of cartilage instead of bone, such as sharks and rays.
Small, tooth-like scales in the skin of sharks and rays.

gewusst: The saw keeps growing throughout life, but lost teeth remain gaps for ever.
So that the mother is not hurt at birth, the saw of the young is at first soft and sheathed.

teile.einleitung: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly, that is, the young animal that hatches from the egg. Caterpillars eat almost without a break, mostly leaves, and grow very fast as they do so. Later they turn into a pupa and change into a butterfly.
wichtigste: Caterpillars are the larvae of butterflies and moths.
After hatching, many caterpillars first eat their own eggshell.
Caterpillars like best to eat leaves, often only from particular plants.
Caterpillars crawl forwards with many small legs.
Birds like to eat butterfly caterpillars very much.
Some caterpillars protect themselves with hairs and bristles, others with camouflage or warning colours.
From the caterpillar, via the pupa, a butterfly develops, which is called metamorphosis.

abschnitte.text: A caterpillar has a soft, elongated body made of many **segments** and a hard head with strong mouthparts. At the front there are three pairs of true legs, and further back usually up to five pairs of stubby **prolegs** with small hooks. In this way it can hold on well to leaves and branches. Many caterpillars are green, others are brightly patterned, hairy or covered with spines.

Caterpillars are real eating machines and eat mainly **leaves**. Many species are very choosy: the caterpillars of the peacock butterfly and the small tortoiseshell eat almost only nettles, and the cabbage white loves cabbage. Because the skin does not grow with them, a caterpillar has to **moult** several times. Within a few weeks it often becomes a hundred times heavier than when it hatched.

The life of a butterfly has four stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa and adult. When the caterpillar is fully grown, it turns into a **pupa**, also called a chrysalis in butterflies that fly by day. In the pupa its body is completely rebuilt until a butterfly with wings hatches. This complete transformation is called **metamorphosis**.

Caterpillars have many enemies, above all **birds**, which feed their young with them, but also wasps and spiders. Some caterpillars are green or brown and hardly to be told apart from leaves and branches. Others carry **stinging hairs** or bristles that scare off predators. Bright warning colours show that the caterpillar is poisonous or inedible, and some have large eyespots that look like a snake's head.

The caterpillar of the **silk moth** spins a cocoon from a single thread several hundred metres long, from which silk is made. Other caterpillars can do damage, such as the box tree moth, which since about 2007 has been eating box trees bare in Switzerland. The hairs of the **oak processionary moth** can cause an itchy rash in humans. That is why the rule is: better not to touch hairy caterpillars.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
Shedding the old skin that has become too tight.
A resting stage in which the caterpillar rebuilds itself into a butterfly.
The complete transformation of an animal into a quite different shape.

gewusst: Caterpillars have up to several thousand muscles, many more than a human.
Geometer caterpillars have only a few prolegs and move by making a hump, as if they were measuring the ground.
The caterpillar of the spurge hawk-moth eats poisonous plants and so becomes inedible for birds itself.

teile.einleitung: Smoking is a very old method of preserving meat, fish or cheese with smoke and making it flavourful. Even in the Stone Age, people hung their stores over the fire. In Swiss cooking, too, smoking is popular, for example with smoked whitefish or bacon.
wichtigste: Smoking makes food last longer through smoke, drying and salt.
People distinguish cold smoking, warm smoking and hot smoking.
Mostly hardwood such as beech or alder is used.
Substances in the smoke hold back bacteria and give a typical taste.
In the kitchen, whitefish are often fried as a fillet or smoked.
Well-known smoked products are bacon, ham, sausages, smoked fish and smoked cheese.
Heavily smoked foods should be eaten only in moderation.

abschnitte.text: In **smoking**, food is hung or placed in the smoke of slowly smouldering wood. The smoke draws water out of it, colours it golden brown and gives it a spicy aroma. Substances in the smoke, for example **phenols**, slow the growth of bacteria and mould. Usually the food is salted beforehand, which improves how long it keeps.

In **cold smoking**, the temperature is below about 25 degrees and the smoking takes days or weeks, which produces raw ham, bacon or smoked salmon. In warm smoking it is somewhat warmer, for example for sausages. In **hot smoking**, the temperature is 60 to over 90 degrees, and the food is cooked at the same time. This produces, for example, smoked trout, whitefish or mackerel, which can be eaten at once.

People have smoked their food for many thousands of years, probably since they began to use fire. In the past, many farmhouses had a **smoke kitchen** without a chimney, in which sausages and hams hung in the smoke under the ceiling. In this way meat could be kept all winter after the autumn slaughter. Today there are fridges for that, but people smoke mainly for the taste.

In Switzerland there are many smoked specialities. On Lake Constance, Lake Zurich or Lake Lucerne, **smoked whitefish** and trout are popular. Also well known are farmhouse bacon, the Vaudois saucisson and smoked sausages such as the Bernese tongue sausage. Bündnerfleisch, by contrast, is not smoked, but air-dried.

When wood burns, substances are also produced that can be harmful in larger amounts, for example so-called **PAHs**. That is why heavily smoked and charred foods should not be eaten every day. Modern smokehouses filter the smoke and pay attention to the right temperature. Anyone who smokes food at home should use only untreated, dry wood and never varnished or painted wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: A room or cabinet in which food hangs in smoke.
Substances in smoke that hold back bacteria and provide the smoky aroma.
Smoking at a high temperature, in which the food is cooked at the same time.
Short for substances that are produced when things burn and can be unhealthy.

gewusst: The Bückling is a hot-smoked herring.
For a special note, some cooks smoke with wood from fruit trees, juniper or even hay.
Cheese, salt, paprika and tea can also be smoked.

teile.einleitung: The reindeer, in North America called the caribou, is a species of deer that lives in the far north of the Earth. It is perfectly adapted to cold and snow and has been kept as a domestic animal by some peoples for centuries.
wichtigste: The reindeer lives in the tundra and the northern forests of Europe, Asia and North America.
In North America the reindeer is called the caribou.
In the reindeer, both males and females carry antlers.
Its hairs are hollow and insulate superbly against cold.
In winter it finds lichens under the snow with its good sense of smell.
Reindeer can perceive ultraviolet light.
The Sami people in northern Europe traditionally keep herds of reindeer.
The calves are usually born in spring or early summer.

abschnitte.text: A reindeer has a shoulder height of about 90 to 140 centimetres. Depending on subspecies and sex, it weighs about 60 to 300 kilograms. The coat is darker in summer and paler and very dense in winter. Its hairs are **hollow** and filled with air, so they insulate like a down jacket. Legs and ears are rather small and well insulated, so that little heat is lost.

Reindeer live in the **tundra** and in the coniferous forests of the far north, for example in Norway, Finland, Russia, Alaska and Canada. Some caribou herds migrate thousands of kilometres every year. In summer, reindeer often move to higher, windier areas, because there are fewer annoying insects there. Their broad hooves carry them well over snow and soft ground. When they walk you often hear a clicking, which comes from tendons in the foot.

In summer the reindeer eats grasses, herbs, leaves and mushrooms. In winter it feeds mainly on lichens such as **reindeer lichen**. It finds these with its fine sense of smell even under a thick blanket of snow. With its hooves and antlers it scrapes the snow away to get at the food. Lichens give it a lot of energy in the cold season.

The reindeer is the only species of deer in which the females also carry **antlers**. The bulls use them for fights over rank in the rutting season in autumn. After the rut, usually in winter, the bulls shed their antlers, and the females often keep theirs until spring. Reindeer can also see **ultraviolet light**. In this way they can better make out lichens, the urine of enemies or wolves in the white snow.

The calves are usually born in spring or early summer. Shortly after birth they can already stand and run. This is important because the herd soon has to move on. The calves drink their mother's milk for a few months. Enemies such as wolves, wolverines and bears go mainly for young or weak animals.

The **Sami** people in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia have kept herds of reindeer for centuries. These domesticated reindeer provide meat, hide and milk, and in the past served as draught and pack animals. In Siberia, too, several peoples live from reindeer herding. Reindeer are also well known as the animals that pull Santa Claus's sleigh. In Switzerland reindeer do not occur in the wild, but you can see them in some animal parks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for the reindeer in North America.
A treeless, cold landscape in the far north with mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.
Tamed by humans and bred as a domestic animal.
The mating season of deer, in which the males fight over the females.

gewusst: In winter, the eyes of reindeer change colour from golden yellow to blue so that they can see better in the dark.
A reindeer calf can follow its mother already about an hour after birth.
Reindeer are good swimmers and even cross wide rivers on their migrations.

teile.einleitung: The Baltic Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic in the north of Europe. Its water is only slightly salty, which is called brackish water, and so sea animals and freshwater fish live side by side there. So even the perch occurs here, which in Switzerland is known as the ‘Egli’.
wichtigste: The Baltic Sea lies in the north of Europe between Scandinavia and the mainland.
Its water is brackish, that is, only slightly salty.
So sea fish such as herring and cod live there next to freshwater fish such as the perch.
Nine countries border the Baltic Sea.
The Baltic Sea is relatively shallow and has hardly any tides.
Typical mammals are the grey seal, the harbour seal and the harbour porpoise.
Over-fertilisation and lack of oxygen are big problems for the animals of the Baltic Sea.

abschnitte.text: The Baltic Sea lies between Sweden, Finland, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany and Denmark. Through narrow straits near Denmark it is connected with the **North Sea** and so with the Atlantic. On average it is only about 50 metres deep, but at its deepest point over 450 metres. In the north lies the **Gulf of Bothnia**, which often freezes over in winter.

Many rivers bring fresh water into the Baltic Sea, while only a little salty water flows in from the North Sea. That is why its water is **brackish water**, much less salty than the open sea. In the west it is still saltier, in the north and east almost fresh. Such a body of water is equally a challenge for sea animals and freshwater animals.

In the Baltic Sea live sea fish such as **herring**, sprat, cod and flounder. At the same time, in the slightly salty water one finds freshwater fish such as pike and **perch**. Altogether fewer species live in the Baltic Sea than in the North Sea, because many animals cannot cope with the changing salt content. Cod was for a long time an important food fish, but is now heavily overfished.

Three species of seal live in the Baltic Sea, the **grey seal**, the harbour seal and the ringed seal. The only whale that occurs here regularly is the small **harbour porpoise**. In the middle part of the Baltic Sea only a few hundred harbour porpoises are left, and they are severely threatened. Many seabirds such as eider ducks and cormorants spend the winter on the coasts.

Many nutrients get into the Baltic Sea from farming, which is called **over-fertilisation**. Then huge carpets of algae grow, and when they die, the oxygen in the deep water is used up. In such low-oxygen zones hardly any animals can survive. Overfishing, rubbish and shipping also burden the sea.

The Baltic Sea is a young sea that came into being about 10,000 years ago after the last **ice age**. Because the Baltic Sea is almost completely enclosed by land, there are hardly any tides. On its beaches one sometimes finds **amber**, a fossilised tree resin. Many Swiss families spend their holidays on the Baltic coast in Germany or Denmark.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that is saltier than fresh water but less salty than sea water.
A sea that is partly enclosed by land and connected with an ocean.
Too many nutrients in the water, which lead to heavy algal growth.
Fossilised resin of trees that lived millions of years ago.

gewusst: In the Baltic Sea one can find pike and herring in the same water.
Because the water is so slightly salty, the Baltic Sea freezes over more easily than the North Sea.
In some pieces of Baltic amber ancient insects are trapped.

teile.einleitung: The Indian rhinoceros is a large rhinoceros from Asia whose thick skin lies in folds and looks like a knight's armour. It lives in India and Nepal and has just a single horn on its nose. A good hundred years ago it was almost extinct, but thanks to protection measures there are again several thousand animals today.
wichtigste: The Indian rhinoceros lives in Asia, mainly in India and Nepal.
It has only one horn.
Its skin lies in thick folds that look like armour plating.
After the white rhinoceros, it is one of the largest rhinoceros species.
Indian rhinoceroses eat grasses and water plants and are good swimmers.
Today about 4,000 Indian rhinoceroses live in the wild again (as of 2022).
In 1956 the first Indian rhinoceros ever born in a zoo came into the world at Basel Zoo.

abschnitte.text: The Indian rhinoceros is called **Rhinoceros unicornis** in science, which means one-horned rhinoceros. Its grey skin is very thick and lies in deep **skin folds** that look like the plates of a suit of armour. Males can weigh over 2 tonnes. The single **horn** is made of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails, and is usually 20 to 30 centimetres long.

Indian rhinoceroses live in the north of India and the south of Nepal. They like damp **floodplains** with tall grass, swamps and rivers at the foot of the Himalayas. The most animals live in Kaziranga National Park in the Indian state of Assam, which is home to about two thirds of all Indian rhinoceroses. Another important protected area is Chitwan National Park in Nepal.

The Indian rhinoceros is a **herbivore** and eats mainly tall grasses, but also leaves, fruit and water plants. It likes to wallow in mud and bathes in water for hours to cool down. It is also a good swimmer and can even dive. The animals mostly live alone, and only mothers stay with their young for a few years.

A female is pregnant for about 16 months and then gives birth to a single calf. The young one already weighs about 60 kilograms at birth. It stays with its mother for around two to three years. Indian rhinoceroses can live to 40 years and older.

Around 1900 only about 200 Indian rhinoceroses were left, because they had been hunted and their habitat destroyed. Thanks to strictly protected areas and rangers, the population grew again to about 4,000 animals (as of 2022). The greatest danger remains **poaching**, because in some countries people wrongly believe that the horn is a medicine. The Indian rhinoceros is now considered vulnerable, but no longer endangered with extinction.

**Basel Zoo** is known worldwide for its Indian rhinoceroses. In 1956 the first Indian rhinoceros ever born in a zoo came into the world there. Since then many more young animals have grown up in Basel, and some were passed on to other zoos. The zoo takes part in the **breeding programme** that aims to preserve the species in human care.

begriffe.erklaerung: The horn-like substance that rhinoceros horns, hair and fingernails are made of.
Places where the thick skin lies in layers on top of each other.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
Rolling in mud to cool down and to protect against insects.

gewusst: In 1515 the artist Albrecht Dürer made a famous woodcut of an Indian rhinoceros without ever having seen one.
Indian rhinoceroses use shared dung sites, which work like signposts for other rhinoceroses.
Despite its weight, an Indian rhinoceros can run at over 40 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: A saddle is the seat that a rider puts on the back of a horse. It spreads the weight and gives support when riding. Together with the stirrups, the saddle became one of the most important inventions in dealing with horses.
wichtigste: The saddle is the piece of equipment on which you sit on the horse's back when riding.
It spreads the rider's weight evenly over the horse's back.
It is fastened to the horse's belly with a girth.
The rider rests the feet in the stirrups.
There are different saddles, for example for dressage, jumping or Western riding.
A saddle must fit the horse exactly, otherwise it will be in pain.

abschnitte.text: A saddle is a padded seat made of leather or plastic. Inside it has a firm frame, the **saddle tree**. Under the saddle lies a soft blanket that soaks up sweat and prevents chafing. The saddle is placed on the back behind the horse's shoulders.

Important parts are the **seat**, the saddle flaps at the sides and the padding underneath. From the saddle hang the stirrup leathers with the **stirrups**. The girth runs under the horse's belly and holds everything in place. At the front and the back the saddle is slightly raised, so that you do not slip.

In a **dressage saddle** you sit deep with long legs, and in a jumping saddle shorter and further forward. The all-purpose saddle is a compromise for all areas. The Western saddle is large and heavy and has a horn at the front, to which cowboys used to fasten the lasso. For racehorses there are very light saddles that weigh only a few hundred grams.

At first people rode without a saddle or only on blankets. More than 2,000 years ago, riding peoples in Asia used padded saddles. The **stirrups** came from Asia and spread in Europe in about the 6th to 8th century. They gave riders much more support, which was important for knights, for example.

A saddle must be adjusted to the horse's back by a **saddler**, because every horse's back is different. If the saddle presses, the horse can get pain and pressure sores. You should clean the leather regularly and care for it with leather grease. When saddling up, you always check whether the girth is tight enough.

begriffe.erklaerung: The firm frame inside the saddle.
A metal loop in which the rider puts the feet.
A broad strap that holds the saddle on the horse.
A craftsman who makes and adjusts saddles and other leather goods.

gewusst: Camels, donkeys and even elephants can also carry saddles.
With proper care, a good leather saddle can last many decades.

teile.einleitung: The brown hyena, in German Schabrackenhyäne, is a rather rare species of hyena from southern Africa. It has long, shaggy, dark brown fur. On the coast of the Namib it even looks for food on the beach and is therefore also called the beach wolf.
wichtigste: The brown hyena lives only in southern Africa.
It is rather rare and is regarded as near threatened.
Its long, dark brown fur and the pale mane around the neck are typical.
It eats mainly carrion, that is, dead animals, but also fruit, eggs and insects.
On the coast of Namibia it also eats young seals and things washed ashore.
It lives in small clans, but usually looks for its food alone.

abschnitte.text: The brown hyena has long, shaggy **fur** that hangs down over the back like a blanket. That is where the German name Schabracke comes from, an old word for a saddle cloth. The neck and shoulders are paler, and the legs are striped. It weighs about 40 to 45 kilograms and is thus smaller than the spotted hyena.

It lives in dry areas of **southern Africa**, for example in the Kalahari and the Namib Desert. You find it in Namibia, Botswana, South Africa, Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries. It gets by on very little water. On the Atlantic coast it roams the beaches at night.

The brown hyena is above all a **scavenger**. With its fine nose it finds carcasses over long distances. Its strong jaws can even crunch up bones. It also eats fruit such as wild melons, insects and eggs, and on the coast also young **seals** and fishes washed ashore.

Brown hyenas live in groups called a **clan**, usually of up to about a dozen animals. They are out and about mainly at night and mostly look for food alone. The young grow up together in a den. Other members of the clan bring food to the young at the den.

There are only a few thousand adult brown hyenas left. Farmers often kill them because they fear that the hyenas attack their cattle, although they rarely hunt. Traps and poison are also a danger. In **protected areas** such as the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park they are better protected.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that eats dead animals.
A family group of hyenas.
A decorated blanket that is laid under or over a horse's saddle.
A large dry region in southern Africa.

gewusst: Brown hyenas mark their territory with a sticky paste from a gland at the rear.
In the Kalahari the brown hyena can go a long time without drinking water, because it takes in liquid from wild melons and its food.

teile.einleitung: The European robin, in German Rotkehlchen, is a small, plump songbird with an orange-red breast and one of the best-known garden birds in Switzerland. It is often not very shy and comes close to people who are working in the garden. You can see it in winter too, and on many Christmas cards.
wichtigste: The robin is a songbird from the order of the passerines.
Typical are the orange-red breast and throat.
Males and females look the same, and both sing.
It defends its territory with its red breast puffed up.
The nest lies well hidden in dense undergrowth close to the ground.
A female usually lays five to six eggs.
In Great Britain the robin is closely connected with Christmas.

abschnitte.text: The robin is about 14 centimetres long and weighs only around 16 to 22 grams, about as much as five sugar cubes. Face, throat and breast are **orange-red**, the back olive brown and the belly whitish. Males and females can hardly be told apart from the outside. Young robins do not yet have a red breast, but brown-spotted plumage.

Robins live in forests with plenty of undergrowth, in parks, hedges and gardens. They occur in almost the whole of Europe, also in western Asia and in North Africa. In Switzerland the robin is a common **breeding bird**. Many Swiss robins migrate in autumn to the Mediterranean region, while birds from the north spend the winter with us.

Robins eat insects, spiders, worms and small snails. In autumn and winter, berries and seeds are added. They like to wait near people who are digging in the garden, because **worms** and larvae come to light as they dig. In winter they also visit feeding places on the ground.

The robin has a varied, bubbling **song** and sings almost all year round, even in winter. The females also sing, especially when they defend a territory of their own in winter. If a strange robin intrudes, the owner threatens with his red breast puffed up. Robins are astonishingly aggressive in this and sometimes fight fiercely.

The female builds the nest of **moss**, leaves and roots, often in dense undergrowth, on banks or in holes in walls close to the ground. She usually lays five to six eggs and incubates them for about two weeks. The young are fed by both parents. Many pairs breed twice a year, because cats, birds of prey and martens eat many eggs and young birds.

In **Great Britain** the robin is a symbol of Christmas and appears on many Christmas cards. This probably comes from the fact that postmen used to wear red jackets and had the nickname “Robin”, like the bird. In 2015 the British chose the robin in a poll as their favourite bird. In Switzerland too, in winter it is one of the few birds that you can hear singing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest order of birds, which includes almost all songbirds.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.
A bird that builds its nest in an area and raises young there.
All the feathers of a bird together.

gewusst: Robins sometimes even sing at night, when street lamps light up the garden.
On migration, robins find their way partly by the Earth's magnetic field.
In their first weeks, young robins do not yet have a red breast at all.

teile.einleitung: The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland on Earth and lies in the heart of South America. Most of it belongs to Brazil, with smaller parts in Bolivia and Paraguay. Here live more jaguars, caimans and waterbirds than almost anywhere else.
wichtigste: The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland in the world.
Most of it lies in Brazil.
In the rainy season, a large part of the area is flooded.
Particularly many jaguars live in the Pantanal.
Other typical animals are capybaras, spectacled caimans and hyacinth macaws.
Part of the Pantanal has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2000.
Fires and drought threaten the area.

abschnitte.text: The Pantanal lies in the west of **Brazil**, in the states of Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul. Smaller parts belong to Bolivia and Paraguay. It covers around 150,000 square kilometres, which is more than three times the size of Switzerland. The **Paraguay River** flows through the area with many tributaries.

The name Pantanal comes from the Portuguese word pântano, which means swamp. In the **rainy season**, from about November to March, the rivers burst their banks and flood large parts of the plain. In the dry season the water withdraws, leaving lagoons and pools. Many animals then gather at the last watering places, which makes them easy to watch.

One of the densest **jaguar** populations in the world lives in the Pantanal. The jaguars here are especially large and good swimmers, and they even hunt caimans in the water. Other typical animals are the **capybara**, the largest rodent in the world, the spectacled caiman, the giant otter and the marsh deer. In the sky you can see the blue hyacinth macaw and the jabiru, a large stork.

Only a few people live in the Pantanal, and most of the land belongs to large farms. For centuries people here have kept **cattle**, which graze on the grasslands in the dry season. The cattle herders are called Pantaneiros. **Ecotourism** is becoming more and more important, because many travellers come to watch jaguars and other animals.

In 2020, after an extreme drought, huge areas of the Pantanal burned down and many animals died. New fields, dams and waterways also change the natural water balance. In 2000 part of the area was named a **UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site**. Conservation organisations work with farmers so that jaguars and cattle can live side by side.

begriffe.erklaerung: A landscape that is often or permanently under water, such as swamps and bogs.
The time of year with a great deal of rain in tropical regions.
Travel into nature that is as gentle as possible on the environment and the local people.
A particularly valuable natural area that has been recognised by UNESCO.

gewusst: Millions of spectacled caimans live in the Pantanal.
Pantanal jaguars often kill caimans with a single bite to the head.
A capybara can grow as heavy as a grown-up person.

teile.einleitung: Mammals are animals whose young drink their mother's milk. They include animals as different as the elephant, the jaguar, the bat, the whale and also humans. Most have fur and a constant body temperature.
wichtigste: Mammals suckle their young with milk, and that gave them their name.
The elephant, the jaguar, the snow leopard and the Cape buffalo are mammals.
Almost all mammals have hair or fur.
They are warm-blooded, so their body temperature stays almost always the same.
More than 6,000 species are known worldwide.
The largest mammal is the blue whale, and one of the smallest is the Etruscan shrew.
Humans are also mammals.

abschnitte.text: The most important feature is the **mammary gland**: mothers suckle their young with milk. A young snow leopard, for example, drinks only milk in the first weeks. Mammals also have hair, three small bones in the middle ear and a diaphragm for breathing. They are **warm-blooded** and can stay active even in the cold.

The **monotremes** such as the platypus lay eggs, but still suckle their young. The **marsupials** such as the kangaroo and the koala give birth to tiny young, which go on growing in the pouch. The largest group is the placental mammals, in which the young develops for a long time in the mother's belly. They include, for example, elephants, big cats, rodents and monkeys.

Mammals live almost everywhere on Earth. Whales and dolphins live in the sea, bats can fly, and moles dig under the ground. Jaguars hunt in the rainforest, Cape buffaloes roam the savanna, and polar bears live in the polar regions. The largest group of species is the **rodents**, followed by the bats.

The **blue whale**, at up to about 30 metres, is the largest animal that has ever lived. The African elephant is the largest land mammal. The Etruscan shrew weighs only about 2 grams. The cheetah is the fastest land animal and for short bursts reaches about 100 kilometres per hour.

In Switzerland live, among others, red deer, chamois, ibex, fox, badger, marmot and hedgehog. Of **bats** alone there are about 30 species here. Large predators such as the lynx and the wolf have returned in recent decades. The ibex was wiped out in the 19th century and was reintroduced from 1911.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organ in which the mother makes milk for her young.
The body temperature stays the same, whether it is warm or cold.
An organ in the mother's body that supplies the young with food.
Mammals whose young grow up in a pouch on the mother's belly.

gewusst: Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae, the giraffe just like the mouse.
Whales are mammals, and they have to come to the surface of the water to breathe.

teile.einleitung: An ox is a male bovine that has been castrated. Oxen are calmer and easier to lead than bulls. In the past they were indispensable on farms as strong draught animals.
wichtigste: An ox is a castrated male bull.
Through castration the animal becomes calmer and less aggressive.
For thousands of years oxen were harnessed to ploughs and carts as draught animals.
In doing so they wear a wooden yoke on the neck or forehead.
Today oxen are kept mainly for their meat.
In many Swiss villages an inn is called ‘Ochsen’ (‘Ox’).

abschnitte.text: In domestic cattle the male animal able to breed is called a **bull**. If a young bull is castrated, it is called an ox. The female animal is the cow, and a young animal is called a calf. Oxen can no longer father offspring.

In **castration** the testicles are removed or made ineffective. As a result the body produces fewer male hormones. The animal becomes calmer, more peaceable and easier to lead. For work in the field and for life in a herd this was a great advantage.

Thousands of years ago people already harnessed oxen to ploughs and carts. In doing so the animals wear a **yoke**, a curved piece of wood on the neck or on the horns. Oxen are slower than horses, but very strong and tough. Until tractors spread in the 20th century they also pulled ploughs and hay wagons in Switzerland.

Today oxen are kept mainly for **meat production**. Ox meat is regarded as especially tender and well marbled. In some countries of Africa and Asia, however, oxen still work in the fields. Expressions such as ‘oxtail soup’ also recall the long history of these animals.

In many Swiss places there are inns called ‘Ochsen’. Such names date from the time when carters travelled with ox teams. At processions and traditional festivals you can sometimes still see decorated **teams**. Some farms even work with draught oxen again out of pleasure in tradition.

begriffe.erklaerung: An operation after which an animal can no longer father young.
A wooden harness with which draught animals are hitched to a plough or cart.
An animal that pulls loads, carts or ploughs.
Two or more animals that pull a cart together.

gewusst: The musk ox, despite its name, is not a bovine, and is more closely related to sheep and goats.
The letter A probably contains an ox head, because the sign comes from an old picture for ‘ox’.
A well-trained draught ox can pull loads that are heavier than itself.

teile.einleitung: Pill millipedes, in German Saftkugler, are small millipedes that roll up in a flash into a ball when in danger. They belong to the diplopods and live in the leaf litter of our forests. Many people confuse them with pill woodlice.
wichtigste: Pill millipedes belong to the diplopods, a group of the millipedes.
Their special feature is that they can roll up into a ball.
They are mostly only about 1 to 2 centimetres long.
They eat dead leaves and so help to form humus.
For defence they give off a foul-smelling fluid, which is where their German name comes from.
In Switzerland the margined pill millipede is common.

abschnitte.text: Pill millipedes have a domed, glossy **back shell** made of a few broad plates. They are black, brown or spotted and often marked with pale edges. Depending on sex, adult animals have 17 to 19 pairs of legs. So they have far fewer legs than many other millipedes.

When a pill millipede is touched, it rolls itself up in seconds into a firm **ball**. Head and legs then lie protected inside, and on the outside there is only the hard shell. In this way ants or beetles can hardly attack it. In addition, they give off through pores a bitter **defensive fluid** that scares off enemies.

Pill millipedes live in damp deciduous forests, under stones, moss and dead wood. They eat rotting leaves and fungal threads. In doing so they break up the leaves, so that bacteria and fungi can break them down more easily. In this way they help to form fertile **humus**.

Pill millipedes look confusingly similar to the **pill woodlouse**. Woodlice, however, are crustaceans and not millipedes. One difference is the number of back plates: pill millipedes have about 12, pill woodlice more and narrower ones. Pill millipedes also have a large, semicircular shield at the rear end.

In Switzerland and in central Europe live several species of the genus **Glomeris**. Especially common is the margined pill millipede, with pale edges on the plates. You often find it in spring and autumn under leaves in the forest or in the garden. Pill millipedes are harmless and can be watched without danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: Millipedes that carry two pairs of legs on most body rings.
The dark, fertile layer in the soil made of decomposed plant remains.
A small crustacean on land that can also roll up.
The scientific name of the main genus of pill millipedes.

gewusst: Giant pill millipedes in Madagascar can roll up into balls as big as a golf ball.
Pill millipedes can live for several years.

teile.einleitung: The giant isopod, in German Riesenassel, is a crustacean from the deep sea that looks like a gigantic woodlouse. The largest species grows up to 50 centimetres long. It lives on the dark sea floor and eats mainly what sinks down from above.
wichtigste: The giant isopod is a very large isopod that lives on the sea floor.
It is related to the woodlouse and belongs to the crustaceans.
The largest species, Bathynomus giganteus, grows up to 50 centimetres long.
Giant isopods live at depths of about 150 to over 2,000 metres.
They eat mainly dead animals that sink to the sea floor.
Giant isopods can go without food for a very long time.
When in danger they roll up into a ball.

abschnitte.text: Giant isopods form a genus with the scientific name **Bathynomus**. They belong to the **isopods**, a group of the crustaceans. Related to them are the small woodlice that you find under stones and in leaf litter. The best-known species is Bathynomus giganteus. It was described in 1879 by the French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards.

Giant isopods grow up to 50 centimetres long and can weigh over 2 kilograms. Their body is flattened and covered with a hard **shell** made of many segments. They have seven pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae. Their large compound eyes also pick up faint light. The colour is mostly a pale grey to brownish.

Giant isopods live on the sea floor at depths of about 150 to over 2,000 metres. There it is dark and cold, and the water pressure is enormous. The best-known species occurs in the western Atlantic, for example in the Gulf of Mexico and in the Caribbean. Other species live in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Because the **deep sea** is so hard to study, little is yet known about their life.

Giant isopods are mainly **scavengers**. They feed on dead fish, whales and squid that sink to the sea floor. Sometimes they also catch slow animals such as sea cucumbers or sponges. Because food is rare in the deep sea, they really stuff themselves when they find some. After that they can **go hungry** for a very long time.

The female carries her eggs in a brood pouch on the underside of her body. The eggs of the giant isopod are among the largest eggs of any invertebrate sea animals. From them hatch young isopods that already look almost like their parents. There is no larval stage as in many other crustaceans. After that the young only have to grow and moult several times.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small crustacean with a flat body made of many armour plates.
The dark, cold part of the sea below about 200 metres.
An animal that eats dead animals.
When animals of a group grow much larger than their relatives, like the giant isopod in the deep sea.

gewusst: A giant isopod in a Japanese aquarium ate nothing for over five years and went on living anyway.
A giant isopod is about twenty times as long as a woodlouse from the garden.
Giant isopods are among the largest isopods in the world, and most isopod species are only a few millimetres long.

teile.einleitung: Imprinting is a special form of learning in young animals. A newly hatched gosling takes the first moving creature it sees for its mother and follows it everywhere. What is learned in this short window of time often stays for a lifetime.
wichtigste: Imprinting is fast learning in a short, sensitive phase of life.
Goslings take the first moving creature after hatching for their mother.
The window of time for imprinting is called the sensitive period.
What has been imprinted can hardly be changed later.
The Austrian researcher Konrad Lorenz made imprinting famous with greylag geese.
Imprinting occurs mainly in birds that hatch as precocial young.
Fish such as salmon are also imprinted, namely on the smell of their home river.

abschnitte.text: Imprinting is a learning process in which a young animal builds up a bond to a particular living thing or stimulus in a short time. This happens in the **sensitive period**, which often lasts only a few hours or days. Before and after, this kind of learning does not work. What is learned usually sits very firmly and can hardly be undone.

The Austrian behavioural researcher **Konrad Lorenz** raised greylag geese in the 1930s. After hatching, the goslings first saw him and then followed him as if he were a mother goose, even when swimming in the water. One of these geese was called Martina and became famous through his books. For his research, Lorenz received the Nobel Prize in 1973 together with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch.

Geese, ducks and chickens are **precocial birds**, and their chicks can walk shortly after hatching. They have to know quickly whom to follow so that they do not get lost or eaten. In nature the first moving creature is almost always their own mother. Imprinting is therefore a clever shortcut that normally works exactly right.

Besides imprinting on the mother, there are other forms. In **sexual imprinting**, young birds learn what a later partner should look like. Young salmon imprint on the smell of their home stream and find their way back to exactly that place after years in the sea. Some songbirds learn the song of their species in an early phase.

Anyone raising orphaned young birds must take care that they are not imprinted on humans. Otherwise they later seek the company of humans rather than of their own species and can survive poorly in the wild. That is why care centres feed some chicks with **hand puppets** that look like a parent bird. In reintroduction projects, people have even accompanied imprinted birds on their migration routes in microlight aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fast, lasting learning in a short phase in the life of a young animal.
A short period of time in which a particular imprinting is possible.
A young chick of a goose.
Young animals that can walk and leave the nest shortly after birth.

gewusst: Goslings can even be imprinted on wellington boots or a ball if these move during the sensitive period.
Konrad Lorenz was often photographed with a flock of geese waddling along behind him.

teile.einleitung: The red fox, in German Rotfuchs, is the best-known predator in Europe and lives almost everywhere in Switzerland, from the forest to the middle of cities. It is clever, adaptable and easy to recognise by its red coat and the white tip of its tail. It belongs to the canids and so is related to the wolf and the dog.
wichtigste: The red fox belongs to the canids (Canidae).
It is active mainly at dusk and at night.
In most red foxes the tip of the tail is white.
It eats mice, birds, insects, fruit and berries.
With its very good hearing it finds mice even under the snow.
Over short distances it runs at up to about 50 km/h.
Young foxes leave their family in autumn and look for a territory of their own.

abschnitte.text: A red fox is about 60 to 90 centimetres long, plus a bushy tail of around 40 centimetres. It usually weighs 5 to 8 kilograms, about as much as a large cat. The coat is reddish brown, the chest and throat are white, and the **tip of the tail** is usually white too. Its large, pointed ears can hear even the faint rustle of a mouse.

The red fox is the most widespread wild **predator** in the world. It lives in Europe, Asia, North America and North Africa and was even taken to Australia by people. In Switzerland it occurs everywhere, from the Central Plateau up into the Alps. Many foxes today also live in cities such as Zurich, Basel or Bern, where they find food in gardens and parks.

The fox is an **omnivore** and eats whatever it happens to find. Most important are mice, plus birds, insects, earthworms, fruit, berries and scraps. When it hears a mouse under the snow, it jumps high into the air and pounces down with its front paws. This typical jump is called the **mouse pounce**.

Red foxes are mostly out and about at dusk and at night and are very cautious. When they hear people or dogs, they flee quickly and quietly. In snow they place their hind paws exactly in the prints of the front paws, so that the track looks almost like a straight line. This track is called **lacing** in the hunters' language, Schnüren in German.

The mating season, the **rut**, called Ranz in German, is in January and February. In spring the vixen, called the Fähe, gives birth in an underground **den** to usually 4 to 6 young. The young play and tumble a lot with one another and so practise hunting. In autumn most young foxes move away and look for a territory of their own.

Adult foxes have only few natural enemies in Switzerland, such as the lynx, the wolf or the golden eagle. In the past, foxes often passed on the dangerous **rabies**. From 1978, Switzerland was the first country to vaccinate foxes against it with vaccine baits laid out, and it has counted as rabies-free since 1999. Because foxes can carry the fox tapeworm, you should wash berries from near the ground well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female fox, in German Fähe, and the male is called a dog fox.
An underground burrow in which foxes raise their young.
The mating season of foxes in winter, called Ranz in German.
An animal family that includes the wolf, dog and fox.
A dangerous viral disease that can affect animals and people.

gewusst: Foxes can probably use the Earth's magnetic field to aim when doing the mouse pounce.
Foxes bark, scream and chatter and can make over 20 different sounds.
In some Swiss cities there live more foxes per square kilometre than in the countryside.

teile.einleitung: Omnivores, in German ‘Allesfresser’, are animals that eat both plants and meat. Humans, brown bears and wild boar are among them. Because they can eat so many things, they find food almost everywhere.
wichtigste: Animals that eat both meat and plants are called omnivores.
The word comes from Latin: ‘omnis’ means ‘all’, ‘vorare’ means ‘to devour’.
Well-known omnivores are humans, brown bears, wild boar, raccoons and crows.
Omnivores often have teeth that are both sharp and flat.
They can adapt well to new habitats.
Besides omnivores there are plant eaters (herbivores) and meat eaters (carnivores).

abschnitte.text: Omnivores eat both **plant** and animal food. This includes, for example, fruit, seeds, roots, insects, eggs and meat. By contrast, **herbivores** eat only plants and **carnivores** mainly meat. Many omnivores adapt their menu to the season.

Omnivores usually have versatile teeth. At the front sit incisors for biting off, next to them pointed canines for holding. At the back lie broad **molars** with bumps that can grind plants. In humans and in pigs these molars look surprisingly similar.

The **brown bear** eats grass in spring, berries and insects in summer and salmon or nuts in autumn. Wild boar root about for roots, acorns, worms and mice. Crows, raccoons, rats and chimpanzees are also omnivores. Many birds such as the blackbird eat both worms and berries.

Omnivores find food even when something becomes scarce. That is why they can survive in very different habitats. Many even live in cities and eat rubbish, like foxes, crows and rats. This adaptability is called **generalism**.

Many omnivores live in Switzerland, for example wild boar, badger, fox, hedgehog and carrion crow. The brown bear turns up now and then in the canton of Graubünden when it migrates in from Italy. Wild boar can cause great **damage** in fields when they look for maize and potatoes. That is why one should never feed wild animals.

Humans are omnivores by nature. Our ancestors gathered plants and hunted animals. A balanced diet with plenty of plants supplies us with all the important **nutrients**. Some people deliberately choose to live as vegetarians or vegans, which can also be healthy with good planning.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant eater.
A meat eater.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A broad tooth at the back of the mouth for grinding food.

gewusst: Although it counts as a carnivoran, the brown bear often eats more plants than meat.
The giant panda is also a carnivoran, but feeds almost only on bamboo.
Rats eat such a wide variety of things that they occur almost everywhere in the world where people live too.

teile.einleitung: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish with a shimmering blue sail, but it is not a true jellyfish. It is a colony of many specialised individual animals that can only survive together. Its long tentacles contain a strong poison that is very painful even for humans.
wichtigste: The Portuguese man o' war is called Physalia physalis in science.
It belongs to the phylum of cnidarians, the class of hydrozoans and the order of siphonophores.
It is a colony of many individual animals with different tasks.
A gas-filled float, the pneumatophore, keeps it at the surface of the water.
In fully grown animals the float is about 15 to 30 centimetres long.
Its tentacles are usually around ten metres long and full of stinging capsules.
Carl von Linné first described it scientifically in 1758.

abschnitte.text: On top, the float called the **pneumatophore** drifts on the water, usually shimmering transparent blue to violet. In adults it is about 15 to 30 centimetres long and bears a crest that works like a sail. The man o' war cannot swim by itself, and the wind drives it across the sea. Its English name “man o' war” recalls a sailing warship, and the German name Galeere also refers to an old warship.

abschnitte.titel: A colony instead of a single animal
abschnitte.text: The Portuguese man o' war is not a true jellyfish but a **colony**. It consists of many small individual animals, the polyps, all of which arise from a single egg. Some polyps catch prey, others digest the food and still others are responsible for reproduction. None of them can survive alone, but together they work like a single living thing.

Beneath the float hang blue **tentacles**, which are usually about ten metres long, but sometimes grow much longer. They are covered with thousands of stinging capsules, which shoot tiny poison harpoons on contact. In this way the man o' war stuns and kills small fish and crustaceans and pulls them up to the feeding polyps. For humans, contact is extremely painful and can cause welts, fever and difficulty breathing, but deaths are very rare.

The Portuguese man o' war lives in warm seas, mainly in the Atlantic, but also in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Strong wind sometimes drives hundreds of them onto beaches, for example in Spain, Portugal or on the Canary Islands. Even washed-up animals can still sting for a long time, which is why you must never touch them. Some animals are protected against its poison, for example the blue sea slug **Glaucus atlanticus**, which eats the stinging capsules and uses them for itself.

Carl von Linné described the species in 1758 and at first placed it in the genus Holothuria. In 1801 Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck put it in the new genus **Physalia**. The name comes from the Greek word physalis, which means bladder. Today it is counted among the siphonophores, a group of cnidarians that all live in colonies.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gas-filled float with which the man o' war drifts at the surface.
A tiny poison capsule that shoots a thread with poison into the skin on contact.
A community of many connected individual animals that work together like one living thing.
A group of cnidarians made up of colonies of specialised individual animals.
A long catching arm or thread of an animal.

gewusst: There are man o' wars with the sail slanting to the left and to the right, so the wind drives them in different directions.
The little man-of-war fish lives among the poisonous tentacles and is protected from enemies there.
Even a dead, washed-up Portuguese man o' war can still sting painfully.

teile.einleitung: The pelagic zone is the area of open water in a lake or sea, far from the shore and not on the bottom. Here, for example, the whitefish swim in our Swiss lakes. In the sea, the pelagic zone is the largest habitat on the whole Earth.
wichtigste: The pelagic zone is the open-water zone of a body of water.
It lies away from the shore and above the bottom of the water.
The bottom area is called the benthic zone, the shore area the littoral zone.
Plankton and free-swimming animals such as fish live in the pelagic zone.
In Swiss lakes, whitefish mostly swim in open water.
In the sea, the pelagic zone is divided into several zones according to depth.

abschnitte.text: The word pelagic comes from the Greek word “pelagos”, which means “open sea”. It refers to all the water that is not directly at the shore and not at the bottom. The bottom of a body of water is called the **benthic zone**, the shore area the **littoral zone**. The pelagic zone is therefore like a huge, freely floating body of water.

In the sea, the pelagic zone is divided by depth. The top layer, down to about 200 metres, is called the **epipelagic zone**, and there is enough light there for plants. Below it follow the mesopelagic zone down to about 1,000 metres, the pitch-dark bathypelagic zone and, deeper still, the abyssopelagic zone. The deeper you go, the colder and darker it gets, and the water pressure rises sharply.

Two large groups of living things live in the pelagic zone. **Plankton** drifts with the current, and includes tiny algae and small animals such as water fleas. **Nekton** are animals that can actively swim against the current, for example fish, squid and whales. Many animals in the open sea are silvery or transparent, so that they are hard to see.

abschnitte.titel: The pelagic zone in Swiss lakes
abschnitte.text: In large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Geneva or Lake Lucerne there is an extensive pelagic zone. This is where the **whitefish** live, which feed on plankton. Arctic char and lake trout also often hunt in open water. Fishers therefore use floating nets in open water to catch whitefish.

In the upper, bright layer, tiny algae grow that make food using sunlight. They are the start of the **food chain** in open water. Small animals eat the algae, fish eat the small animals, and larger predators eat the fish. Dead living things sink slowly into the depths and feed other animals there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The open-water zone of a lake or sea, away from the shore and the bottom.
The habitat at the bottom of a body of water.
The shore area of a body of water, where light reaches the bottom.
All animals that can swim independently in water, such as fish.

gewusst: By volume, the pelagic zone of the oceans is the largest habitat on our planet.
Many animals from the depths rise to the top every night to feed and dive down again in the morning.
Some deep-sea animals in the dark pelagic zone make light themselves.

teile.einleitung: The pterostigma, in German called Flügelmal, is a small, dark spot on the front edge of the wings of dragonflies and many other insects. It looks like a blob of paint, but it has an important job. It stabilises the wing when the insect flies fast.
wichtigste: The pterostigma is a thickened, usually dark patch near the wing tip.
In German it is called Flügelmal, meaning wing mark.
It occurs in dragonflies, bees, wasps and other insects.
The wing mark is slightly heavier than the rest of the wing.
It stabilises the wing in fast flight and prevents fluttering.
In many dragonfly species, its colour helps to identify the species.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek: **pteron** means wing and stigma means mark or spot. The pterostigma is a small cell on the front edge of the wing, just before the tip. It is filled with blood fluid and has a thicker wall, which is why it looks darker. Dragonflies have a wing mark on each of their four wings.

In fast wingbeats, thin wings can start to tremble and **flutter**. This costs energy and makes the flight unsteady. The wing mark acts like a small counterweight at the wing tip. In the 1970s a Swedish researcher showed that dragonflies without a wing mark start to flutter at a lower speed.

Dragonflies can fly forwards, backwards and sideways and can hover in the air. Large species such as the **emperor dragonfly** reach speeds of over 30 kilometres per hour. Each of their four wings can move independently. The pterostigma helps to steer the wings calmly and precisely.

The colour, shape and length of the wing mark are slightly different in each dragonfly species. In some it is black, in others brown, yellow, red or even two-coloured. Experts use these differences to **identify** species. Around 75 species of dragonfly live in Switzerland, many of them at ponds, bogs and slow streams.

Technology also knows the problem of fluttering, for example in aircraft wings or rotor blades. Engineers prevent it, among other things, with extra weights at certain places. The principle is therefore similar to the dragonfly's wing mark. Learning from nature for technology is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark, heavier patch on the front edge of an insect's wing, also called the wing mark.
Uncontrolled trembling of a wing at high speed.
The science that uses ideas from nature for technology.
Predatory insects with four long wings and large eyes.

gewusst: Dragonflies existed long before the dinosaurs, and some ancient dragonflies had a wingspan of over 60 centimetres.
Bees and wasps also have a wing mark, but it is usually smaller and harder to see than in dragonflies.

teile.einleitung: Orb-weaver spiders are a large family of spiders that build artful, round capture webs. The best-known example is the garden spider, whose web you often see in the garden in late summer. The shape of this web is called an orb web, because it looks like a wheel with spokes.
wichtigste: Orb-weaver spiders build round webs with spokes and a spiral.
The shape of the garden spider's web is called an orb web.
There are over 3,000 species of orb-weaver spiders worldwide.
The capture spiral is covered with sticky droplets of glue.
Many orb-weaver spiders eat their old web and build a new one every day.
Well-known species in Switzerland are the garden cross spider and the wasp spider.
The orb-weaver spiders of Switzerland are harmless to humans.

abschnitte.text: Like all spiders, orb-weavers have eight legs and a body made up of a front part and an abdomen. The abdomen is often thick and rounded and in many species bears a pattern. The **garden cross spider** has a white cross of spots on its back, and the **wasp spider** has yellow and black stripes like a wasp. The females are mostly much larger than the males.

abschnitte.titel: How an orb web is made
abschnitte.text: First the spider stretches a **bridge thread**, which the wind often carries from branch to branch. Then it builds a frame and pulls many **spokes** to the centre, the so-called hub. After that it lays a dry auxiliary spiral and finally the sticky **capture spiral**. For a whole web, a garden spider often needs less than an hour.

Orb-weaver spiders catch mainly flying insects such as flies, mosquitoes and wasps. The spider sits in the middle of the web or hides beside it and holds a **signal thread**. When an insect struggles, it feels the vibrations at once, bites and stuns it with **venom**. Then it wraps the prey in silk and eats it later.

Spider silk is made in **silk glands** in the abdomen and comes out of the spinnerets. In proportion to its weight it is stronger than steel and at the same time very stretchy. Many orb-weaver spiders eat their old web and so reuse the valuable protein for the new web. The wasp spider also weaves a zigzag band into the web, which is called a **stabilimentum**.

Several dozen species of orb-weaver spiders live in Switzerland. Most often you see the garden cross spider in gardens, hedges and on house walls, especially in **late summer and autumn**, when the animals are fully grown. The wasp spider lives in sunny meadows and has spread strongly in recent decades. Orb-weaver spiders are useful because they catch many mosquitoes and flies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round spider web with spokes and a spiral in the middle.
Small organs on the abdomen from which the silk threads come.
A conspicuous zigzag band of silk that some spiders weave into the web.
The centre of the web, where all the spokes meet.

gewusst: Not only orb-weaver spiders build orb webs, some species from other spider families do too.
After mating, the males of the wasp spider are often eaten by the much larger female.
Morning dew makes orb webs especially easy to see in autumn, because the drops glitter on the threads.

teile.einleitung: The bobcat, in German Rotluchs, is a small wild cat from North America and a close relative of our Eurasian lynx. It is clearly smaller than the lynx and has a short stub of a tail. Its English name “bobcat” means roughly a cat with a bobbed tail.
wichtigste: The bobcat is one of four lynx species.
It lives in many regions of North America, from southern Canada to Mexico.
It is smaller than the Eurasian lynx.
Its tail is short and black on top at the tip.
It hunts mainly hares, rabbits and rodents.
The bobcat is adaptable and not threatened.

abschnitte.text: The bobcat is about twice as big as a house cat and usually weighs between 6 and 13 kilograms. Its coat is yellow-brown to reddish with dark spots and stripes. Typical are the small **ear tufts** and the ruff of fur on its cheeks. Its short **stub tail** is white on the underside and black on top at the tip.

The bobcat lives in North America, from southern Canada across almost the whole of the USA to Mexico. It occurs in forests, swamps, semi-deserts, mountains and even on the edge of cities. In this it is much more adaptable than the other lynx species. In the far north with deep snow, by contrast, lives its relative, the **Canada lynx**.

The bobcat is a **predator** and hunts mainly hares and rabbits. It also eats mice, squirrels, birds and sometimes young deer. It sneaks up quietly or lies in wait in hiding and then pounces in a flash. It is mostly active at **dusk** and at night.

Bobcats are loners and mark their territory with urine, droppings and scratch marks. Only at the mating season in winter and spring do males and females meet. In a sheltered den, the female gives birth to usually two to four young. The young stay with the mother for a few months and learn hunting from her.

Worldwide there are four lynx species: the **Eurasian lynx**, the Canada lynx, the Iberian lynx from Spain and Portugal and the bobcat. The Eurasian lynx is the largest of them and can weigh over 25 kilograms. The bobcat is the smallest species and has the shortest ear tufts. All lynxes have short tails and long legs.

In Switzerland no bobcat lives, but the Eurasian lynx. This had been wiped out in the 19th century and was **reintroduced** from 1971. Today a few hundred lynx live again in the Jura and in the Alps. The bobcat can be seen here only in some zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tufts of hair at the tips of the lynx's ears.
An animal that mostly lives alone.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
An area that an animal claims for itself and defends.

gewusst: The English name “bobcat” comes from the short tail that looks as if it had been cut off.
Bobcats are good climbers and often flee up trees when in danger.

teile.einleitung: The red wood ant is one of the best-known ants in Europe and builds the large anthills that you see in the forest. In one nest live at least several thousand, and in large nests even hundreds of thousands of ants together. In Switzerland it is protected, because it is so important for the forest.
wichtigste: The red wood ant builds dome-shaped mounds of needles and small twigs.
Beneath the mound lies a nest with many tunnels and chambers.
It eats other insects and the sweet honeydew of aphids.
For defence it sprays formic acid.
Wood ants are useful because they eat many pests.
In Switzerland the red wood ant is protected by law.
The mound uses the warmth of the sun to keep the nest warm.

abschnitte.text: Workers of the red wood ant are about 4 to 9 millimetres long, and the queens somewhat larger. Head and abdomen are dark brown to black, and the chest is **reddish brown**. Wood ants have no sting. Instead they can spray **formic acid** from the abdomen at attackers and in addition bite with their jaws.

The visible mound is made of spruce needles, small twigs, bits of resin and plant remains. It is usually **dome-shaped** and can grow over a metre high. Beneath it the nest, with many tunnels and chambers, reaches deep into the ground. The ants open and close entrances in order to regulate warmth and moisture.

In spring, many workers bask in the sun on the mound. With their warmed-up bodies they carry the **warmth** into the inside of the nest. The sloping dome also catches a lot of sunlight. In this way it stays warm enough inside for eggs, larvae and pupae to develop well.

Wood ants hunt caterpillars, beetles, flies and other insects. Very important too is the **honeydew**, a sweet liquid that aphids excrete. The ants look after the aphids almost like a herd and protect them from enemies. On their ant trails they carry large amounts of food into the nest every day.

A large colony can capture a great many insects in one day, including pests that weaken trees. Wood ants also spread plant seeds and loosen the soil. They are themselves food for animals such as the black woodpecker, the green woodpecker and the **capercaillie**. That is why they are sometimes called the health police of the forest.

In Switzerland, the mound-building wood ants are under **nature protection**. You may not destroy or damage their nests or take ants from them. They are endangered mainly by forestry work, road building and the loss of sunny forest edges. Anyone who finds a nest should therefore watch it only from a distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sharp liquid that wood ants spray in defence.
A sweet sap that aphids excrete and that ants like to eat.
The female in the nest who lays the eggs.
An ant that builds, looks for food and cares for the young, but lays no eggs.

gewusst: A wood ant nest can be run by several queens at the same time.
Birds sometimes sit on anthills on purpose, so that the formic acid drives parasites out of their plumage.

teile.einleitung: Reptiles, in German also called Kriechtiere, are cold-blooded vertebrates with a dry, scaly skin. They include turtles, crocodiles, lizards and snakes. They already lived in the time of the dinosaurs and today occur almost everywhere in the world.
wichtigste: Reptiles are also called Kriechtiere in German, meaning creeping animals.
They are cold-blooded, and their body temperature adapts to the surroundings.
That is why lizards like to bask on warm stones.
Their skin is covered with horny scales or horny plates.
Most reptiles lay eggs with a shell, and a few give birth to live young.
Reptiles do not feed their young with milk, and they are not mammals.
In Switzerland live almost 20 native species of reptile.

abschnitte.text: Reptiles are **vertebrates**, so they have a backbone like fish, birds and mammals. Their skin is dry and covered with **horny scales**, which protect against drying out. Because the skin does not grow with them, many reptiles shed their skin regularly. They breathe with lungs, even when they live in water like turtles. Worldwide, over 11,000 species are known.

The reptiles include the **turtles** with their hard shell. Crocodiles, alligators and gharials are the largest reptiles alive today. The largest group are the squamates, with lizards, geckos, iguanas and snakes. Then there is the tuatara from New Zealand, which looks like a living fossil. The dinosaurs also belonged to this animal relationship, and the birds descend from them.

Reptiles are **cold-blooded**, that is, their body temperature depends on the surroundings. In the morning, lizards lie in the sun to warm up and become mobile. If it gets too hot, they creep into the shade. In winter, reptiles fall into a cold torpor and hide frost-free in the ground. Because they do not have to produce heat themselves, they need much less food than mammals.

Most reptiles lay eggs with a leathery or hard **shell**. The grass snake, for example, likes to lay its eggs in warm compost heaps. A few species such as the slow worm or the common lizard give birth to live young. The young mostly already look like small versions of their parents. In many turtles and crocodiles, the temperature in the nest decides whether males or females hatch.

In Switzerland live almost 20 native species. They include lizards such as the **sand lizard**, the wall lizard and the common lizard, as well as the slow worm, a lizard without legs. Among the snakes there are harmless colubrids such as the grass snake and the venomous vipers, the adder and the asp viper. The only native turtle is the European pond turtle. Many of these species are endangered because their habitats such as dry-stone walls and wetlands are disappearing.

All native reptiles are protected in Switzerland. You may not catch, kill or disturb them. In the garden, piles of stones, dry-stone walls, piles of leaves and a pond help. Cats are a great danger for lizards. Anyone who sees a snake is best off leaving it in peace and watching it from a distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body temperature changes with the temperature of the surroundings.
The German word for reptiles.
Shedding the old skin when the animal grows.
A state in winter in which cold-blooded animals rest almost motionless.

gewusst: The slow worm looks like a snake, but is a lizard without legs.
Some lizards can drop their tail when in danger, and it then wriggles for a while.
Birds are the closest living relatives of the crocodiles.

teile.einleitung: Parthenogenesis, also called virgin birth, is reproduction without fertilisation. A new living thing develops from an unfertilised egg cell, with no male at all. In aphids this happens very often in summer.
wichtigste: Parthenogenesis means virgin birth.
In it, an offspring arises from an unfertilised egg cell.
Aphids often multiply by parthenogenesis in summer.
In honeybees, the males, the drones, develop from unfertilised eggs.
Water fleas, stick insects and some lizards can also reproduce this way.
The Geneva naturalist Charles Bonnet observed virgin birth in aphids in the 18th century.
In mammals, parthenogenesis does not occur in nature.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: parthenos means virgin and genesis means origin. Normally in reproduction an **egg cell** and a sperm cell fuse. In **parthenogenesis**, however, the egg cell goes on developing without fertilisation. The offspring therefore have only the mother's genes and are often very similar to her.

**Aphids** are the best-known examples of virgin birth. In spring and summer the females give birth to live daughters without any males, and these sometimes already carry the next generation inside them. In this way huge colonies build up in a short time on roses or beans. Only in autumn do males appear again, and the females lay fertilised eggs that survive the winter.

In the **honeybee**, the queen decides whether an egg is fertilised. Fertilised eggs become females, that is, workers or queens. Unfertilised eggs hatch into the males, which are called **drones**. Many stick insects and water fleas also reproduce wholly or at times without males.

Among some lizards there are species made up only of females, for example certain whiptail lizards in North America and rock lizards in the Caucasus. In 2006, Komodo dragons in two English zoos had offspring even though they had never had contact with a male. Virgin birth has also been observed in sharks in aquariums and in some snakes. In **mammals** it does not occur in nature.

Around 1740 the Geneva naturalist **Charles Bonnet** raised a single aphid completely shielded from others. It still had many young, and so Bonnet recognised virgin birth. His observation was a sensation in science at the time. He is therefore regarded as one of the discoverers of parthenogenesis.

The great advantage is that the animals can multiply very quickly, because every animal has offspring. A single female can even found a new colony on her own. The disadvantage is that the genes hardly mix and the offspring are very similar. As a result, they are less able to **adapt** to new diseases or changes in the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for parthenogenesis, reproduction without fertilisation.
The female reproductive cell from which a new living thing can develop.
The fusing of an egg cell and a sperm cell.
A male honeybee.

gewusst: In aphids, a baby can already carry its own daughters inside it while still in its mother's body.
Some species of whiptail lizards are made up only of females.
A drone has a mother but no father.

teile.einleitung: The red-eared slider, in German Rotwangen-Schmuckschildkröte, is a freshwater turtle from North America with a striking red stripe behind each eye. In the past it was sold in its millions as a pet. Many animals were later released and today are a problem for native nature in Europe.
wichtigste: The red-eared slider comes from North America.
Its mark is a red patch behind each eye.
It lives in calm, warm waters and likes to bask.
It can live for several decades.
In the past it was a very popular pet.
Released turtles can displace native species and pass on diseases.
In the EU it now counts as an invasive species.

abschnitte.text: The red-eared slider has an olive green to brown **shell** with yellow lines. Behind each eye sits a broad red stripe, the red cheek, which gives it its German name. The females grow larger and reach a shell length of up to about 28 centimetres. The males are smaller and have very long claws on the forelegs.

Originally it lives in the area of the **Mississippi** in the USA and in the north-east of Mexico. There it inhabits ponds, lakes, swamps and slow-flowing rivers with a soft bottom. It loves places with water plants and tree trunks on which it can bask. As a **cold-blooded** animal, it needs the sun to warm its body.

The turtle is an **omnivore**. Young animals eat mainly insects, snails, tadpoles and small fish, older ones more water plants. In cold regions it hibernates in torpor on the bottom of the water. With good care it can live to 30 years and older.

From the 1950s, millions of tiny baby turtles were sold all over the world. Many buyers did not know that the animals grow large and live for decades. That is why numerous turtles were **released** in ponds and lakes. The EU banned imports in 1997 and today lists it on its list of invasive species.

Released sliders eat spawn, tadpoles, insects and small fish. They can displace native species and pass on **diseases**. Especially endangered is the **European pond turtle**, the only native turtle in Switzerland, which is very rare anyway. Both species compete for basking places and food.

In Switzerland it is forbidden to release alien animals into the wild. Anyone who can no longer keep a turtle should turn to an animal shelter or a **rescue centre** for reptiles. Before buying, you should think carefully about whether you can really look after an animal for many decades. Freshwater turtles also need a large tank with a basking place and a heat lamp.

begriffe.erklaerung: An alien animal or plant species that spreads and harms native species.
The body temperature adapts to the surroundings.
A hard casing of bony plates that protects the turtle's body.
A place where animals that have been handed in or found are cared for.

gewusst: In many turtles, the temperature in the nest decides whether a male or a female hatches from an egg.
In courtship, males wave their long claws in front of the female's face.

teile.einleitung: Poikilotherm means cold-blooded: the body temperature of such an animal depends on its surroundings. Fish such as the lake trout, but also frogs, lizards and insects, are poikilotherms. When it is cold, they become slow, and when it is warm, they are nimble.
wichtigste: Poikilothermic animals are cold-blooded.
Their body temperature depends on the temperature of the surroundings.
In the lake trout, body temperature depends on the water temperature.
Fish, amphibians, reptiles and most invertebrates are poikilotherms.
Birds and mammals, by contrast, are warm-blooded.
Cold-blooded animals need much less food than warm-blooded ones.

abschnitte.text: The word **poikilotherm** comes from Greek: “poikilos” means changing and “thermos” means warm. A poikilothermic animal has no fixed body temperature, and it rises and falls with the surroundings. The opposite is called **homeothermic** or warm-blooded, like us humans at about 37 degrees. Instead of poikilotherm, people also often say ectothermic, because the heat comes from outside.

The **lake trout** lives in large Swiss lakes such as Lake Geneva, Lake Constance or Lake Lucerne. Because it is cold-blooded, it has almost the same temperature as the water around it. In the cold winter it is therefore less active and eats less. Trout need cool, oxygen-rich water, and waters that are too warm become dangerous for them.

All **fish** are cold-blooded, as are amphibians such as frogs and newts, and reptiles such as lizards, snakes and turtles. Insects, spiders, snails and worms are also poikilothermic. Many of them can, however, influence their temperature through their **behaviour**. A sand lizard, for example, basks on a warm stone in the morning before it goes hunting.

Because they do not have to produce their own heat, cold-blooded animals need much less **energy** and food. A snake can go for weeks without food after a large meal.
