The disadvantage: in the cold they become slow and can hardly flee or hunt. That is why fewer reptiles and amphibians live in cold regions than in warm ones.

In winter, many cold-blooded animals in Switzerland fall into a **cold torpor**. Frogs hibernate in the mud at the bottom of ponds, and lizards and snakes in holes in the ground or piles of stones. Their bodies then work very slowly until it gets warm again in spring. Fish stay active in winter, but much calmer, because the water at the bottom of a lake usually gets no colder than about 4 degrees.

begriffe.erklaerung: Cold-blooded, that is, with a body temperature that depends on the surroundings.
Warm-blooded, with an almost constant body temperature.
An animal that gets its heat mainly from outside.
A state in which a cold-blooded animal becomes almost motionless in the cold.

gewusst: Fish that live in the Arctic Ocean have special substances in their blood that work like antifreeze.
A cold-blooded animal needs only a fraction of the food of a mammal of the same size.
Bumblebees can shiver with their flight muscles and so warm themselves up, even though they are insects.

teile.einleitung: Roe, in German Rogen, is the technical term for the eggs of fish while they are still in the female's belly or have just been taken out. Depending on the species, a female fish can carry from a few hundred to many millions of such eggs. Roe is also known as a delicacy, for example as caviar.
wichtigste: Roe is the name for the eggs of fish.
A female fish with eggs is sometimes called a Rogner in German.
The sperm fluid of male fish is called milt, and the male is called a milter, in German Milchner.
Fish eggs that have been laid in the water are called spawn.
Some fish lay millions of eggs at once.
Salted roe from the sturgeon is called caviar.
Roe contains a lot of protein and healthy fats.

abschnitte.text: **Roe** is the word for the eggs of fish. They form in the **ovary** of the female and lie there close together as small beads. A female carrying roe is called a Rogner in German. The male is called a Milchner, meaning milt bearer, because his sperm fluid looks milky white and is called Milch, or milt. As soon as the eggs have been laid in the water, people usually speak of spawn.

Most fish lay their eggs in the water, which is called **spawning**. At the same time the male releases his milt over them, and so the eggs are fertilised. From the fertilised eggs develop larvae, which at first live off a yolk sac. In trout in Swiss streams, this takes several weeks in the cold winter water. Only a tiny part of the eggs later becomes an adult fish.

The number of eggs varies greatly among fish species. A brown trout lays, depending on size, a few hundred to a few thousand eggs. A carp can have several hundred thousand eggs. The cod even lays several million eggs. Those that lay many eggs mostly do not care for their offspring, because the sheer number secures the **survival** of the species.

Salted roe from the **sturgeon** is called **caviar** and is among the most expensive foods in the world. Because wild sturgeon are heavily endangered, caviar today comes almost only from farms. Cheaper is the orange roe of salmon or trout. In Japan, people like to eat salmon roe on sushi. In Mediterranean countries, dried roe of the grey mullet is sold as bottarga.

In Switzerland too there are fish farms that obtain roe. For some years, caviar has even been produced in Switzerland from sturgeon farms. In **fish hatcheries**, the roe is taken from lake trout, whitefish and other fish and fertilised. The young fish are later released into lakes and rivers. In this way the cantons help to strengthen fish stocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs of a fish.
The sperm fluid of male fish.
The eggs of fish or amphibians that have been laid in the water.
Salted roe from the sturgeon.

gewusst: The ocean sunfish can carry hundreds of millions of eggs, more than almost any other fish.
A salmon egg, at about half a centimetre, is much larger than the tiny eggs of many sea fish.
In some fish such as the seahorse, the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch.

teile.einleitung: A pack, in German Rudel, is a group of animals that live closely together and hunt, migrate or raise their young together. Best known is the wolf pack, but with dogs, lions or deer too, people speak of packs. In a pack there is often a clear order of who has which role.
wichtigste: A pack is a group of closely living animals.
Wolves, dogs and lions live in packs.
A group of deer or chamois is also called a pack in German.
A wolf pack is usually a family of parents and their young.
In many packs there is a ranking order.
The ranking order is a social sequence of who submits to whom.
Wolf packs have been living in Switzerland again since 2012.

abschnitte.text: A **pack** is a group of animals of one species that stay together for a longer time. The word is used mainly for predators such as wolves, dogs and lions. In hunters' language, however, people also speak of packs with red deer and chamois. For other animals there are words of their own, for example herd for cattle, sounder for wild boar or shoal or flock for fish and birds.

A wolf pack usually consists of a **pair of parents** and their young from the last one to two years. Often there are about five to ten animals. The parents lead the pack, and as a rule only they have young. When the young wolves are adult, they leave the pack and look for a partner and a territory of their own.

In a pack, wolves can also bring down large animals such as deer, which a single wolf could hardly manage. They work together, drive the prey and take turns. **Lions** also hunt together, and usually the females take on the hunt. The pack also defends its **territory** against strange members of its species.

In many animal groups there is a **ranking order**, that is, a sequence of who submits to whom. It regulates, for example, who eats first or gets the best resting place. In this way there does not have to be constant fighting, because each animal knows its place. In the past, people spoke of the “alpha animal” in the wolf, but today researchers know that in free packs it is usually simply the parents who lead.

Dogs descend from the wolf and are also **social animals**. When a dog lives together with people, the family becomes a kind of group for it. It needs clear rules, attention and activity in order to feel well. If a dog is often left alone, it can become lonely and restless.

After the wolf had been wiped out in Switzerland, it returned from Italy from 1995. In 2012 the first pack formed on the **Calanda**, between Graubünden and St Gallen. Since then the number of packs has grown strongly and stood at several dozen around 2024. Because wolves also kill sheep, there is much discussion in Switzerland about how to deal with wolf packs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals living closely together, for example wolves.
A social sequence of who submits to whom in a group.
An area that a group of animals claims for itself.
An animal that likes to live, and mostly lives, in groups.

gewusst: Wolves howl to call their pack together and to show other packs where their territory is.
A wolf pack can have a territory of over 200 square kilometres, larger than the canton of Zug.

teile.einleitung: Baboons are large, strong monkeys that live mainly in Africa. Because of their long, dog-like muzzle they are also called dog-faced monkeys. They live in large groups and are very clever.
wichtigste: Baboons make up the genus Papio and belong to the Old World monkeys.
Most baboon species live in Africa, and one species also on the Arabian Peninsula.
Because of their long muzzle they are also called dog-faced monkeys.
Baboons spend most of the day on the ground.
They live in groups with several males and many females with young.
A female usually has only one young at a time.
In the wild, baboons live to about 20 to 30 years.

abschnitte.text: Baboons have a strong body, long arms and legs and a long, dog-like **muzzle**. The males are clearly larger than the females and have long, sharp **canine teeth**. On the rump, baboons have bare, hardened sitting pads, on which they can sit comfortably. In females, the skin on the rump swells and turns red around ovulation, which shows the males that they are ready to mate.

Baboons live in savannas, steppes, semi-deserts and rocky mountains. Well-known species include the **olive baboon**, the chacma baboon, the yellow baboon, the Guinea baboon and the **hamadryas baboon**. The hamadryas baboon lives in north-east Africa and on the Arabian Peninsula, and the males wear a silvery-grey mane like a cloak. Where it is dry, baboons dig for water in dried-up riverbeds.

Baboons are **omnivores** and not fussy. They eat grasses, roots, seeds, fruit and tubers, but also insects, eggs and sometimes small animals. With their skilful hands they dig food out of the ground. If they live near settlements, they get used to human food and sometimes raid rubbish bins, fields or even cars.

Most baboon species live in groups called **troops**, with several males and many females with their young. In the group there is a clear pecking order. The animals groom each other's fur, which is called **grooming** or picking lice, and it strengthens friendships. If an enemy such as a leopard appears, the group defends itself together, especially the strong males.

A female baboon is pregnant for about six months and usually has a single young. The newborn has dark fur and at first clings to its mother's belly. Later it rides along on her back, like a little jockey. Only after several years is a young baboon fully grown.

In ancient Egypt the hamadryas baboon was regarded as a sacred animal of the god **Thoth**, the god of wisdom and writing. Today baboons live in many zoos, including in Europe. In Africa they sometimes come into conflict with farmers because they raid fields. Most baboon species are currently not considered seriously threatened, but in some places they are losing their habitat.

begriffe.erklaerung: Monkeys from Africa and Asia whose nostrils lie close together and point downwards.
Thick, hard cushions of skin on the rump on which baboons sit.
The name for a group of baboons that lives and moves around together.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.

gewusst: Baboons communicate with barks, grunts and screams, but also with gestures such as yawning, which shows their large canine teeth.
A male baboon can grow twice as heavy as a female.
At night baboons like to sleep on rocks or tall trees, where they are safe from predators.

teile.einleitung: The tufted duck, in German Reiherente, is a black and white diving duck with a funny tuft of feathers on the back of its head. In winter you can see it in the thousands on Swiss lakes, where it dives for mussels. It gets its German name from the tuft, which is reminiscent of the plumes of a heron.
wichtigste: The tufted duck is a diving duck that dives under water for food.
The male is black with white flanks and has yellow eyes.
On the back of its head it carries a hanging tuft of feathers.
It eats mainly small mussels, snails and insect larvae from the bottom of the water.
In winter many tufted ducks come from northern and eastern Europe to Swiss lakes.
Switzerland is an important wintering area for this duck.

abschnitte.text: The tufted duck is about 40 to 47 centimetres long and so somewhat smaller than a mallard. The **male** is glossy black with bright white flanks and has golden yellow eyes. The female is dark brown with paler sides and has a shorter tuft. Typical of both is the **tuft of feathers**, which hangs down at the back of the head.

The tufted duck belongs to the **diving ducks** and can dive especially well. It usually dives several metres deep, sometimes deeper, and often stays under water for half a minute. On the bottom it searches for small **mussels**, snails, small crustaceans and insect larvae. Unlike dabbling ducks such as the mallard, it has to run across the water first in order to take off.

An important food of the tufted duck is the **zebra mussel**, also called the three-cornered mussel. This small mussel was introduced into Swiss lakes in the 1960s and multiplied strongly. Since then, far more tufted ducks spend the winter in Switzerland than before. The ducks swallow the mussels whole and crack the shells in their strong stomach.

Tufted ducks breed in large parts of northern and central Europe and Asia, especially in Scandinavia and Russia. In autumn many move south and west into areas with ice-free lakes. In Switzerland you can watch them in winter in large flocks on **Lake Constance**, Lake Geneva and Lake Neuchâtel. A few pairs also breed in Switzerland, mostly on quiet shores with dense vegetation.

Because so many tufted ducks live on Swiss lakes in winter, Switzerland has a special **responsibility** for this species. Several lakes and river stretches are protected as waterbird and **migratory bird reserves**. There the birds are supposed to be able to rest and feed undisturbed. Disturbance by boats or drones costs the ducks a lot of energy, which they urgently need in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A duck that dives completely under water to look for food.
A duck that only dabbles, that is, puts its head and neck into the water.
A small, striped mussel that has been introduced into many lakes.
An area in which migratory birds spend the cold season.

gewusst: In winter, tens of thousands of tufted ducks can gather on a single Swiss lake.
The closely related scaup looks similar, but has a grey back and no tuft.
Tufted ducks often sleep on the water, with the head tucked into the plumage on the back.

teile.einleitung: The large kangaroos, in German Riesenkängurus, are the biggest kangaroos and belong to the marsupials of Australia. They hop on their powerful hind legs and carry their young in a pouch on the belly. They include four large species, among them the red kangaroo.
wichtigste: The large kangaroos include four large kangaroo species.
The red kangaroo is the largest marsupial in the world.
Large kangaroos live in Australia.
They get around with big leaps on their hind legs.
The young one grows up in its mother's pouch.
The strong tail serves as a support and for balance.
Large kangaroos eat grasses and herbs.

abschnitte.text: The large kangaroos include four large species. The **red kangaroo** lives in the dry areas in the interior of Australia. The eastern grey kangaroo and the western grey kangaroo live in forests and grassland in the east and west. The fourth species is the antilopine kangaroo in the north of Australia. All belong to the kangaroo family, which exists only in Australia and New Guinea.

A fully grown male red kangaroo can, standing upright, be about as tall as an adult human. It then weighs up to about 85 kilograms. The females are clearly smaller and lighter. Large kangaroos have long, strong **hind legs**, short forelegs and a thick, muscular tail. They can turn their long ears one at a time in order to locate sounds.

abschnitte.titel: Hopping as a way of moving
abschnitte.text: Large kangaroos hop on both hind legs at the same time. A single leap can be several metres long. Over short distances they reach speeds of over 50 kilometres per hour. The **tendons** in the legs act like springs and save a lot of energy. They move slowly by supporting themselves on the tail and the forelegs.

Kangaroos belong to the **marsupials**. The young one is born after only about a month of pregnancy and is then hardly bigger than a bean. It crawls by itself through the fur into its mother's pouch and attaches itself to a teat. There it grows up over several months. A young kangaroo is called a **joey** in English.

Large kangaroos are **plant eaters** and eat mainly grasses and herbs. They are mostly active at dusk and at night and rest in the shade by day. They often live in loose groups called a mob. Males sometimes fight one another by supporting themselves on the tail and kicking with the hind legs. They can also manage for a long time with little water.

The kangaroo is an emblem of Australia and appears in the country's coat of arms. Large kangaroos are very common, and there are many millions of them. Farmers sometimes see them as competitors for their cattle. At night they often collide with cars. In Switzerland you can watch kangaroos in some **zoos**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young are born very small and go on developing in a pouch.
The English word for a young kangaroo.
A group of kangaroos.
An animal that feeds on plants.

gewusst: A kangaroo cannot hop backwards well.
A newborn large kangaroo weighs less than a gram.
A female kangaroo can have a young one in the pouch, one beside her and an embryo in her belly at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The red kite, in German Rotmilan, is a large, elegant bird of prey with reddish-brown plumage and a deeply forked tail. It lives almost only in Europe, and in Switzerland it can now be seen commonly in many places. Typical is its wavering soaring flight over fields and meadows.
wichtigste: The red kite is a bird of prey with a deeply forked, reddish tail.
It lives almost exclusively in Europe.
A particularly large part of the world population lives in Germany.
It is most often confused with the black kite.
Its call is a high, plaintive whistle.
It eats mice, other small animals and carrion.
Wild red kites can live to be over 25 years old.

abschnitte.text: The red kite has a **wingspan** of about 1.4 to 1.7 metres, but weighs only around one kilogram. Its plumage is reddish brown, and the head is pale grey and streaked. Under the wings it has large white patches. The tail is reddish with dark cross bands and deeply **forked**, which is where the old German name Gabelweihe, meaning fork harrier, comes from.

The red kite is most often confused with the **black kite**. This is darker brown, somewhat smaller and has a tail that is only weakly forked. The black kite often lives near lakes and rivers. Both species sometimes fly together over freshly mown meadows.

The red kite hunts mainly mice, young birds, earthworms and insects. Often it catches weakened or sick animals and likes to eat **carrion**. That is why it sometimes flies low over roads, where animals that have been run over lie. When farmers mow their fields, it circles over the fresh meadows and looks for mice and injured animals.

The red kite builds its nest, the **eyrie**, high up in trees at the forest edge. Sometimes it uses an abandoned crow's nest as a base. It often decorates the eyrie with pieces of plastic, paper or scraps of cloth. The female usually lays two to three eggs, and at about 2 to 3 years the young birds themselves become sexually mature.

The red kite occurs almost only in Europe, especially in Germany, France, Spain and Switzerland. A particularly large part of the world population breeds in **Germany**. Many red kites from the north move in autumn to south-western Europe, which is why you then see especially many in Switzerland. More and more red kites, however, also stay in Switzerland over the winter and spend the night in large roosts.

Red kites can poison themselves when they eat carrion with remains of **lead ammunition**. Further dangers are wind turbines, power lines, road traffic and poisoned baits. In Switzerland the population has increased strongly since the 1970s. That is why Switzerland today bears a special responsibility for this bird.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with a hooked beak and sharp claws that hunts animals.
The large nest of a bird of prey.
The body of a dead animal.
The distance from one wing tip to the other.

gewusst: The red kite steers with its long forked tail as with a rudder and keeps twisting it back and forth.
For their nest, red kites sometimes even collect socks, plastic bags or string.

teile.einleitung: A trunk, in German Rüssel, is a long, mobile extension of the nose that some animals use like a tool. The most famous trunk belongs to the elephant, which can use it to grasp, smell, drink and even greet friends. But tapirs, weevils and butterflies also have a kind of trunk.
wichtigste: The elephant's trunk consists of the nose and upper lip, which have grown together.
It has no bones, but tens of thousands of bundles of muscle.
Elephants use the trunk for grasping, smelling and drinking.
The tip of the trunk is especially sensitive and important for feeling.
To greet one another, elephants touch and smell each other with the trunk.
Tapirs, elephant shrews and many insects also have a trunk.

abschnitte.text: In the elephant, the **trunk** has grown together from the nose and the upper lip. In a large African elephant it can grow about two metres long. In the trunk there are no bones, but very many **muscles**, over 40,000 bundles of muscle according to estimates. That is why it is strong enough to lift tree trunks and at the same time fine enough to pick up a peanut.

The elephant uses its trunk like a hand, a nose and a hose all at once. With it, it tears off grass, leaves and branches and puts them in its mouth. To drink, it sucks water into the trunk and then squirts it into its mouth, because it does not drink through the trunk itself. With it, it can also **shower** itself with water or dust in order to cool down and to protect itself from insects.

Elephants have an excellent **sense of smell** and smell water and other elephants from a great distance. The **tip of the trunk** is especially sensitive and full of nerves. The African elephant has two finger-like projections there, the Asian elephant only one. With these, elephants can feel and grasp even small things.

When elephants greet each other, they **touch** and smell each other with the trunk, sometimes they even put it in the other's mouth. Mothers stroke and steer their young with the trunk. When swimming, elephants stick the trunk out of the water like a snorkel. Newborn elephants cannot yet use their trunk properly and have to learn it first.

The **tapir** also has a short trunk with which it grasps leaves. Butterflies have a long **proboscis**, which they unroll to drink nectar and roll up again afterwards. Weevils have an elongated head with the mouthparts at its tip. In the pig, the strong nose is also called a snout, with which it roots in the ground.

In Switzerland you can see elephants, for example, at **Zurich Zoo** in the Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park. There Asian elephants live in a large enclosure with bathing pools. A very long time ago, an animal with a trunk also lived in Switzerland: during the Ice Age the **mammoth** roamed across the Central Plateau. Its bones and tusks have been found in many places in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The elongated, mobile nose of an animal, in the elephant fused with the upper lip.
A tube-shaped mouthpart with which butterflies drink nectar.
An animal group that includes elephants and the extinct mammoth.
The ability to perceive smells.

gewusst: An elephant can suck up several litres of water at once in its trunk.
Young elephants sometimes suck on their trunk, much as babies suck their thumb.

teile.einleitung: Poison dart frogs are small, often brightly coloured frogs from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their bright colours warn enemies: many species have a strong poison in their skin. The golden poison frog is even one of the most poisonous animals in the world.
wichtigste: Poison dart frogs form the family Dendrobatidae with around 200 species.
Their sister group is the family Aromobatidae.
The genus name Dendrobates means “tree walker”.
Indigenous hunters coated blowpipe darts with the skin poison, which is where the name comes from.
It is proven that only species of the genus Phyllobates were used for this.
The golden poison frog lives only in Colombia and contains batrachotoxin.
The bright colours warn enemies about the poison.

abschnitte.text: Most poison dart frogs are small, many only 1.5 to 5 centimetres long. They glow red, yellow, blue, green or orange, often with black spots. These bright **warning colours** tell birds and snakes: watch out, I am poisonous! The genus name Dendrobates means “tree walker”, although many species also live on the forest floor.

Poison dart frogs live in tropical **rainforests** from Nicaragua to Bolivia and Brazil. The family Dendrobatidae now includes around 200 species, and its closest relative is the family Aromobatidae. The **golden poison frog** (Phyllobates terribilis) lives only in Colombia, on the Pacific coast. Its range is smaller than 5,000 square kilometres and lies from sea level up to about 200 metres in height.

The golden poison frog grows to about 5 centimetres and is bright yellow. Its skin poison is called **batrachotoxin** and paralyses nerves and muscles. Even the amount in a single frog could kill several people, which is why its species name “terribilis” means terrible. The frogs do not make the poison themselves but take it in with their food, mainly through ants and mites.

Indigenous hunters in Colombia coated the tips of their **blowpipe darts** with the frogs' skin poison. In this way they could bring down birds and monkeys. It is proven that only species of the genus **Phyllobates** were used for this, even though all species of the family carry the name. Many other poison dart frogs are only weakly poisonous.

Poison dart frogs look after their young remarkably well. The eggs are laid on land in damp leaves and guarded by one of the parents. After hatching, the male often carries the **tadpoles** on his back to small pools of water, for example in the leaf axils of bromeliads. In some species the female even feeds the tadpoles with unfertilised eggs.

Many poison dart frogs are threatened because rainforest is being cut down. A dangerous **fungal disease** is also affecting amphibians worldwide. In the past many animals were caught for the pet trade, but today the trade is strictly regulated. Incidentally, poison dart frogs bred in zoos and terrariums are not poisonous, because they lack the poisonous food.

begriffe.erklaerung: A striking colour that shows enemies that an animal is poisonous or inedible.
A very strong nerve poison from the skin of some poison dart frogs.
A long tube through which small darts are shot with the breath.
The larva of a frog, which lives in water and breathes with gills.

gewusst: Poison dart frogs bred in captivity lose their poison because they eat different insects.
Poison dart frogs are active by day, while many other frogs are out at night.
A species of snake in South America can withstand the poison of some poison dart frogs and still eats them.

teile.einleitung: The giant squid is a huge cephalopod that lives in the deep sea. It has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom and, with its feeding tentacles, can grow about 12 to 13 metres long. For a long time it was known only from legends about sea monsters.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the giant squid is Architeuthis dux.
It belongs to the molluscs and to the family Architeuthidae.
It has eight arms and two long feeding tentacles.
The largest females grow, with tentacles, about 12 to 13 metres long.
Its mantle grows at most about 2.25 metres long.
Its eyes reach a diameter of around 25 centimetres.
According to estimates, females weigh at most about 275 kilograms.
Its most important enemy is the sperm whale.

abschnitte.text: The giant squid bears the scientific name **Architeuthis dux**. The word “dux” is Latin and means leader or prince. It belongs to the family Architeuthidae and to the animal phylum of the **molluscs**, like snails and mussels. Within the molluscs it counts among the cephalopods, like octopuses and cuttlefish. The genus was scientifically described in 1857 by the Danish researcher Japetus Steenstrup.

The body without the head and arms is called the **mantle** and grows at most about 2.25 metres long. On the head there are eight arms and two much longer feeding tentacles with suckers. According to reliable estimates, the largest females reach about 12 to 13 metres with their tentacles. Older figures of 18 metres and more should be treated with caution, because the tentacles of dead animals stretch a lot. Females weigh at most about 275 kilograms, and males are smaller.

The giant squid has the largest **eyes** in the animal kingdom, and they can reach about 25 centimetres in diameter. That is about as big as a football. In the dark deep sea it uses them to catch even faint light. A well-known study from 2012 suggests that in this way it recognises approaching sperm whales early. When a sperm whale swims, it makes tiny glowing organisms light up.

Giant squid live in all oceans, mostly at depths of a few hundred metres. There they hunt fish and other squid. With the long **feeding tentacles** they grab their prey and pull it to the arms and the sharp beak. Their main enemy is the **sperm whale**, which dives deep to eat them. On the skin of sperm whales you often find round scars from suckers.

For a long time giant squid were known only from dead animals that were washed up on beaches or caught in nets. Only in 2004 did Japanese researchers manage to photograph a living giant squid in the depths. In 2012 a team filmed a giant squid in its natural habitat for the first time, off Japan. To this day, encounters with living animals are very rare. Many questions about its life are still open.

Sailors used to tell of a huge sea monster, the **Kraken**. Probably some of these stories go back to sightings of giant squid. In novels such as “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” by Jules Verne, too, people fight against giant cephalopods. In reality, giant squid do not attack ships. They live shyly in the depths, far away from people.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molluscs with arms on the head, for example squid, octopuses and cuttlefish.
The main body of a cephalopod without the head and arms.
Two especially long arms with which the squid grabs prey.
The scientific name of the giant squid.

gewusst: The eyes of the giant squid are about as big as a football.
A giant squid has three hearts and blue blood.
Even larger eyes and more weight are probably reached only by its relative, the colossal squid from the Antarctic.

teile.einleitung: Prairie dogs are not dogs but sociable rodents from the squirrel family. They live in huge underground colonies in the grasslands of North America. They owe their name to their barking warning calls.
wichtigste: Prairie dogs belong to the squirrel family (Sciuridae).
All prairie dogs belong to the genus Cynomys, which literally means dog mouse.
There are five species alive today.
The name prairie dog comes from their barking warning calls.
The black-tailed prairie dog weighs about 0.7 to 1.5 kilograms.
The males are generally larger and heavier than the females.
Prairie dogs live in large colonies with branching burrows.

abschnitte.text: Prairie dogs are sturdy rodents about 30 to 40 centimetres long, with a short tail and sandy-brown fur. They belong to the genus **Cynomys**, which is part of the squirrels, and their closest relatives are marmots and ground squirrels. The five species are the black-tailed, the white-tailed, the Gunnison's, the Utah and the Mexican prairie dog. The black-tailed prairie dog is easiest to recognise by its black tail tip.

Prairie dogs live in the open grasslands of North America, from Canada through the USA to Mexico. There they dig deep burrows with many tunnels, living chambers and exits. Around the entrances they pile up mounds of earth, which serve as lookout points and as protection against flooding. Many burrows together form a **prairie dog town**, which can be huge.

In the colonies the animals live together in small family groups called **coteries**. Guards keep watch for enemies such as coyotes, eagles or badgers. When they see danger, they give barking warning calls, and everyone disappears into the holes in a flash. Researchers found that the calls even sound different depending on whether a human, a hawk or a coyote is approaching.

On the famous Lewis and Clark expedition, Meriwether Lewis called the black-tailed prairie dog the “barking squirrel”. In 1805 the expedition sent a live prairie dog to President **Thomas Jefferson**. The scientific species name ludovicianus comes from the Louisiana Territory. The Gunnison's prairie dog is named after the US Army officer John W. Gunnison.

Prairie dogs eat mainly grasses, herbs and roots and so keep the plants in their colony short. Their burrows loosen the soil and offer shelter to many other animals, such as burrowing owls. The rare **black-footed ferret** feeds almost only on prairie dogs. Because farmers fought them as pests and diseases such as plague wiped out many colonies, their numbers have shrunk greatly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals of one species that live together in one place.
A small family group of prairie dogs within a colony.
A sound with which animals warn others of their species of danger.
Wide, flat grassland in North America.

gewusst: Around 1900 there is said to have been a single prairie dog town in Texas with hundreds of millions of animals.
Black-tailed prairie dogs greet each other by touching teeth, which looks like a kiss.
When excited, they stretch up and give a call so forceful that they sometimes almost topple over.

teile.einleitung: Dung beetles are beetles that shape round balls out of animal dung and roll them away. The balls serve them as food or as a nursery for their young. In ancient Egypt the dung beetle was even revered as a sacred animal.
wichtigste: A dung beetle is a beetle that rolls dung into balls.
It usually rolls the ball backwards with its hind legs.
It rolls it away as straight as possible to save it from rivals.
Dung beetles can find their way by the sky, even by the Milky Way.
The best-known species is the sacred scarab.
In ancient Egypt, as the scarab, it was a symbol of the sun.

abschnitte.text: Dung beetles belong to the family of **scarab beetles** and are usually black and sturdily built. The best-known genus is called Scarabaeus, and the sacred scarab grows to about 2 to 4 centimetres long. On the head they have a kind of shovel with points, with which they work the dung. Their front legs are broad and toothed, ideal for digging and shaping.

A dung beetle cuts a piece from the fresh dung of herbivores and shapes it into a round **dung ball**. It rolls this backwards with its hind legs while walking on its front legs. The ball can be much larger and heavier than the beetle itself. It rolls it away as straight as possible so that no rival can steal it.

Before a dung beetle rolls off, it often climbs onto its ball and turns around as if in a dance. In doing so it takes its bearings from the sun, the moon or the polarised light in the sky. In 2013, researchers in South Africa discovered that some dung beetles even line themselves up by the **Milky Way** at night. When the beetles were given little caps that blocked out the sky, they wandered around in circles.

For their young, dung beetles bury a ball in the ground. The female lays an egg in it, often in a pear-shaped brood ball made of dung. The **larva** that hatches eats the ball from the inside and grows up protected inside it. When it has pupated and transformed, the finished beetle digs its way up to the surface.

Dung beetles live mainly in warm, dry regions, such as around the Mediterranean, in Africa and in Asia. In central Europe there is a rare relative, the little **pill beetle**, but true dung beetles are absent from Switzerland. Dung beetles are very useful because they bury droppings, fertilise the soil and leave flies fewer breeding places. In Australia, dung beetles from other countries were therefore introduced to get rid of cow dung on the pastures.

In ancient Egypt the sacred scarab was revered as the **scarab**. People saw in the rolling ball an image of the sun travelling across the sky. The beetle stood for the sun god Khepri and for new beginnings. Scarabs made of stone or clay were worn as lucky charms and seals, and many of them can be found today in museums.

begriffe.erklaerung: The droppings of animals, especially of herbivores such as cows.
A family of beetles with fan-shaped antennae, which also includes cockchafers.
Another name for the sacred scarab beetle, a sacred symbol in ancient Egypt.
A young animal that still looks quite different from the adult animal.

gewusst: Dung beetles are the first known animals proven to find their way by the Milky Way.
A dung beetle can roll a ball that weighs many times its own weight.
Dung beetles also climb onto their ball to cool their feet on hot sand.

teile.einleitung: The r/K selection theory explains why some animals have very many young and others only a few. Mice have many young, while elephants have only one every few years. The theory assigns such differences to two strategies, the r strategy and the K strategy.
wichtigste: The theory was made well known in 1967 by the ecologists Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson.
The letter r stands for the growth rate of a population.
The letter K stands for the capacity, that is, how many animals a habitat can feed.
r strategists have many offspring with little parental care.
K strategists have few offspring, which they look after for a long time.
Most living things lie somewhere between the two extremes.
Today the theory is seen as a simplified but useful model.

abschnitte.titel: What do r and K mean?
abschnitte.text: The letters come from a mathematical formula for the growth of animal populations. **r** is the rate at which a population grows when there is enough food and space. **K** is the **capacity**, that is, the highest number of animals that a habitat can feed in the long term. Depending on which of the two matters more for a species, people speak of r selection or K selection.

**r strategists** rely on quantity: they have very many, mostly small offspring. The parents hardly look after them or not at all, so most of the young die early. Examples are mice, many insects, frogs or the cod, whose female lays millions of eggs. This strategy pays off in uncertain habitats that change quickly.

**K strategists** rely on quality: they have few, but large and well-developed young. The parents look after them for a long time, and many young survive. Examples are elephants, whales, great apes and also humans. An elephant cow carries her calf for almost 22 months and has a young one only every few years.

The ecologists **Robert MacArthur** and **Edward O. Wilson** presented the idea in 1967 in a book about life on islands. Later the biologist Eric Pianka developed it further and listed typical features of both strategies. For example, r strategists mostly live a short time and mature early. K strategists, by contrast, often grow old and reproduce only late.

In nature, many species do not fit neatly into one box. Sea turtles lay many eggs but live a very long time, and trees such as oaks bear thousands of acorns every year. That is why experts today prefer to speak of **life histories** and to look at many features at the same time. Even so, the r/K theory remains a good tool for understanding the basic idea.

In a Swiss garden you can find both strategies. Aphids multiply explosively in spring and are typical r strategists. The **ibex**, by contrast, usually has only one kid a year, which stays with its mother for a long time. The field vole, which multiplies in huge numbers in good years, is also a well-known example of an r strategist.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the animals of one species that live together in an area.
The highest number of animals that a habitat can feed in the long term.
Everything that parents do to protect and look after their young.
Natural selection: those that are better adapted have more offspring.

gewusst: A single female cod can lay several million eggs in one season.
In summer, aphids can reproduce without males and give birth straight away to live young.
Humans are among the most pronounced K strategists, because children need many years of care.

teile.einleitung: Horses come in many different colours, and each colour has its own name. A black horse is called a black, a reddish-brown one a chestnut and a white one a grey. Anyone who knows these names can describe horses the way experts do.
wichtigste: A black horse is simply called black.
A horse with reddish-brown fur is called a chestnut.
A white or light grey horse is called a grey.
A bay has brown fur with a black mane and a black tail.
Greys are usually born dark and only turn light over the years.
White markings on the head and legs are called markings.

abschnitte.text: The three basic colours in horses are **black**, **chestnut** and **bay**. A black horse is completely black, with a black mane and a black tail. A chestnut has reddish-brown fur, and its mane is the same colour or lighter. A bay has brown fur but a black mane, a black tail and usually dark legs.

A **grey** looks white or light grey. Most greys are born dark and only get lighter and lighter over the years. The Lipizzaners are well known for this, as their foals are born black or brown. In between, young greys often have a spotted coat, which is called dapple grey.

A **dun** has a sand-coloured or greyish-brown coat and often a dark stripe along the back, the dorsal stripe. A palomino is golden yellow with a light, almost white mane. Horses with large white and coloured patches are called **pintos**. Leopard-spotted horses have many small dark spots on a light coat, as seen in Appaloosas.

White areas on the head and legs are called **markings**. A small white patch on the forehead is called a star, and a long white stripe down the face is called a blaze. A white patch between the nostrils is called a snip. Markings help to identify a horse unmistakably, which is why they are also written in the horse passport.

The colour a horse has is determined by its **genes**, which it inherits from its mother and father. Some breeds are almost always the same colour: Friesians are black, and Haflingers are chestnuts with a light mane. Swiss Franches-Montagnes are mostly bays or chestnuts. In other breeds, such as the Icelandic horse, by contrast, a great many colours occur.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horse with black fur, a black mane and a black tail.
A horse with reddish-brown fur.
A horse with white or light grey fur.
White areas on a horse's head or legs.

gewusst: A grey is usually not white from birth, but only turns light with time.
Under the white coat of a grey, the skin is mostly dark.
The German word “Fuchs” for a chestnut horse comes from the reddish colour that is reminiscent of a red fox.

teile.einleitung: Propolis is a sticky resin that bees use to seal their hive. They collect it from tree buds and mix it with wax and saliva. Because propolis holds back germs, it is a kind of medicine cabinet for the bee colony.
wichtigste: Propolis is a sticky resin with which bees seal their hive.
Bees collect the resin mainly from the buds of poplars, birches and conifers.
Propolis is also called bee glue.
Propolis holds back the growth of bacteria and fungi.
Bees even cover dead intruders with it that are too big to carry out.
People use propolis in ointments, tinctures and toothpastes.
Some people are allergic to propolis.

abschnitte.text: Many trees protect their buds and wounds with sticky **resin**. Certain worker bees scrape this resin off with their jaws, mainly from poplars, birches, chestnuts and conifers. They carry it like pollen in the baskets on their hind legs to the hive. There they mix it with **beeswax** and saliva to make propolis.

With propolis, bees close cracks and gaps in their home. In autumn they often use it to make the entrance narrower, so that less cold air and fewer enemies get in. The inner walls and the cells of the honeycomb are also covered with a thin layer. For beekeepers propolis is a nuisance, because it glues frames and lids firmly together.

In a beehive it is warm and damp, ideal for **bacteria** and fungi. Propolis contains many substances that hold back germs. In this way it protects the brood and the stores from disease. If a mouse gets into the hive and is stung to death, the bees cover it with propolis so that it does not rot and spread disease.

Propolis was already used in ancient Egypt and ancient Greece. Today you find it in ointments, lozenges, mouthwashes and tinctures. In **natural medicine** it is used for small wounds or sore throats, but its effect in humans is not well proven scientifically in all cases. Because propolis can cause an **allergy**, you should try it carefully.

Propolis can be yellow, red, brown or almost black, depending on which plants the resin comes from. It smells spicy and resinous, and is soft when warm and hard and brittle when cold. Beekeepers obtain it by scraping propolis off the frames or by placing special **propolis grids** in the hive. A bee colony usually supplies only about 50 to 150 grams a year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for propolis, because bees use it to seal gaps.
A sticky sap with which trees protect buds and wounds.
Wax that bees secrete from glands on the belly to build honeycomb.
Healing methods that mainly use natural substances from plants and animals.

gewusst: The word propolis comes from Greek and means roughly in front of the city, because bees use it at the entrance to their hive.
Bees can even embalm a whole mouse with propolis, much like a mummy.

teile.einleitung: The broad-bodied chaser is a dragonfly with a strikingly broad, flat abdomen. In the male this abdomen is sky blue, in the female yellowish-brown. In Switzerland the broad-bodied chaser is one of the best-known dragonflies and often visits garden ponds too.
wichtigste: The broad-bodied chaser is a dragonfly species widespread in Switzerland.
Its scientific name is Libellula depressa.
The male has a blue, powdery abdomen, the female a yellowish-brown one.
The abdomen is broad and flat, hence the name.
The larvae live in the water for one to two years.
The broad-bodied chaser likes to colonise new ponds and pools.

abschnitte.text: The broad-bodied chaser belongs to the family of **skimmers** and grows to about 4 to 5 centimetres long. Its abdomen is strikingly broad and flat, as if someone had sat on it. In the adult male it is covered with a **bloom** that makes it look sky blue, and in the female it is yellowish-brown with yellow patches at the sides. At the base of all four wings, the broad-bodied chaser has dark brown patches.

The broad-bodied chaser lives at small, sunny waters such as pools, ponds, gravel pits and **garden ponds**. It is regarded as a **pioneer species**, because it is often one of the first dragonflies to colonise newly created waters. It is found in almost all of Europe and as far as Asia. In Switzerland it is widespread in the lowlands and also occurs at lower elevations in the Alpine valleys.

Like all dragonflies, the broad-bodied chaser is a skilful **predator**. It likes to sit on a lookout, such as a reed stalk, and sets off from there on short hunting flights. With its large eyes it spots mosquitoes, flies and other insects and catches them in flight. The males defend their small territory at the water against other males.

After mating, which takes place only briefly in the air, the female lays her eggs by tapping her abdomen into the water. **Larvae** hatch from the eggs, living at the bottom of the water and hunting small water animals there. After one to two, rarely three years, the larva climbs out of the water on a plant stem. Then its skin splits open, and the finished dragonfly slips out.

In Switzerland you see the broad-bodied chaser mainly from May to August. It is not considered threatened here, because it also uses small and new waters. Anyone who builds a nature-friendly **garden pond** without fish can often watch it in the very first summer. Similar-looking species are the black-tailed skimmer and the four-spotted chaser, which are more slenderly built.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flying insect with four wings and a long abdomen that hunts other insects.
A fine, waxy layer that makes the abdomen look blue.
A species that is one of the first to colonise new habitats.
The young form, which in dragonflies lives in water.

gewusst: Dragonflies existed long before the dinosaurs, and some ancient dragonflies had a wingspan of around 70 centimetres.
A dragonfly can move its four wings separately and can therefore even hover in the air.
Dragonflies cannot sting and are completely harmless to people.

teile.einleitung: PanEco is a Swiss foundation that works to protect orangutans and their habitat. It was founded in the 1990s by the biologist Regina Frey and is based in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich. It is also active in protecting nature in Switzerland.
wichtigste: PanEco is a nature conservation foundation from Switzerland.
It was founded by the biologist Regina Frey.
Its headquarters are in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich.
PanEco works for orangutans in Indonesia, especially on Sumatra.
The foundation rescues orphaned orangutans and prepares them for life in the forest.
In Switzerland, PanEco runs the Thurauen Nature Centre in the Zurich Weinland.

abschnitte.text: PanEco is a non-profit **foundation** that was founded about 30 years ago by the Swiss biologist Regina Frey. As early as the 1970s, Regina Frey was working with orangutans in Indonesia. The foundation is based in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich. It works in Indonesia and in Switzerland and combines species protection with environmental education.

In the wild, orangutans now live only on the islands of **Borneo** and Sumatra. PanEco works for these seriously threatened great apes, with its main focus on **Sumatra**. Together with Indonesian partners, the foundation runs a station where injured or orphaned orangutans are cared for. There, young animals learn to climb and find food before they are released into protected forests.

Orangutans can only survive if their **rainforest** is preserved. The greatest danger is deforestation, for example to make way for oil palm plantations. That is why PanEco also works to have forests placed under protection and to replant areas that have been destroyed. The foundation also supports farming families on the spot in using nature-friendly farming methods.

In Switzerland, PanEco runs the **Thurauen Nature Centre** near Flaach in the Zurich Weinland. There the River Thur was restored to a more natural state, so that a **floodplain landscape** rich in species could develop. Visitors can discover beavers, kingfishers and dragonflies on an adventure trail. The foundation also includes a bird of prey station in Berg am Irchel, which cares for injured birds of prey.

PanEco offers materials for school classes and organises guided tours and excursions. Children and young people learn how the rainforest and Swiss nature are connected. One example is our own shopping: anyone who chooses products with sustainable **palm oil** is helping the orangutans. Many people also support the foundation with donations or sponsorships.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that uses donated money to pursue a particular good cause.
Letting an animal that has been in human care go back into nature.
A natural landscape along a river that is flooded regularly.
The group of apes that includes orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos.

gewusst: Young orangutans stay with their mother for about seven to eight years, longer than almost any other animal.
The word orangutan comes from Malay and means forest person.
A Swiss foundation helps great apes on the other side of the world and, at the same time, beavers in the canton of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: The horse is one of the most important domestic animals for humans. For thousands of years horses have carried riders, pulled carts and ploughs and been faithful companions. Horses are fast, clever animals of flight that live in herds.
wichtigste: Horses live in groups called herds.
A wild herd of horses is often led by an older, experienced mare.
Horses eat mainly grass and hay, preferably in many small portions.
A horse has only one toe on each foot, the hoof.
A mare carries her foal in her belly for about 11 months.
Horses live to be about 25 to 30 years old.
Horses can breathe only through the nose.

abschnitte.text: A horse stands on four long legs, and on each foot it has only one toe, protected by a hard **hoof**. Its size is measured as the **height at the withers**, from the ground to the withers, the highest point of the back. The nostrils are especially large so that the horse can breathe in plenty of air when running. Because its throat is built the way it is, a horse can breathe only through its nose and not through its mouth.

Horses are herbivores and eat mostly **grass and hay**. In nature they eat for up to 16 hours a day, in small portions again and again. For this they have large molar teeth, which wear down and keep growing. A horse cannot vomit, so spoiled food or wrong feeding can cause dangerous **colic**.

Horses are **animals of flight**: when in danger, they would rather run away than fight. With their eyes set at the sides, they can see almost all the way round. In a wild herd an older, experienced mare often leads the group to food and water. In a stable, horses need contact with other horses and enough exercise, otherwise they become unhappy.

A female horse is called a mare, a male a stallion and a young one a **foal**. The mare carries her foal in her belly for about 11 months. Shortly after birth the foal can already stand and run, so that it can keep up with the herd. It drinks its mother's milk for several months.

Horses move in three basic gaits: **walk, trot and canter**. At a gallop, racehorses reach over 60 kilometres per hour. When a horse exerts itself hard, it sweats all over its body, a bit like a person. Horses can even doze while standing, because their legs can lock into place as if with a latch.

Humans tamed the horse a few thousand years ago in the steppes of Eurasia. After that, horses changed farming, trade and warfare. The best-known Swiss horse breed is the **Franches-Montagnes** from the Jura, a versatile, calm horse. In Avenches in the canton of Vaud there is the Swiss National Stud Farm, and today horses are kept mainly for sport and leisure.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard horny shoe at the end of each horse's leg.
A female horse.
A young horse.
An animal that runs away when in danger instead of fighting.
The size of a horse, measured from the ground to the withers.

gewusst: A horse's eyes are among the largest of all land mammals.
Horses can sleep standing up, but they lie down for deep sleep.
Experts can estimate a horse's age from its teeth.

teile.einleitung: A pedigree dog is a dog that belongs to a particular dog breed and whose parents also belong to this breed. From the tiny Chihuahua to the huge St Bernard, there are hundreds of breeds. They all descend from the wolf and were bred by humans for particular tasks or a particular appearance.
wichtigste: A pedigree dog belongs to a recognised dog breed with fixed features.
The features of a breed are described in a breed standard.
The international umbrella organisation FCI recognises about 350 dog breeds.
Most of today's breeds came into being from the 19th century onwards.
Through breeding for outward features, the genetic diversity of many breeds fell sharply.
Some breeds therefore often suffer from inherited diseases.
Well-known Swiss breeds are the Bernese mountain dog and the St Bernard.

abschnitte.text: All domestic dogs descend from the **wolf** and were tamed by humans many thousands of years ago. A **dog breed** is a group of dogs with a similar build, coat and character. A pedigree dog has parents of the same breed and often a **pedigree certificate**, a kind of family tree. Dogs whose parents belong to different breeds are called crossbreeds.

Early on, people bred dogs for particular tasks, such as herding, hunting or guarding. From the **19th century**, people in England and other countries began to define breeds exactly and to hold dog shows. For each breed a **breed standard** was written, describing size, colour and body shape. The world federation FCI was founded in 1911 and today recognises about 350 breeds.

Switzerland has several breeds of its own. Well known are the four **Sennenhunde**, or Swiss mountain dogs: the Bernese mountain dog, the Greater Swiss mountain dog, the Appenzeller and the Entlebucher. In the past they helped on farms, drove cattle and pulled milk carts. The **St Bernard** was bred at the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass and is the national dog of Switzerland.

Because often only a few animals were used for breeding, many dogs of one breed are closely related to one another. As a result, **genetic diversity** fell sharply, and hereditary diseases occur more often. Dogs with a very short nose, such as the pug or the French bulldog, often have breathing problems. When animals are bred for features that harm them, it is called **breeding that causes suffering**, which is forbidden in Switzerland by animal protection law.

Anyone who wants a dog should first think about which breed suits their own life. A herding dog such as the Border Collie needs a lot of exercise and activity. Responsible breeders pay attention to **health** and character and show the parent animals. In animal shelters, too, many pedigree dogs and crossbreeds are waiting for a new home.

begriffe.erklaerung: A description of how a dog of a particular breed should look and behave.
The family tree of a pedigree dog with its parents, grandparents and other ancestors.
The variety of inherited traits within a group of living things.
Breeding in which the animals suffer or fall ill because of their features.
Fédération Cynologique Internationale, the world federation of dog breeding.

gewusst: A Chihuahua can weigh less than 2 kilograms, and a Great Dane or a St Bernard more than 60 kilograms, and yet both belong to the same species.
The famous St Bernard Barry is said to have saved over 40 people in the mountains in the 19th century.
On average, crossbreeds are no less clever or loyal than pedigree dogs.

teile.einleitung: The ecological niche describes how a species lives in its habitat and what role it plays there. So it is not about a place, but about the ‘job’ of a species in nature. It includes what it eats, when it is active and which conditions it needs to live.
wichtigste: The ecological niche is the sum of all environmental requirements and the functional role of a species in its habitat.
A niche is not a place, but rather the ‘job’ of a species.
A niche includes food, time of activity, temperature, nesting sites and much more.
Two species with exactly the same niche cannot exist side by side for long.
Through different niches, many species can live in the same habitat.
The term was coined in the early 20th century by biologists such as Joseph Grinnell and Charles Elton.

abschnitte.text: Every species has certain demands on its environment, such as for food, temperature, moisture or hiding places. At the same time it fulfils a task, for example as a hunter, plant eater or **decomposer**. All of this together is called the ecological niche. You can imagine it as the job of a species, while the habitat is its address.

If two species need exactly the same thing, the stronger displaces the weaker. This is called the **competitive exclusion principle**. The Russian researcher Georgy Gause showed this in the 1930s with paramecia. That is why species that live together usually differ in at least one important point.

In Swiss forests several species of tits live side by side. The larger great tit often looks for food on the ground and on thick branches, the light blue tit more on thin twig tips. Owls and birds of prey hunt similar prey, but at different times, the former at night, the latter by day. In this way they share the **resources** of the forest.

On the Galápagos Islands many different **Darwin’s finches** developed from one bird species. Each species got a beak that suits a particular food, such as hard seeds, insects or cactus flowers. In this way the finches occupied different niches. Charles Darwin observed these birds in 1835 on his voyage.

The American biologist Joseph Grinnell used the term niche in 1917 for the living requirements of a species. The Briton Charles Elton stressed in 1927 the role of a species in the **food chain**. Later George Evelyn Hutchinson described the niche as a space made up of many environmental factors. Today a distinction is made between the potential niche without competition and the niche actually used.

Anyone who knows the niche of a species understands why it lives in one place and is absent elsewhere. This is important for **species conservation**, because a species needs all parts of its niche. Introduced species can contest the niche of native species. In climate change too, this knowledge helps to predict which species will get into trouble.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something a living thing needs to live, for example food, water or nesting sites.
The contest between living things for the same resources.
The place where a species lives, for example a forest or a lake.
Living things such as fungi and bacteria that break down dead matter.

gewusst: Woodpeckers, nuthatches and treecreepers all look for food on the tree trunk, but each in its own way.
On islands especially many new species often arise, because there many niches are still free.
The human niche is unusually broad, because humans can live almost anywhere on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The basking shark, in German Riesenhai, is, after the whale shark, the second-largest fish in the world. Although it grows up to about 10 metres long, it is completely harmless to people. It swims through the sea with its mouth wide open and filters tiny plankton out of the water.
wichtigste: The basking shark is the second-largest fish in the world.
Only the whale shark is larger.
Basking sharks usually grow 6 to 8 metres long, and large animals reach about 10 metres.
It feeds on plankton, which it filters out of the water.
For people the basking shark is harmless.
It lives in cooler seas all over the world.
The basking shark is regarded as endangered.

abschnitte.text: The basking shark has the scientific name **Cetorhinus maximus**. It is grey-brown to blackish and has a large triangular dorsal fin. Striking are its huge gill slits, which reach almost all the way round the head. It can open its mouth about a metre wide. Its teeth are tiny and play hardly any role in feeding.

Basking sharks live in the cool and temperate seas of the whole world. In Europe you often see them in summer off the coasts of Great Britain, Ireland and Norway. They also occur in the Mediterranean. They like to swim slowly near the **surface of the water**, where a lot of plankton drifts. In winter they dive to greater depths and migrate over long distances.

The basking shark is a **filter feeder**. It swims with its mouth open through clouds of tiny crustaceans, fish larvae and other **plankton**. The water streams out through the gills, and the food stays caught on the gill rakers. In this way it filters well over a million litres of water per hour. As it does so it swims only about as fast as a person walks at a leisurely pace.

Little is yet known about the reproduction of the basking shark. The young develop inside the mother's body and are born alive. Researchers suspect that the gestation period lasts over a year. Basking sharks mature only late and have only a few young. That is why their populations recover only very slowly.

In the past, basking sharks were hunted heavily, above all for their huge **liver**. The oil from it was used as lamp oil and for other purposes. The fins are also in demand, and many animals die as bycatch in fishing nets. Today the basking shark is protected in many countries. On the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, it counts as **endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that sieves tiny food out of the water.
Tiny plants and animals that drift in the water.
Sieve-like growths on the gills on which the food gets caught.
Animals that get caught in the fishing net unintentionally.

gewusst: In the past, sailors sometimes took dead basking sharks, whose gills had rotted away, for sea monsters.
The liver of a basking shark can make up about a quarter of its body weight.
Although it is so large, the basking shark eats only animals that are often smaller than a grain of rice.

teile.einleitung: Comb jellies, in German Rippenquallen, are transparent, jelly-like sea animals that look like jellyfish but belong to an animal group of their own. They swim with eight rows of tiny plates of cilia, which shimmer in rainbow colours in the light. Unlike true jellyfish, they have no stinging cells to sting with.
wichtigste: Comb jellies belong to an animal group of their own and are not true jellyfish.
They have no stinging cells and cannot sting people.
They swim with eight rows of plates of cilia, the combs.
These combs shimmer in rainbow colours in the light.
Many comb jellies catch prey with sticky cells.
Comb jellies live in all seas.
Some species can make light themselves.

abschnitte.text: Comb jellies form an **animal phylum** of their own with the name Ctenophora, which means comb bearers. They look similar to jellyfish, but are only distantly related to them. Their body consists almost entirely of water and is transparent as glass. About 150 to 200 species are known. They belong to the oldest animal groups on Earth.

On their body run eight rows of tiny **plates of cilia**, which are called combs. The plates beat one after another like small oars and push the animal slowly through the water. When light falls on them, it is refracted, and the combs shimmer in all the **colours of the rainbow**. This is not a glow of its own, but a light effect like that on a soap bubble. Comb jellies are the largest animals that move around using cilia.

True jellyfish catch prey with **stinging cells** that inject poison. Comb jellies instead have sticky cells, which are called **colloblasts**. Many species have two long catching threads on which small crustaceans and fish larvae get stuck. Other species swallow their prey with the wide-open mouth. For people, comb jellies are completely harmless.

In the North Sea and the Baltic Sea lives the **sea gooseberry**, which is about as big as a gooseberry. Venus's girdle is ribbon-shaped and can grow over a metre long. The sea walnut comes from the western Atlantic and was introduced into other seas in the ballast water of ships. In the Black Sea it multiplied in huge numbers in the 1980s. It ate so much plankton and fish larvae that fishing suffered badly.

Many comb jellies can produce light themselves, which is called **bioluminescence**. They glow mostly blue or green, especially when they are disturbed. In the deep sea live species that were discovered only with diving robots. Because their body is so delicate, they often fall to pieces in nets. That is why little is yet known about many species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A jelly-like sea animal with eight rows of plates of cilia.
Cells of jellyfish that shoot out a poisonous thread on contact.
Sticky cells of comb jellies for catching prey.
The ability of living things to make light themselves.

gewusst: Some comb jellies eat other comb jellies that are almost as large as themselves.
The rainbow-like shimmer of the combs arises because the plates refract the light.
Comb jellies consist of over 95 per cent water.

teile.einleitung: Pacing is a gait in which an animal moves both legs on one side of its body forward at the same time. Camels and giraffes walk like this, and as they do they sway from one side to the other. Some horse breeds, such as the Icelandic horse, also master a special form of pacing.
wichtigste: In pacing, both legs on one side of the body move at the same time.
Camels walk with a pacing gait.
Giraffes and some bears also use this gait.
In pacing, the body sways from side to side.
Pacing is the counterpart of the trot, in which diagonal legs move together.
Icelandic horses can do the fast flying pace.

abschnitte.text: In **pacing**, both left legs first start moving at the same time and then both right legs. The body is therefore carried alternately on the left and on the right side. That is why an animal pacing sways like a boat. Camels are therefore also called ships of the desert.

Most four-legged animals, such as dogs, horses or cows, move to a different beat. In the **trot**, the legs move crosswise, so the left front leg moves together with the right hind leg. This gait is also called the **diagonal gait**. It is very stable, because the animal always stands on diagonally opposite legs.

Besides the **camel**, giraffes also pace when walking slowly. Some bears, elephants and a few dogs, especially when tired, also show pace-like movements. In animals with long legs, pacing has an advantage, because the front and hind legs do not knock into each other. This gait also saves energy when an animal covers long distances.

Some horse breeds can pace naturally, and they are called **gaited horses**. The best known is the **Icelandic horse**, which besides walk, trot and canter can also do the tölt and the fast flying pace. Icelandic horses are very popular in Switzerland too, and there are many farms and competitions for them here. In North America, in some harness races, horses even run at the pace instead of the trot.

In the Middle Ages, horses with a pacing gait were highly valued because they were comfortable to ride. Travellers, merchants and fine ladies therefore liked to ride on so-called **palfreys**. As better roads and carriages were built, these horses were needed less. In Iceland, however, the tradition has survived to this day, because for a long time there were hardly any roads there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way an animal moves its legs when it moves along.
A gait in which both legs on one side of the body move forward together.
A gait in which diagonally opposite legs move together.
A particularly comfortable gait of Icelandic horses with no moment of suspension.

gewusst: Camels are called ships of the desert because of their swaying pace, and some riders even get seasick from it.
A flying pace in Icelandic horses can be as fast as a canter.
In the Middle Ages, pacers were often much more expensive than ordinary horses.

teile.einleitung: The grape phylloxera, in German Reblaus, is a tiny insect that sucks at the roots of grapevines. In the 19th century it was brought from North America to Europe and destroyed huge vineyards, in Switzerland too. Only a clever trick by the winegrowers saved European wine.
wichtigste: The grape phylloxera is a plant louse, related to the aphids.
It comes from North America and arrived in Europe in the 19th century.
It sucks at the roots of grapevines and can kill European vines.
From about 1860 it destroyed large parts of the vineyards in France and all over Europe.
In Switzerland it was first discovered in 1874, near Geneva.
Winegrowing was saved by grafting European vines onto American roots.
This method is still used almost everywhere today.

abschnitte.text: The grape phylloxera is only about 1 millimetre in size and yellowish to brownish. It pierces the **roots** of the vine with its proboscis and sucks plant sap. Swellings form on the roots and later rot. On American vines it also forms small growths on the leaves, which are called **galls**.

abschnitte.titel: How did it come to Europe?
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, plant lovers brought American **vines** to Europe in order to experiment with them. With them, the phylloxera travelled unnoticed across the Atlantic. From about 1863 it was noticed in the south of France, where whole vineyards died. In the following decades it spread over almost the whole of Europe.

The phylloxera disaster destroyed huge areas of vineyards in France. Many winegrowing families lost their income and emigrated. In Switzerland the phylloxera was discovered in **1874** in Pregny near Geneva, and later also in Vaud, in Valais and in German-speaking Switzerland. Some old grape varieties almost completely disappeared in this period.

People noticed that American vines can withstand the phylloxera, because their roots close the wounds quickly. That is why today a shoot of a European variety is cut off and set on an American **rootstock**, that is, a root stock. This technique is called **grafting**. In this way the well-known grapes such as Chasselas or Pinot Noir grow above, and resistant roots protect them below.

The phylloxera has not disappeared, and it lives in many vineyards to this day. As long as the vines are grafted, however, it does hardly any damage. Only in a few areas with sandy soil or in remote winegrowing regions are there still **ungrafted** vines. In Switzerland, vines are planted almost exclusively grafted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Joining a shoot of one plant to another plant so that the two grow together.
The root part of a grafted plant on which the noble variety grows.
A growth on a plant that is caused by an animal.
A vine that grows on its own roots and is not grafted.

gewusst: The grape phylloxera has a complicated life cycle, with forms that live on the roots and others that have wings.
Because almost all vineyards had to be replanted, many vineyards in Europe look quite different today from 150 years ago.
Against the phylloxera, people at first even tried to flood vineyards or to inject poison into the soil.

teile.einleitung: Plankton are tiny living things that float in water and drift with the current. Most are so small that you can only see them under a microscope. Even so, plankton is enormously important: it is the food basis of almost all life in lakes and seas.
wichtigste: Plankton are living things that drift in water and cannot swim against the current.
Plant plankton is called phytoplankton, animal plankton zooplankton.
Phytoplankton makes food and oxygen using sunlight.
Young whitefish at first feed on tiny plankton.
Even huge whales such as the blue whale eat plankton.
The name comes from Greek and means “the wanderer”.

abschnitte.text: **Plankton** includes all living things that float in water and are carried by the current. The term was introduced in 1887 by the German marine researcher Victor Hensen. It comes from the Greek word for “the wanderer”. Most plankton organisms are tiny, but even large jellyfish count as plankton, because they drift with the current.

**Phytoplankton** consists of tiny algae and bacteria, for example diatoms with shells of glass. Like plants, they use sunlight to make sugar and **oxygen**, which is called photosynthesis. A large part of the oxygen on Earth comes from the phytoplankton of the seas. That is why it lives mainly in the upper, bright layers of water.

**Zooplankton** are tiny animals, for example water fleas, copepods and rotifers. The larvae of many fish, mussels and crustaceans also drift in the water as plankton at first. Many zooplankton animals migrate upwards every night to eat algae, and back down into the dark depths by day. In the Southern Ocean, **krill** forms huge swarms that whales, penguins and seals live on.

Swiss lakes are also teeming with plankton. Young **whitefish** at first eat tiny plankton, and adult whitefish also feed mainly on zooplankton. When too many nutrients get into the water, algae multiply strongly, which is called an **algal bloom**. The Burgundy blood alga used to turn Lake Murten red at times, and according to legend it was meant to be the blood of the Burgundians from the Battle of Murten in 1476.

Plankton stands right at the start of the **food chain** in water. Small fish eat plankton, larger fish eat small fish, and so on up to predatory fish, seals and humans. Even the largest animals in the world, such as the blue whale and the whale shark, feed on plankton. Without plankton there would be hardly any life in lakes and seas.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny algae and bacteria that float in water and carry out photosynthesis.
Tiny animals that drift in water, such as water fleas.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen.
A strong multiplication of algae that can colour the water.

gewusst: Every second breath we take contains oxygen that comes from marine plankton.
Some plankton glows at night when the water is disturbed, making waves glitter blue.
With a fine plankton net you can also catch plankton in a Swiss pond and look at it under a magnifying glass.

teile.einleitung: Pythons are large, non-venomous giant snakes from Africa, Asia and Australia. They kill their prey by wrapping their powerful body around it. According to today's classification, the python family (Pythonidae) includes around 40 species, among them some of the longest snakes in the world.
wichtigste: Pythons form the snake family Pythonidae.
The family includes around 40 species.
Pythons live naturally in Africa, Asia and Australia.
They are non-venomous and kill their prey by constriction.
Pythons lay eggs, whereas most boas give birth to live young.
With heat-sensing pits in their lips they sense the body heat of their prey.
The name comes from a serpent in Greek legend that Apollo killed at Delphi.

abschnitte.text: Pythons have a muscular body and a beautifully patterned skin of scales. Sizes vary greatly: the small pygmy python grows only about 60 centimetres long. The **reticulated python** from South-East Asia, by contrast, is regarded as the longest snake in the world and can grow to over 6 metres. Beside the vent sit small claws, the **anal spurs**, which are remains of the hind legs with a stunted thigh bone.

Pythons live naturally in Africa south of the Sahara, in South and South-East Asia and in Australia. They are found in rainforests, savannas, swamps and rocky areas. Some species live on the ground, others climb trees well. In Florida the Burmese python was brought in by humans and is now an **invasive species** there, eating many native animals.

Many pythons have small **pit organs** on their lips with which they sense heat radiation. In this way they track down warm-blooded prey such as mice or birds even in the dark. In pythons these pits lie in the lip scales themselves, in boas, by contrast, between the scales. A study found in 2010 that a protein called TRPA1 works in these organs as an infrared sensor.

Pythons lay eggs, and in this they differ from most **boas**, which give birth to live young. The females of many species coil around their clutch and guard it. In the Burmese python they even warm the eggs by rhythmic shivering of their muscles. The males use their anal spurs when mating, to stimulate the female and position her.

The name python comes from Greek legend. There a giant serpent called Python guarded the **oracle** of Delphi until the god Apollo killed it. The French naturalist François Marie Daudin set up the genus Python in 1803. Today the species are assigned to several genera, which together form the family Pythonidae.

The **royal python** from West Africa is a popular terrarium animal because it is calm and curls up into a ball when in danger. Large species, however, need a lot of space, warmth and experience.
