Many pythons are threatened by loss of habitat, hunting for their skin and the animal trade. For humans, most pythons are harmless, and only very large animals can become dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake that wraps itself around its prey and kills it that way instead of poisoning it.
A sense organ on the lips with which a snake senses heat.
A small claw beside the vent, a remnant of the hind legs.
An animal or plant that was brought in by humans and spreads strongly.

gewusst: After a large meal, a python can go for weeks or even months without food.
The programming language Python is not named after the snake, but after the British comedy group Monty Python.
While digesting a large prey, a python's heart can grow noticeably larger.

teile.einleitung: Beneficial animals are animals that help people by eating pests or pollinating plants. The best-known beneficial animal is the ladybird, which devours aphids. Farmers and gardeners use beneficial animals deliberately in order to have to spray less poison.
wichtigste: Beneficial animals are animals that are used deliberately for pest control.
Ladybirds and their larvae eat aphids.
Lacewings, parasitic wasps and predatory mites are also important beneficial animals.
Bees and bumblebees count as beneficial animals because they pollinate flowers.
The use of beneficial animals is called biological pest control.
Whether an animal is beneficial or a pest is decided by the human point of view.

abschnitte.text: A beneficial animal is an animal that brings people an advantage. Usually it eats **pests**, that is, animals that damage plants or stored food. Other beneficial animals pollinate flowers or break down leaves into fertile soil. The classification is a human one, because in nature every animal has its own role.

The **ladybird** and its larvae eat large numbers of aphids. The larvae of the lacewing are even called ‘aphid lions’. Tiny **parasitic wasps** lay their eggs in pests, which are then eaten from the inside. Predatory mites hunt spider mites, which harm cucumbers and beans.

In greenhouses beneficial animals are often released deliberately, and you can even buy them. In Switzerland Trichogramma parasitic wasps have been used on maize fields for decades against the European corn borer. This method is called **biological pest control**. It saves chemical plant protection products and spares other animals.

In the garden too there are many helpers: hedgehogs eat slugs, birds peck caterpillars, and bats hunt mosquitoes at night. Earwigs devour aphids in fruit trees. Anyone who wants to encourage beneficial animals leaves hedges, deadwood and piles of leaves standing. An **insect hotel** offers wild bees a place to breed.

Some animals are useful or a nuisance depending on the situation. A mole loosens the soil and eats larvae, but throws up hills in the lawn. Wasps hunt many insects, but disturb at the cake table. For nature the rule is: all animals are part of an **ecosystem**.

Many beneficial animals are becoming rarer through insecticides, a lack of flowers and tidied-up landscapes. **Flower strips** at the edge of a field offer them food and shelter. In Switzerland farmers receive payments if they create such areas. In this way you help nature and agriculture at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that damages plants, stored food or objects.
Fighting pests with the help of their natural enemies instead of with poison.
The young form of an insect, which often looks quite different from the adult animal.
The transfer of pollen so that fruit and seeds form.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva eats several hundred aphids during its development.
Some parasitic wasps used against pests are smaller than half a millimetre.
Over a thousand years ago Chinese farmers already used ants in citrus trees against pests.

teile.einleitung: The Iberian lynx is the smallest lynx in the world and lives only in Spain and Portugal. For a long time it was considered the most endangered cat species on Earth. Thanks to large conservation programmes, it has recovered remarkably well in recent years.
wichtigste: The Iberian lynx lives on the Iberian Peninsula, in Spain and Portugal.
It is the smallest lynx in the world.
For a long time it was considered the most endangered cat species in the world.
Its main food is wild rabbits.
Around 2002 there were fewer than 100 animals.
Thanks to breeding and release into the wild, over 2,000 Iberian lynxes live there again today (as of 2024).
In Switzerland, by contrast, the larger Eurasian lynx lives.

abschnitte.text: The Iberian lynx is called **Lynx pardinus** in science. It weighs about 9 to 15 kilograms, and males are heavier than females. Its yellowish-brown fur is covered with strong dark spots, a bit like a leopard's. Typical features are the **ear tufts** with black bunches of hair and a striking ruff of fur on the cheeks.

The Iberian lynx lives only on the **Iberian Peninsula** in the south-west of Europe. Most of the animals live in Andalusia, for example in the Sierra Morena and around Doñana National Park. Thanks to releases, there are now populations again in other parts of Spain and in Portugal. It likes a mix of scrubland, woods and open areas.

The Iberian lynx is a specialist, because **wild rabbits** make up by far the largest part of its food. A grown-up lynx needs roughly one rabbit a day. When diseases such as **myxomatosis** decimated the rabbits, the lynxes went hungry too. Now and then it also eats birds, mice or young deer.

Hunting, road building, the destruction of its habitat and a shortage of rabbits caused the population to fall sharply. Around the year 2002, fewer than 100 Iberian lynxes lived in the wild. At that time it was considered the most endangered cat species in the world. Many animals also died in **road accidents**.

Spain and Portugal started a large **breeding programme** and built breeding stations. Young lynxes were released in suitable areas, and rabbits were also resettled. By 2024 the population had grown to over 2,000 animals. As a result, in 2024 the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the Iberian lynx down from endangered to **vulnerable**.

In Switzerland it is not the Iberian lynx that lives, but the larger **Eurasian lynx**. It had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1971. Today it roams through the Jura and the Alps and hunts mainly roe deer and chamois there. The two lynx species are closely related.

begriffe.erklaerung: The peninsula in the south-west of Europe that contains Spain and Portugal.
Ears with long tufts of hair at the tip, typical of lynxes.
Letting animals from breeding or care go out into nature.
A dangerous viral disease in rabbits.

gewusst: The Iberian lynx is the best-known example of how an almost extinct cat species can be saved.
In Spain, special tunnels were built under roads so that lynxes can safely cross beneath the carriageway.
An Iberian lynx is only about half as heavy as a large Eurasian lynx.

teile.einleitung: Romulus and Remus are the twins from the famous founding legend of the city of Rome. According to the legend, they were abandoned as babies and suckled and saved by a she-wolf. Later Romulus is said to have founded the city of Rome.
wichtigste: Romulus and Remus are twin brothers from a Roman legend.
A she-wolf is said to have suckled the abandoned babies.
A shepherd named Faustulus then brought up the twins.
According to the legend, Romulus founded the city of Rome in 753 BC.
In a dispute over the city, Romulus killed his brother Remus.
The she-wolf with the twins is still the emblem of Rome today.

abschnitte.text: The mother of the twins was the king's daughter **Rhea Silvia**, and the father was the god of war, Mars. Her uncle Amulius had seized the throne from her father Numitor. He feared that the children might later take power from him. That is why he ordered the babies to be drowned in the River Tiber.

The servants set the twins out on the Tiber in a basket, but the basket ran aground on the bank. There a **she-wolf** found the hungry children and suckled them. A woodpecker is also said to have brought them food, because both animals were regarded as sacred to Mars. Finally the shepherd **Faustulus** discovered them and brought them up with his wife Acca Larentia.

As adults, the brothers put their grandfather Numitor back on the throne as king. After that they wanted to build a city of their own where they had been rescued. But they quarrelled over who should found and name the city, and asked the flight of birds about it. Romulus chose the hill **Palatine**, Remus the Aventine, and the Romans later celebrated 21 April 753 BC as the founding day.

Romulus drew a furrow as the boundary for the new city wall. Remus jumped over it in mockery, and Romulus killed him in anger. In this way Romulus became the first king of Rome, and the city received his name. Historians see in this a **legend**, because in reality Rome slowly arose from several villages.

The most famous depiction is the **Capitoline Wolf**, a bronze figure in the Capitoline Museums in Rome. For a long time it was believed to be over 2,000 years old. More recent studies suggest that it was cast only in the Middle Ages. The two children beneath her were certainly added only in the Renaissance.

The she-wolf with the twins is still the symbol of the city of Rome. You see her on coats of arms, coins, stamps and in the badge of the football club AS Roma. The legend shows that in antiquity the **wolf** was regarded not only as dangerous, but also as strong and protective. Real wolves, however, do not bring up human children.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old tale with a true core or entirely invented, which often explains how something came about.
Two siblings who are born at the same birth.
One of the seven hills of Rome, on which Romulus is said to have founded the city.
A famous bronze figure of a she-wolf in Rome, beneath which the twins sit.

gewusst: The name Rome is said to come from Romulus, but many researchers suspect that it was rather the other way round.
In the watching of the birds, Remus is said to have seen six vultures, but Romulus twelve.
Rome still celebrates its birthday every year on 21 April.

teile.einleitung: The earwig is a small brown insect with a pair of pincers at the rear end, which lives in gardens all over Switzerland. The German word ‘Ohrwurm’ has, however, a second meaning: it is also the name for a song that will not leave your head, in English an earworm. Both are harmless, even if you do not get rid of them so easily.
wichtigste: The common earwig is an insect with pincers on its abdomen.
It is nocturnal and hides by day in narrow crevices.
Earwigs eat aphids and are therefore useful in the garden.
The mother cares for her eggs and young, which is rare in insects.
A song that will not leave your head is also called an Ohrwurm in German.
The English word ‘earworm’ was taken over from German.

abschnitte.text: The **common earwig** is the best-known member of the earwigs in Europe. It grows to about 1 to 1.5 centimetres long and is glossy brown. At the rear end it carries pincers, which are strongly curved in males and almost straight in females. For people it is completely harmless.

Earwigs are **nocturnal** and hide by day under bark, stones or in flowers. They eat aphids and small insects, but also parts of plants and ripe fruit. Gardeners often hang flowerpots filled with straw upside down in fruit trees. In them earwigs find a hiding place and eat aphids at night.

In autumn or winter the female lays a few dozen eggs in a small hollow in the ground. She guards the eggs and licks them clean so that they do not go mouldy. The newly hatched young too are looked after for a time. This **brood care** is rather unusual in insects.

A musical **earworm** is a short melody that repeats itself in your head constantly. Usually they are catchy refrains with simple rhythms. Experts speak of an involuntary memory of music. Almost everyone knows it, and it is completely normal.

Often it helps to listen to the song once all the way to the end. Some people chew gum or solve a tricky puzzle to distract the brain. Another song can also push out the earworm. Usually the **musical earworm** goes away by itself after some time.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that is on the move at night and sleeps by day.
The care of parents for eggs and young.
The two hard appendages at the rear end of the earwig.
The part of a song that repeats several times.

gewusst: In the past people believed that earwigs crawled into the ears of sleeping people at night, which is not true.
The English word ‘earworm’ is a literal translation from the German.
Musical earworms are mostly only a short piece of a song, rarely the whole song.

teile.einleitung: Sand eels are small, eel-like sea fishes that bury themselves in the sand in a flash. Despite their name they are not true eels. For many seabirds, seals and large fishes they are one of the most important sources of food.
wichtigste: A sand eel is a small, eel-like sea fish that buries itself in the sand.
Sand eels form a family of their own and are not related to the true eels.
They live in large shoals above sandy sea floors.
Well-known species in the North Sea are the small sand eel and the greater sand eel.
Puffins and other seabirds often feed their chicks with sand eels.
In the North Sea, sand eels are caught in large quantities and made into fishmeal.

abschnitte.text: Sand eels have a long, thin, silvery body with a pointed snout. Depending on the species they grow to about 15 to 35 centimetres long. The lower jaw sticks out, and **pelvic fins** are mostly missing. Their slim body is ideal for boring into the sand.

Sand eels live in coastal waters with loose **sandy bottoms**, for example in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea and the Atlantic. By day they swim in shoals, and at night and in winter they bury themselves in the sand. When danger threatens, they vanish head first into the bottom within seconds. If the sand is too muddy, they cannot live there.

Sand eels eat mainly **plankton**, that is, tiny crustaceans and fish larvae in the water. They hunt by sight and snap at single prey animals. In spring and summer they build up a layer of fat. They live on it in winter, when they rest in the sand.

Sand eels are a central link in the **food web** of the sea. Puffins, kittiwakes, terns, seals, cod and mackerel eat them. In photos, puffins often carry several sand eels crosswise in their beaks. If there are too few sand eels, many seabird chicks starve.

In the North Sea, sand eels are caught in very large quantities, above all by Danish ships. They are hardly eaten, but are made into **fishmeal** and fish oil, which is used as feed in fish farms. Because seabirds suffer as a result, Great Britain banned sand eel fishing in its waters of the North Sea in 2024. The warming of the seas also harms sand eels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of fishes that swim together.
Tiny living things that drift in the water.
Ground, dried fish that is used as animal feed.
All the feeding relationships between the living things of a habitat.

gewusst: A puffin can carry more than ten sand eels crosswise in its beak at once.
Sand eels can bury themselves so fast that all you see is a small cloud of sand.

teile.einleitung: Omega-3 fatty acids are especially valuable fats that our body needs for the brain, eyes and heart. It cannot make some of them itself, so we have to take them in with our food. A lot of them are found in oily sea fish such as salmon.
wichtigste: Salmon flesh gives humans especially large amounts of omega-3 fatty acids.
Omega-3 fatty acids are among the unsaturated fatty acids.
Alpha-linolenic acid is essential, because the body cannot make it itself.
Fish take in omega-3 fatty acids through algae and plankton.
Good plant sources are linseed, rapeseed oil, walnuts and chia seeds.
Omega-3 fatty acids are important for the brain, eyes and heart.

abschnitte.text: Fats consist to a large extent of **fatty acids**, long chains of carbon atoms. In unsaturated fatty acids there are so-called double bonds in the chain. In omega-3 fatty acids the first double bond lies at the third carbon atom from the end of the chain. This end is called omega, after the last letter of the Greek alphabet.

The three best-known omega-3 fatty acids are called ALA, EPA and DHA. **ALA** (alpha-linolenic acid) occurs mainly in plants and is essential for humans. **EPA** and **DHA** are found mainly in oily sea fish. From ALA the body can make only small amounts of EPA and DHA.

Oily fish such as salmon, herring, mackerel and sardines are especially rich in EPA and DHA. The fish do not make them themselves, however, but get them through **algae** and plankton in their food. Plant sources are linseed, linseed oil, rapeseed oil, walnuts and chia seeds. For people who do not eat fish there is oil from algae.

abschnitte.titel: What does the body need them for?
abschnitte.text: DHA is an important building block of the brain and of the **retina** in the eye. That is why omega-3 fatty acids are especially important for growing children and in pregnancy. They also contribute to a healthy heart and normal blood fat levels. The body also uses them to make messenger substances that influence inflammation.

Around 1930 researchers in the USA showed that rats fall ill without certain fatty acids. In this way it was recognised that some fats are **essential**. In the 1970s Danish researchers studied the Inuit in Greenland, who ate a lot of fish and seal meat. They found that heart attacks were comparatively rare there, which greatly increased interest in omega-3.

The Swiss dietary recommendations advise eating fish once or twice a week. In doing so one should pay attention to sustainably caught or farmed fish, because many seas are **overfished**. Anyone who eats little fish can add a little rapeseed oil or a handful of walnuts every day. A spoonful of ground linseed in the muesli also provides omega-3.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of fats that consists of a chain of carbon atoms.
Necessary for life and not something the body can make itself.
The light-sensitive layer in the eye with which we see.
A fatty acid with double bonds, usually liquid at room temperature.

gewusst: The omega-3 fatty acids in salmon originally come from tiny algae in the sea.
Our brain consists to a large extent of fat, and DHA is one of its most important fats.
Baumnüsse, as walnuts are called in Switzerland, are one of the best plant sources of omega-3.

teile.einleitung: Pelicans are large waterbirds with a huge bill and a stretchable throat pouch beneath it. With it they catch fish like with a landing net. There are eight species of pelican worldwide, living on lakes, rivers and coasts.
wichtigste: The pelican family (Pelecanidae) includes eight species alive today.
Pelicans belong to the order Pelecaniformes.
Their closest relatives are the shoebill and the hamerkop.
The throat pouch of a large pelican holds about 11 litres of water.
The Australian pelican has the longest bill of all birds, at up to about 50 cm.
The Dalmatian pelican is the heaviest species, the brown pelican the smallest.
In pelicans, all four toes are joined by webbing.

abschnitte.text: Pelicans have a long neck, short legs and a very long bill with a **throat pouch** of stretchable skin. On their feet, all four toes are joined by **webbing**, so they paddle well. Under the skin and even into the bones they have many air sacs, which give them buoyancy in the water. In great heat they flutter the skin of the throat and throat pouch to cool down.

The **Dalmatian pelican** is regarded as the heaviest species and is one of the heaviest flying birds in the world. Its wings can reach a span of over three metres. The Australian pelican has the longest bill of all birds, at up to about 50 cm. The **brown pelican** from the Americas is the smallest of the eight species.

Pelicans eat mainly fish. Many species swim side by side in groups and drive fish into shallow water, where they scoop them out with their throat pouch. Then they let the water drain out at the sides and swallow the catch. The brown pelican, by contrast, plunges head first into the sea from the air to catch fish.

Pelicans live on every continent except Antarctica. In Europe the **great white pelican** and the Dalmatian pelican breed, mainly in south-eastern Europe, for example in the Danube Delta. Pelicans breed in colonies, often on islands or in reeds. In Switzerland you see pelicans almost only in zoos, or very rarely as lost visitors.

The name “pelican” comes from the ancient Greek word **pelekys**, which means “axe”, probably because of the shape of the bill. The Swedish naturalist Carl von Linné described the genus Pelecanus in 1758. Molecular studies show that the shoebill and the hamerkop are the closest relatives of the pelicans. Earlier, people thought that cormorants and gannets were their closest relatives.

Some pelican species are threatened by drained wetlands, disturbance at nesting sites and fishing nets. The Dalmatian pelican was rare in Europe for a long time, but its numbers are partly recovering thanks to **conservation projects**. In Christian art the pelican is an old symbol of self-sacrifice. According to a legend it is said to have fed its young with its own blood, which is not true.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stretchable pocket of skin under the bill with which pelicans catch fish.
Skin between the toes that acts like a paddle when swimming.
A large group of birds that breed close together.
The force that pushes something upwards in water and lets it float.

gewusst: A pelican's throat pouch holds more water than its stomach holds food.
Pelicans can soar for hours, almost without flapping their wings.
Pelicans have existed for a very long time, and fossils show that their bill has looked almost the same for millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Oxygen is an invisible gas that almost all animals need to live. They breathe it in with lungs, gills or through the skin. If oxygen is missing, for example at the bottom of a lake, animals and even their eggs can suffocate.
wichtigste: Oxygen is a chemical element with the symbol O.
Air consists of about 21 per cent oxygen.
Plants and algae release oxygen during photosynthesis.
Animals need oxygen to gain energy from food.
Fishes take the oxygen dissolved in the water with their gills.
Whitefish eggs lie on the lake bed and can suffocate if there is a lack of oxygen.
Some Swiss lakes are therefore aerated artificially.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen is a **chemical element** and has the symbol O. At normal temperature it is a colourless gas without a smell. In the air it occurs as a molecule of two atoms, which is written O2. Oxygen is also contained in water, because water consists of hydrogen and oxygen.

Mammals, birds and reptiles breathe with **lungs**, fishes with **gills**, and insects through fine tubes in the body. In the body, the oxygen is carried by the blood to all the cells. There it slowly burns the food, and that produces energy. Carbon dioxide is produced as waste and is breathed out again.

Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from plants, algae and bacteria. In **photosynthesis** they use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide and release oxygen. A large part comes from the sea, from tiny algae in the plankton. A very long time ago there was still almost no oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.

In water, much less oxygen is dissolved than in air, and warm water contains less than cold. If too many nutrients from fertiliser get into a lake, many algae grow. When they die, bacteria use up the oxygen at the bottom as they break them down. **Whitefish** lay their eggs on the lake bed, where they can then suffocate, which is why lakes such as Lake Baldegg and Lake Sempach have been **aerated artificially**.

Oxygen was discovered in the 1770s, independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Sweden and Joseph Priestley in England. The Frenchman Antoine Lavoisier recognised that oxygen is used up in burning. Without oxygen there is no **fire**. That is why you smother flames, for example, with a fire blanket.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance that cannot be broken down into other substances.
The process by which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen.
The breathing organs of fishes, which take oxygen from the water.
When too many nutrients get into the water and too many algae grow.

gewusst: Liquid oxygen is light blue and is attracted by magnets.
On high mountains such as Mount Everest, you get only about a third as much oxygen with each breath as at sea level.

teile.einleitung: The barn swallow, in German Rauchschwalbe, is an elegant migratory bird with a deeply forked tail that breeds in stables and barns in summer. With its twittering song and its fast flights over meadows, it announces spring in Switzerland. It spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
wichtigste: The barn swallow is about 17 to 19 centimetres long, including the tail.
Its tail is deeply forked with long outer feathers.
It breeds in Europe, Asia and North America.
It likes best to live in open farmland near farms.
It catches insects in flight and flies at up to about 50 to 60 km/h.
It usually raises two, sometimes three broods per summer.
In Switzerland things are getting harder for it, because modern stables often offer no access and insects are lacking.

abschnitte.text: The barn swallow is about 17 to 19 centimetres long, and the **tail streamers** make up a large part of that. Its upperside gleams metallic blue-black, and the forehead and throat are **rusty red**. The belly is white to cream. Males usually have longer tail streamers than females, which matters when choosing a partner.

The barn swallow lives in open **farmland** with meadows, pastures and farms. It builds its cup-shaped nest of small lumps of clay and stalks inside stables, barns and sheds, usually on a beam. Often several pairs breed in loose small **colonies** in the same building. Many return to the same nest every year and only repair it.

Barn swallows feed almost only on **insects** such as flies, mosquitoes and small beetles, which they catch in flight. They often hunt close above the ground or over stretches of water and reach up to about 50 to 60 kilometres per hour. For their young they form many insects into a compact **food ball** in the beak. Before rain they often fly low, because then the insects fly lower too.

The female usually lays 4 to 5 eggs and incubates them for about two weeks. After that both parents feed the young, which fly out after about three weeks. In one summer there are usually two, sometimes three **broods**. In the best case, barn swallows can live up to about 8 years, but many die young.

In September the swallows often gather on power lines and then migrate south together. They cross the Mediterranean and the **Sahara** and spend the winter in Africa south of the desert. In March and April they return, and many find exactly their old stable again. On this **bird migration** they cover thousands of kilometres every year.

In Switzerland the barn swallow is still widespread, but its numbers have fallen. Modern stables are often closed, and there are fewer insects and fewer open puddles with clay for building nests. Farming families can help by leaving a window or an **entrance opening** open. Droppings boards under the nests and meadows with many flowers and insects also support the swallows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that flies back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter area.
A group of animals of one species that breed or live close together.
The eggs or young of a pair of birds from one clutch.
A landscape used by humans, with fields, meadows and farms.

gewusst: The song of the barn swallow sounds like a cheerful, twittering chat and often ends with a buzzing trill.
Barn swallows drink in flight by gliding just above a stretch of water and taking up water with the beak.
The proverb “One swallow does not make a summer” means that a single sign proves nothing yet.

teile.einleitung: Pollen is the fine, mostly yellow dust that flowering plants produce. Each pollen grain carries the male genetic material of a plant and is so small that you can only really see it under a microscope. Bees collect pollen as the most important protein food for their brood.
wichtigste: Pollen is the flower dust produced by the stamens of a flower.
A pollen grain contains the male reproductive cells of the plant.
For seeds and fruit to form, pollen has to reach the stigma of a flower.
Pollen is carried by the wind or by animals such as bees, bumblebees and butterflies.
For bees, pollen is the most important source of protein.
Some people react to pollen with hay fever.
The shell of pollen grains is so resistant that it can last for thousands of years.

abschnitte.text: Pollen is made in the **anthers**, which sit on top of the stamens of a flower. A single pollen grain is usually only about 0.01 to 0.1 millimetres in size. In large amounts, pollen looks like yellow, orange or sometimes even red powder. Each plant species has pollen grains with a shape of its own, and some are round, others spiky or have small air sacs.

When pollen reaches the **stigma** of a flower of the same species, this is called **pollination**. After that a seed can form, from which a new plant grows. Many flowers attract insects with colours, scent and sweet nectar. While the insects drink nectar, pollen sticks to their hairy bodies and is carried to the next flower. Without pollinators there would be far fewer apples, cherries or strawberries.

Grasses, cereals and many trees such as **hazel**, birch or pine are pollinated by the wind. They usually have inconspicuous flowers with no scent. In return they make huge amounts of light pollen, which can fly for kilometres. In spring you sometimes see yellow streaks on puddles and cars, and this is pine or spruce pollen.

Honeybees collect pollen and carry it in the baskets on their hind legs to the hive. There they mix it with nectar and saliva and store it as **bee bread** in the honeycomb. The nurse bees eat the pollen and feed the larvae with it. A bee colony needs, roughly estimated, 20 to 30 kilograms of pollen a year.

In some people the immune system fights against harmless pollen, which is called **pollen allergy** or hay fever. Typical signs are sneezing, a runny nose and itchy, watering eyes. In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss measures at several stations how much pollen is in the air and publishes pollen forecasts. The first pollen of the year often flies as early as January or February, mostly from hazel and alder.

The shell of a pollen grain is built from an extremely resistant substance. That is why pollen is often preserved for thousands of years in lake beds and bogs. Researchers identify it under the microscope and so find out which plants grew in an area in the past. This science is called **pollen analysis** and helps, for example, to research the climate in Switzerland after the last Ice Age.

begriffe.erklaerung: When pollen reaches the stigma of a flower so that a seed can form.
The part of the flower in which pollen is made.
The sticky tip in the middle of the flower that catches pollen.
Pollen stored in the beehive, mixed with nectar, as food for the brood.
Oversensitivity of the body to pollen, also called hay fever.

gewusst: With pollen grains from honey you can find out which area the honey comes from.
A single hazel catkin can release millions of pollen grains.
Pollen grains are sometimes even used in criminal investigation to find out where someone has been.

teile.einleitung: The backswimmer, in German Rückenschwimmer, is a water bug that, as its name says, rows through the water belly up. You find it in almost every pond and pool in Switzerland. It is a skilful predator and can also fly.
wichtigste: The backswimmer is a bug that lives in the water.
It swims with its back down and its belly up.
Unlike the pond skater, it swims under the surface of the water.
It uses its long hind legs like oars.
It breathes air, which it takes under water with it as a silvery supply.
It hunts insects, tadpoles and small fish.
Its sting can be painful for people too.

abschnitte.text: The common backswimmer is about 14 to 16 millimetres long. Its body is shaped like a **boat hull**, with an arched back on which it lies in the water. The hind legs are very long and fringed with fine swimming hairs. The large eyes help it to spot prey and enemies early.

The backswimmer rows with its hind legs in strong strokes, rather like a person with oars. As it does so it always lies upside down in the water. This is how it differs from the **pond skater**, which walks on the surface of the water, while the backswimmer swims beneath it. If it stops rowing, it drifts upwards because of its air supply.

Although it lives in the water, the backswimmer breathes **air**. It fetches it at the surface with the tip of its abdomen and stores it under the wings and between fine hairs on the belly. This air supply gleams silvery like a small bubble. When the air is used up, it swims back up and fetches new.

The backswimmer is a **predator**. It often hangs just under the surface and senses with sensory hairs the ripples made by an insect that has fallen into the water. Then it grabs the prey with its forelegs and stabs it with its **piercing beak**. It injects digestive juice and sucks the prey dry, tadpoles and small fish too.

Backswimmers have wings and can fly well. In this way they find new ponds, pools or garden ponds, often soon after these have been made. In spring the female lays her **eggs** in water plants. The larvae look like small adults without wings and moult several times.

In Switzerland the backswimmer is common in pools, ponds and garden ponds. If you pick it up, it can sting with its beak, which feels like a **bee sting**. That is why it is sometimes also called the water bee. The sting is not dangerous, however, and it stops hurting after a short time.

begriffe.erklaerung: An insect with a beak for piercing and sucking.
A pointed mouthpart with which some insects pierce and suck.
The young form of an insect.
A bug that walks on the surface of the water.

gewusst: Because of its position on its back, the backswimmer's back is pale and its belly dark, the opposite of most animals.
Backswimmers find new waters in flight because they recognise the glitter of water.

teile.einleitung: The pupil is the black hole in the middle of the eye through which light falls into the inside. It gets larger or smaller depending on how bright it is. In animals it has very different shapes, from round to slit-shaped to horizontal.
wichtigste: The pupil is an opening in the coloured iris.
It regulates how much light falls into the eye.
In darkness it becomes wide, in brightness narrow.
Cats have a vertical, slit-shaped pupil, which can regulate light especially precisely.
Sheep have horizontal pupils, which help them to see almost all the way round.
Humans have round pupils.
The pupil looks black because the light is swallowed up in the eye.

abschnitte.text: The pupil is not a part but a hole in the **iris**, the coloured part of the eye. Through this hole light reaches the lens and on to the **retina**, where the image is formed. Because hardly any light comes back out of the eye, the pupil looks black. In flash photos, however, it can glow red, which is the well-known red-eye effect.

In the iris sit two small muscles. A ring-shaped muscle makes the pupil narrow, and another pulls it wide open. In bright light the pupil narrows quickly, which is called the **pupillary reflex**. In this way the eye protects itself from too much light, much like the aperture of a camera.

Cats, foxes, crocodiles and many snakes have vertical **slit pupils**. A slit pupil can open and close much more than a round one. That is why cats see well at dusk and yet are not dazzled by the glare of midday light. Researchers found that it is mainly smaller animals that hunt by ambush that have vertical pupils.

Sheep, goats, horses and deer have horizontal, rectangular pupils. These animals are **prey animals** and have to spot enemies early. The horizontal shape helps them keep the horizon in good view almost all the way round. When a sheep lowers its head to graze, its eyes even rotate so that the pupils stay horizontal.

Cephalopods such as the cuttlefish have a pupil shaped like a W. Geckos have slit pupils with small holes, which widen into a round opening at night. Big cats such as lions and tigers, by contrast, have **round pupils** like us humans. In humans the pupils also change with feelings such as joy, fear or great interest.

Doctors often shine a small light into the eyes. They check whether both pupils narrow equally fast and equally strongly. This shows whether nerves and brain are working properly. At the eye doctor's you sometimes get drops that **dilate** the pupil so that the doctor can see better into the eye.

begriffe.erklaerung: The coloured part of the eye, in the middle of which the pupil lies.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye on which the image is formed.
The automatic narrowing of the pupil in bright light.
An elongated, narrow pupil, such as cats have.

gewusst: In a cat, the area of the pupil can change many times more than in humans.
The name pupil comes from the Latin pupilla, little girl, because you see yourself reflected very small in someone else's pupil.

teile.einleitung: With a territory marking, animals show others that an area is already occupied. To do so they leave scents, scratch marks or droppings, or make loud noises. In this way, disputes can often be settled without a fight.
wichtigste: Territory markings show that an area is occupied.
Many animals mark with scents from special glands.
Cats mark with scent glands on the head and paws as well as with scratch marks.
Dogs and wolves mark with urine.
Birds mark their territory mainly with song.
Markings help to avoid dangerous fights.
Scent marks also reveal which animal has left them.

abschnitte.text: Many animals live in a **territory** of their own and want to keep it for themselves. Instead of keeping watch all the time, they leave signs. These **markings** work like a sign saying “Occupied”. Other animals of the same species recognise the sign and know that someone already lives here. In this way the owner of the territory saves strength and time.

The most common kind of marking is smell. Many mammals have special **scent glands**, for example on the head, feet or rump. Dogs, foxes and wolves lift a leg and put urine on trees or stones. Badgers and rabbits leave droppings at particular places. For the noses of other animals, these scent marks are like a business card with name, age and sex.

A cat marks its territory mainly with scent glands on the head and paws. When it rubs its head on furniture, door frames or on your legs, it leaves its scent. When **scratching** on trees or on the scratching post, visible marks are made and at the same time scent marks from the paws. Tomcats also often mark with urine. People mostly cannot smell these fine scent marks, but other cats can very well.

Many animals show their territory with sounds. Songbirds such as the blackbird, robin and great tit sing from high perches. Woodpeckers drum on wood with the beak, and the sound can be heard far away. **Howler monkeys** in South America call so loudly that you can hear them for kilometres. The howling of wolves also helps to keep packs at a distance.

Some markings can also be seen. In spring the roe buck rubs his antlers on young trees, which is called **fraying**, and leaves scent from glands on his forehead as he does so. Bears scratch and rub themselves on tree trunks. Many birds show themselves in conspicuous colours on their perches. Anyone who looks closely in the forest can often find such traces themselves.

Markings help to avoid **fights** in which animals might be hurt. They also show whether the owner of a territory is still there, because old scent marks fade. Scent marks also reveal whether a female is ready to mate. So markings serve not only to mark boundaries, but also for communication. They are a kind of language without words.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign with which an animal shows that an area belongs to it.
A place in the body that produces a scent.
The rubbing of antlers on trees by roe deer and deer.
A raised place from which a bird sings or watches.

gewusst: When a cat rubs its head on your legs, it is marking you as part of its territory.
Dogs can read from a single scent mark which dog has passed by.
Hippos spread their droppings with their wagging tail in order to mark their area.

teile.einleitung: The roe deer, in German Reh, is the smallest and most common deer in Switzerland and lives in forests, at forest edges and in fields. With its large eyes, its brown colour and the pale patch on its rump, it is easy to recognise. The male, the buck, carries small antlers that fall off every year and grow anew.
wichtigste: The roe deer often lives in Swiss forests, and the male carries antlers.
The male is called a buck, the female a doe, and the young one a fawn.
A fully grown roe deer weighs about 15 to 30 kilograms.
Roe deer like best to eat herbs, leaves and buds.
The buck's antlers fall off every year and grow anew.
The mating season, the rut, is in summer, around July and August.
A fawn lying alone should never be touched, but left in peace.
In the wild, roe deer live to be about 10 years old.

abschnitte.text: A roe deer is about 60 to 75 centimetres high at the shoulder and weighs 15 to 30 kilograms. In summer its coat is reddish brown, in winter greyish brown and denser. On the rump it has a pale patch, the **mirror**, which is easy to see when it flees. The **buck** carries short antlers with usually up to three points per beam, which hunters also call the horns.

Roe deer live in forests, at forest edges, in hedges and in fields, from the lowlands up into the mountains. They are choosy eaters and pick out the best **herbs**, leaves and buds. In winter, when there is little fresh greenery, they eat twigs, buds and bark of trees. Because they like to eat young shoots of firs and maples, they can harm the forest if there are too many.

Roe deer are very cautious and most active at dawn and dusk. When a roe deer notices a person, it often stands still, watches them and then flees quickly. In danger it gives a barking sound, which is called **barking alarm**. In summer roe deer live rather alone or as a mother with a fawn, in winter they join together in small groups, which are called a **herd**.

In summer, around July and August, is the **rut**. Then the buck defends his territory against other bucks and follows the does. The fertilised egg then rests for several months and begins to grow only in winter, which is called **delayed implantation**. In May or June, one or two fawns with white spots are born, which crouch well hidden in the grass.

The buck's antlers are made of bone and are shed every year in autumn or early winter. After that they grow anew, protected by a soft, well-supplied skin, the **velvet**. In spring the antlers are finished, and the buck rubs the velvet off on young trees, which is called **fraying**. With a little luck you can find a shed roe deer antler in the forest.

abschnitte.titel: Roe deer and people in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The roe deer is the most common wild hoofed animal in Switzerland and is hunted in all cantons. Its natural enemies are the lynx, the wolf and, for young fawns, also the fox. Many fawns die during mowing because they crouch in the tall grass instead of fleeing, so volunteers often search the meadows beforehand with **drones**. Anyone who finds a fawn alone should not touch it, because the mother usually comes back and might possibly abandon it because of the human scent.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female roe deer, also called a Geiss in German.
A young roe deer in its first year of life.
The mating season of deer and roe deer.
The soft skin that covers and supplies a growing antler.
The pale patch on the rump of the roe deer.

gewusst: In their first days of life, roe fawns have almost no scent of their own, which protects them from foxes.
Although roe deer mate in summer, the fawns are born only the following spring, because of delayed implantation.
The roe deer is not a child of the red deer, but a species of its own, even if both belong to the deer family.

teile.einleitung: The competence certificate for dog owners, in German Sachkundenachweis or SKN for short, was in Switzerland a compulsory course for dog owners. Anyone who got a dog had to use it to prove basic knowledge of how to handle a dog. Since 2017 it has no longer been required at federal level.
wichtigste: The competence certificate for dog owners was introduced in Switzerland in 2008.
It was meant to show that you have basic knowledge of how to handle a dog.
There was a theory course before acquiring a dog and a practical course with the dog.
At the end of 2016 the requirement was abolished by Parliament.
Some cantons still require courses of their own today.
For other animals, such as wild animals or venomous animals, competence is still required.

abschnitte.text: The **competence certificate** was a certificate that someone had attended a course about dogs. It was set out in the federal Animal Welfare Ordinance. Anyone who wanted to buy a dog for the first time had to attend a **theory course** beforehand. After the purchase, a practical course together with their own dog followed within a year.

The theory course was about what a dog needs: food, exercise, care and activity. You learned to read dogs' **body language**, for example whether a dog is afraid or wants to play. In the practical course you practised everyday situations, such as walking on the lead, meetings with other dogs or recall. The aim was that dog and person live together safely and considerately.

The course was introduced in 2008, after there had been some serious dog bite accidents before. A tragic case in Oberglatt in 2005, in which a child was killed by dogs, triggered a great debate. Later, however, it turned out that the courses reduced the number of accidents hardly measurably. That is why **Parliament** decided in 2016 to abolish the requirement, and since 2017 it no longer applies.

Since the abolition, the **cantons** may issue rules themselves. Some cantons still require courses for all dogs or for certain large dogs. In some cantons, certain dog breeds need a permit or are even banned. Anyone who wants to keep a dog should therefore ask the canton or the municipality.

Even without the requirement, experts recommend attending a course at a **dog school**. A well-trained dog is more relaxed and safer in everyday life. Every dog in Switzerland must be marked with a microchip and registered in the Amicus database. Anyone who has a dog is also responsible for damage that the animal causes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A set of federal rules that lays down how animals must be kept.
A course in which you learn knowledge without practising.
A tiny chip under the dog's skin with a number for identification.
The person who is responsible for a dog.

gewusst: Anyone who had attended the theory course once did not have to do it again for the next dog.
In Switzerland live about half a million dogs (as of around 2024).

teile.einleitung: Penguins are birds that cannot fly but are excellent at swimming and diving. Their wings have turned into strong flippers. Almost all penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, many of them in cold regions around Antarctica.
wichtigste: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim very well.
Most species live in cool or cold regions of the Southern Hemisphere.
They eat fish and small sea creatures such as krill.
Their feathers are tight and oiled with grease, which makes them waterproof.
Parents recognise their chick in the huge colony by its call.
The dark colour of the back camouflages them from enemies above.
Some species are threatened by climate change and a shortage of food.

abschnitte.text: Penguins have a streamlined body, short legs and **flippers** instead of wings. Their short feathers lie close like scales and are oiled with grease from a gland, so they stay waterproof. On their feet they have hardly any feathers, so that they can walk better and do not lose so much heat there. The back is dark and the belly light, and this **camouflage colouring** protects them from enemies above and below.

There are about 18 species of penguin. The **emperor penguin** is the largest, at over a metre tall, and the little penguin, at around 30 to 40 centimetres, is the smallest. Most species live in cool or cold regions of the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Antarctica, South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. The Galápagos penguin even lives at the equator, where cold seawater provides cooling.

Penguins eat fish, squid and small sea creatures such as **krill**. Under water they move with their flippers as if they were flying. Emperor penguins can dive over 500 metres deep and stay under water for more than 20 minutes. To make faster progress, some species leap out of the water like dolphins as they swim.

Many penguins breed in huge **colonies** with thousands of animals. When the partner comes back after breeding, the two recognise each other by their voices, and the parents find their chick by its special call. In the emperor penguin, the male incubates the egg on his feet in the middle of the Antarctic winter, protected by a fold of belly skin. The young penguins are called **chicks** and at first have a fluffy coat of down that is not yet waterproof.

In the sea, leopard seals, sea lions and orcas hunt penguins. On land, skuas are dangerous, as they take young penguins or eggs. Today some species are threatened by **climate change**, because the sea ice is shrinking and there is less food in the sea. Overfishing and oil pollution also cause them problems.

Many zoos build cool pools with rocks to climb so that penguins feel comfortable. At **Zurich Zoo** live king penguins, which in winter, in cool weather, are allowed to go for a walk through the zoo. This penguin walk is very popular with families. Penguins are also bred in zoos to preserve threatened species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals that breed together in the same place.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in huge swarms in the sea.
Colouring that makes an animal hard for enemies to see.
Soft, fluffy feathers that keep warm.

gewusst: Penguins can drink salt water, because a gland above the eyes gets rid of the salt again.
In the Arctic at the North Pole there are no wild penguins.
In winter, emperor penguins huddle close together and constantly swap places so that nobody has to freeze on the outside for too long.

teile.einleitung: Cattle are large even-toed ungulates with horns, and they include the domestic cow, but also buffalo, bison and yak. The domestic cow is one of the most important farm animals in the world and provides milk, meat and leather. In Switzerland, cows on pastures and Alpine pastures shape the picture of the landscape.
wichtigste: An adult male of cattle or buffalo is called a bull.
A female that has already had a calf is called a cow.
The domestic cow descends from the extinct aurochs.
Cattle are ruminants with a stomach made of four parts.
Wild cattle include water buffalo, bison, wisent and yak.
In Switzerland live about 1.5 million cattle (as of about 2023).
Well-known Swiss breeds are Brown Swiss, Simmental and Eringer.

abschnitte.text: The **cattle** include several species of large plant eaters with horns. Besides the domestic cow, these include the water buffalo, the African buffalo, the American bison, the European wisent and the yak from the Himalayas. All are **even-toed ungulates**, so they walk on two toes per foot. Both males and females usually carry horns. These horns grow for a lifetime and are not shed like antlers.

An adult male of cattle or buffalo is called a **bull**. A castrated male is called an ox, and it is calmer and was used in the past as a draught animal. A female that has already had a calf is a cow. A young female before her first calf is often called a Rind in Switzerland, in English a heifer. The young animals are called calves.

Cattle are **ruminants** and have a stomach made of four parts: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. First they swallow grass almost unchewed. Later they bring the food back up in small portions and chew it thoroughly in peace. In the huge rumen, countless microbes help to digest the tough grass. A cow eats many kilograms of grass or hay a day and often drinks over 50 litres of water.

The domestic cow descends from the **aurochs**, a large wild bovine. About 10,000 years ago, people in the Near East began to tame aurochs. Later a second form arose in South Asia, the zebu with its hump. The last wild aurochs died in 1627 in Poland. Today there are over a thousand different breeds of cattle worldwide.

In Switzerland live about 1.5 million cattle (as of about 2023). Well-known breeds are **Brown Swiss**, the Simmental Fleckvieh and the Holstein. In Valais lives the strong, black Eringer cattle, which is known for its cow fights. In summer, many cows spend a few months on the Alp, where cheese is made from their milk. The festive ascent to the Alp and the descent with decorated cows are old customs.

Cattle provide **milk**, from which butter, yoghurt and cheeses such as Emmental or Gruyère are made. There are also meat and leather. In the past, oxen pulled ploughs and wagons. When digesting, however, cattle give off the gas methane, which contributes to climate change. That is why research is being done on feed that produces less methane.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that brings its food back up and chews it again.
The largest part of the cattle stomach, in which microbes break down the grass.
An adult male of cattle or a male buffalo.
An extinct wild bovine from which the domestic cow descends.
A hoofed animal that walks on two toes per foot.

gewusst: A cow gives milk only after she has given birth to a calf.
Cattle see almost all the way round, because their eyes sit on the sides of the head.
The name Eringer comes from the Val d'Hérens in Valais.

teile.einleitung: Coelacanths are ancient fishes with fleshy, leg-like fins. For a long time researchers believed they had been extinct for around 66 million years. But in 1938 a fisherman off South Africa pulled a living coelacanth out of the sea, one of the greatest surprises in zoology.
wichtigste: Coelacanths belong to the lobe-finned fishes (Sarcopterygii), a group of bony fishes.
Today two living species of the genus Latimeria are known.
The first living coelacanth was caught off South Africa on 22 December 1938.
The museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer was the first to realise how special the fish was.
James Leonard Brierley Smith described it in 1939 as Latimeria chalumnae.
A second species, the Indonesian coelacanth, was discovered in 1997 on Sulawesi.
Coelacanths are regarded as “living fossils” and are strictly protected today.

abschnitte.text: A coelacanth can grow almost 2 metres long and weigh well over 80 kilograms. Its body is covered with thick, hard **scales** and is mostly steel blue with pale spots. Especially striking are the **fleshy fins**, which sit on a small stalk of bone and muscle. When swimming, it moves them in alternation, much as a four-legged animal moves its legs when walking.

On 22 December 1938 a fishing boat near the mouth of the Chalumna River in South Africa caught a strange blue fish. The curator **Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer** of the museum in East London realised that it was something special and sent a sketch to the fish researcher **J. L. B. Smith**. Because it was hot and Smith arrived only weeks later, the fish was stuffed and the innards were thrown away. As a result, the gills and inner skeleton could not be studied. In 1939 Smith named the species after the curator and the river: Latimeria chalumnae.

Smith searched for years for a second specimen and handed out leaflets offering a reward. In 1952 a coelacanth was finally caught off the **Comoros**, a group of islands between Africa and Madagascar. Smith at first took it for a genus of its own and named it “Malania” after the prime minister Daniel François Malan. The fishermen there had known the fish for a long time and called it **Gombessa**. So it became clear that the real home of the species lies around the Comoros.

In 1997 the marine biologist **Mark Erdmann** discovered a brown coelacanth at a fish market on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. The fishermen there call it “raja laut”, which means “king of the sea”. It was later described as a species of its own, the **Indonesian coelacanth** (Latimeria menadoensis). The two species live around 10,000 kilometres apart.

Coelacanths live at depths of about 150 to 700 metres on steep underwater slopes of volcanic islands. By day they often rest in **caves**, and at night they slowly go hunting for fish and squid. The females do not lay eggs into the water, but give birth to **live young**. Researchers suspect that coelacanths can live very long, perhaps up to 100 years.

Fossils of coelacanths are up to around 400 million years old. Their close relatives, the early lobe-finned fishes, were the ancestors of the first **land vertebrates**. Because only few animals are left, trade in coelacanths is banned internationally. On the Comoros there probably live only a few hundred animals, and the species is regarded as **critically endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of fishes with fleshy fins, which also includes the lungfishes and the ancestors of land animals.
A living thing that has hardly changed over a very long time.
A woman who is responsible for the collection in a museum.
The name that fishermen on the Comoros give to the coelacanth.

gewusst: Before 1938, coelacanths were known only as fossils, and people thought they had disappeared along with the dinosaurs.
The genus Latimeria bears the name of the museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer.
Coelacanths sometimes swim upside down or backwards when they are searching for prey.

teile.einleitung: The carrion crow, in German Rabenkrähe, is a large, completely black member of the crow family that almost every child in Switzerland knows. It lives in fields, in parks and in the middle of cities. Carrion crows are regarded as especially clever and can even recognise individual people.
wichtigste: The carrion crow has completely black, glossy plumage.
It weighs about 400 to 600 grams.
It is found mainly in Western Europe, including Switzerland.
Carrion crows eat almost anything, even carrion, and so help to keep nature clean.
Both parents feed the chicks in the nest.
Carrion crows become sexually mature at about 2 to 3 years.
Researchers have shown that crows can recognise human faces.

abschnitte.text: The carrion crow is about 45 to 50 centimetres long and so larger than a pigeon. Its plumage is **completely black** and shimmers slightly blue or violet in the sun. Beak and legs are also black, and the eyes of adult birds are mostly dark brown. It can be confused with the much larger **raven** or with the rook, which has pale, bare skin at the base of the beak.

The carrion crow lives mainly in **Western Europe**, also throughout Switzerland north of the Alps. Further east and south lives its close relative, the grey and black **hooded crow**. Where the two species meet, there are also hybrids. Carrion crows like open landscapes with trees, but have also adapted very well to cities.

Carrion crows are **omnivores**: they eat worms, insects, seeds, fruit, mice and sometimes the eggs of other birds. **Carrion**, that is, dead animals, and food scraps are also part of the diet. In this way they fulfil an important task as the health police of nature. Hard nuts they sometimes drop from the air onto stones or roads so that they break open.

Carrion crows often stay with the same partner for life. They build their nest of twigs high up in trees, and the female usually lays 4 to 6 eggs. After hatching, **both parent birds** feed the chicks together. Young crows without a territory of their own live in **flocks** and communicate with many different calls, for example as a warning.

Members of the crow family are among the most intelligent animals of all. Researchers have shown that crows remember the **faces** of people who have once annoyed them and scold these people even years later. They solve tricky tasks and learn from one another. Their natural enemies include larger **birds of prey** such as the goshawk or the eagle owl.

Because carrion crows sometimes damage fresh seed or silage bales in fields, they are not always popular with farmers. In Switzerland the carrion crow counts as a **huntable bird species**, but there are rules for it, such as a closed season during the breeding period. The cantons regulate the details. In cities you often see them on lawns, at bins and on roofs.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that eats both plants and animals.
The body of a dead animal.
The time of year in which an animal may not be hunted.
The bird family that includes crows, ravens, magpies and jays.

gewusst: Carrion crows and hooded crows are so closely related that experts argued for a long time whether they are two species or one.
Crows can pass on their knowledge about a dangerous person to other crows that have never seen him themselves.
Carrion crows belong to the songbirds, even though their croaking does not sound like singing.

teile.einleitung: Palm oil is a vegetable fat that is obtained from the fruits of the oil palm. It is found in very many products, from chocolate spread and biscuits to soap and cosmetics. Because rainforest is often cleared for oil palm plantations, animals such as the orangutan lose their habitat.
wichtigste: Palm oil is obtained from the flesh of the fruit of the oil palm.
It is the most produced vegetable oil in the world.
Most palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia.
For new plantations a great deal of rainforest was cleared.
As a result orangutans, tigers and many other animals lose their habitat.
Anyone who chooses products with sustainable palm oil helps to protect orangutans.
The oil palm yields much more oil per area than other oil plants.

abschnitte.text: Palm oil comes from the fruits of the **oil palm**, which originally comes from West Africa. The plum-sized, reddish fruits grow in large bunches. From the flesh palm oil is pressed, and from the kernel **palm kernel oil**. Palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature and keeps for a long time without going rancid.

Palm oil is found in many foods such as margarine, chocolate spread, biscuits, instant soups and crisps. Soaps, shampoos, lipsticks and detergents also often contain palm oil or substances made from it. It is also used as a **biofuel** for vehicles. On the list of ingredients it is usually given as palm oil, palm fat or vegetable fat from palms.

Oil palms grow only in warm, damp regions near the equator, which is exactly where **rainforests** stand. Above all on Borneo and Sumatra huge areas of forest were cleared for plantations. As a result the **orangutan**, the Sumatran tiger and the Bornean elephant are severely threatened. When forests are burnt, a lot of smoke is also produced, and carbon dioxide is released, which warms the climate.

Giving up palm oil altogether is not necessarily the solution. Other oil plants such as rape, soya or coconut need many times as much land for the same amount of oil. That is why many organisations rely on **sustainable palm oil**, for which no new rainforest is cleared. A well-known label for this comes from the RSPO, a Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, which was founded in 2004.

Switzerland imports palm oil, among other things, for the food industry. In March 2021 Swiss voters narrowly approved a **free trade agreement** with Indonesia. It states that tariff concessions apply only to palm oil that has been produced according to certain sustainability rules. Many Swiss companies say they now use certified palm oil or replace it with local rapeseed oil.

Read the list of ingredients on packaging and look out for notes on sustainable palm oil. Home-cooked food usually contains fewer hidden fats than ready-made products. Organisations such as the Swiss foundation PanEco work directly in Indonesia for orangutans. Less waste and mindful **consumption** also help the rainforest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tropical palm from whose fruits palm oil is obtained.
A large area on which only a single crop is grown.
Removing forest in order to make room for fields or settlements.
Managing things so that nature and people can live well in the future too.

gewusst: An oil palm can bear fruit for over 20 years.
A fruit bunch of the oil palm can weigh more than 20 kilograms.
Around half of all packaged products in the supermarket contain palm oil, environmental organisations estimate.

teile.einleitung: The eastern grey kangaroo is one of the largest kangaroos in Australia. Unlike the red kangaroo, it lives more in woodland and green areas with plenty of grass. With powerful leaps it can hop surprisingly fast and far.
wichtigste: The eastern grey kangaroo lives in the east of Australia and in Tasmania.
It prefers open woodland and green grassland to dry deserts.
Its fur is grey to greyish brown.
It eats mainly grasses and herbs.
Kangaroos live in groups called mobs.
The young grows for many months in its mother’s pouch.
Males are much larger and heavier than females.

abschnitte.text: The eastern grey kangaroo is scientifically called **Macropus giganteus**. It has dense, grey to greyish-brown fur and a pale underside. Standing upright, large males become almost as tall as a grown person and often weigh over 50 kilograms. The long, strong **tail** serves as a support when sitting and for balance when leaping.

This kangaroo lives in the east of Australia, from Queensland to Victoria, and also on the island of **Tasmania**. It likes open woodland, bushland and meadows near trees. Unlike the red kangaroo, it avoids the dry deserts of the interior. By day it often rests in the shade, and to feed it comes out onto the meadows at dusk.

The grey kangaroo is a **herbivore**. It eats mainly grasses, but also herbs and sometimes leaves. Like cows, it has a large, many-chambered stomach in which micro-organisms break down the tough plant food. It gets much of its water from the plants it eats.

The young, which is called a **joey**, is born after a gestation of only about 36 days and is then as tiny as a bean. It crawls into its mother’s **pouch** by itself and fastens onto a teat. There it grows for almost a year before it leaves the pouch for good. Even after that it still drinks milk for a while.

Grey kangaroos live in groups called **mobs**. They move by hopping with both hind legs at the same time and reach over 50 kilometres per hour. A single leap can be about 8 metres long. Males sometimes fight each other by rearing up, wrestling with their arms and kicking with their hind legs.

The eastern grey kangaroo is common and is not regarded as threatened. Besides the red kangaroo it is one of the best-known heraldic animals of Australia. On roads, however, there are often accidents with cars, especially at dusk. Kangaroos belong to the **marsupials**, whose young develop in a pouch.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young go on developing in a pouch after birth.
The name for a young kangaroo.
The name for a group of kangaroos.
An animal that feeds only on plants.

gewusst: A newborn kangaroo weighs less than a gram.
Kangaroos cannot hop backwards well.
When hopping, kangaroos save energy because their tendons work like springs.

teile.einleitung: A territory, in German Revier, is an area that an animal or a group of animals claims for itself and defends against others. In it, the animal looks for food, finds a partner and raises its young. A great tit, for example, breeds and looks for food in its own territory.
wichtigste: A territory is an area that an animal defends against others of its species.
A pair of great tits breeds and looks for food in its territory.
In its territory, an animal finds food, hiding places and a place for its young.
Animals show with song, scent marks or threats that an area is occupied.
The size of a territory depends on how much food there is there.
Some animals have a territory only during the breeding season.
Not all animals defend a territory, and many also live in flocks or herds.

abschnitte.text: A **territory** is an area that an animal regards as its own. It allows no strange members of its own species there, above all no rivals of the same sex. In the territory there are feeding places, sleeping places and often the nest or den. Other animal species are mostly tolerated, because they do not compete for the same food. The territory secures for its owner the means needed for survival.

In spring, the male **great tit** looks for a territory in a forest, park or garden. With his song he shows other males that the place is taken. If a rival comes too close, he is chased away. In the territory the female builds the nest in a tree hole or a nest box. Both parents then collect caterpillars and insects there for the young.

The size of a territory varies a lot. A robin often needs only an area as big as a few gardens. A wolf pack in the Alps, by contrast, roams a territory of several hundred square kilometres. When there is a lot of **food**, a small area is enough. When food is scarce, the territory has to be larger.

Most animals avoid real fights, because these are dangerous. Instead they show with song, calls, scent marks or **threat displays** to whom the area belongs. An intruder thus recognises early on that someone lives here. Usually he withdraws without a fight taking place. The owner of the territory often wins a dispute because he defends his area especially determinedly.

Many birds have a territory only during the **breeding season**. In autumn and winter they then live peacefully together in flocks. The robin is an exception, because with it the females also defend a feeding territory of their own in winter. Fish such as the stickleback defend a small area around their nest during the spawning season. Other animals, such as roe bucks, hold a territory in summer for the mating season.

In Swiss forests, foxes, badgers, woodpeckers and owls, for example, have territories of their own. House cats also take over an area around their home. The word **Revier** is also used in hunting, where it refers to an area in which certain hunters may hunt. Anyone who watches animals can often tell where the borders of a territory lie. Singing blackbirds on rooftop ridges, for example, show their territory.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area that an animal claims for itself and defends.
A technical word for a territory.
A competitor of the same species that wants the same territory or the same partner.
The time in which birds lay eggs and raise their young.

gewusst: Birdsong in the morning is often a message to other males: this territory is taken.
Some fish such as the damselfish even defend a small algae garden on a coral reef.
The owner of a territory often wins a dispute against a stronger intruder, because he has more to lose.

teile.einleitung: Reindeer lichen is a grey, strongly branched lichen that forms whole carpets in the far north. It is the most important winter food of reindeer. Although it looks like a plant, a lichen is a partnership of a fungus and an alga.
wichtigste: Reindeer lichen is not a plant, but a lichen.
A lichen consists of a fungus and an alga that live together.
It gives reindeer a lot of energy in winter.
Reindeer lichens grow very slowly, often only a few millimetres a year.
They grow in the tundra, in coniferous forests and in moors.
Reindeer lichens also occur in the Swiss Alps.
Lichens take up substances from the air and so show how clean the air is.

abschnitte.text: A **lichen** is a close partnership of a fungus and an alga. The fungus forms the framework and protects the alga from drying out. The alga makes sugar with sunlight, like a plant. The fungus lives on this too. Such a living together for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

The true reindeer lichen has the scientific name Cladonia rangiferina. It is grey to whitish and looks like tiny, densely branched little trees. The individual thalli grow about 5 to 10 centimetres high. Many thalli together form soft, spongy **carpets** on the ground. In dry weather it becomes hard and brittle, and in rain soft again.

Reindeer lichens grow mainly in the tundra and in the open coniferous forests of Scandinavia, Siberia, Alaska and Canada. They like nutrient-poor, acid soils on which other plants hardly grow. They are also found in moors and heaths. In Switzerland reindeer lichens grow mainly in the **Alps** and in raised bogs. There you often see them between dwarf shrubs such as bilberries.

In winter, reindeer find hardly any grass or leaves. Then they dig lichens out from under the snow with hooves and antlers. Lichens contain many carbohydrates and so provide a lot of **energy** against the cold. Reindeer have special helpers in their stomach that can digest lichens well. Because the lichen grows so slowly, the herds have to keep moving on so that it can grow back.

Reindeer lichen grows only a few millimetres a year. If a carpet of lichen has been eaten off or trampled, it takes decades to recover. Lichens have no roots and take up water and substances directly from rain and air. That is why they react sensitively to **air pollution**. Researchers therefore use lichens as indicators of clean air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A partnership of a fungus and an alga that often grows on stones, bark or the ground.
A living together in which both partners benefit.
The body of a lichen.
A living thing that shows how healthy or polluted the environment is.

gewusst: After the Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986, lichens in Scandinavia took up radioactive substances, so that the meat of many reindeer was also contaminated.
Dried and dyed reindeer lichen is used as decoration, for example in wreaths or as little trees on model railways.
Lichens can become extremely dry and still survive, and as soon as it rains they become active again.

teile.einleitung: The ocelot is a medium-sized wild cat from Central and South America with a beautifully patterned coat. It is the largest species of the spotted cats of the genus Leopardus and hunts mainly at night in dense forest. Because of its fur it used to be hunted heavily.
wichtigste: The ocelot is scientifically called Leopardus pardalis.
It belongs to the genus Leopardus and is its largest species.
Carl Linnaeus first described it scientifically in 1758.
A fully grown ocelot weighs about 7 to 16 kilograms.
Its coat bears elongated rosettes, often linked like a chain.
Its closest relative is the margay.
The ocelot lives from Texas to northern Argentina.

abschnitte.text: An ocelot has a **head-and-body length** of about 55 to 100 centimetres, plus a tail 30 to 45 centimetres long. At the shoulder it is about 40 to 50 centimetres tall and weighs roughly 7 to 16 kilograms, so about twice as much as a large domestic cat. Its yellowish-brown coat is covered with black-edged **rosettes** that are elongated and often linked like a chain. Every animal has its own pattern, much like a fingerprint.

The ocelot lives from the south of the USA in Texas through Mexico and Central America to northern Argentina. It needs dense plant cover and occurs in **rainforests**, dry forests, mangroves and bushland. In Texas only very few animals are left. Since the reorganisation of the cats in 2017, only two **subspecies** are recognised.

The ocelot hunts mostly at night and alone on the ground. It eats mainly small mammals such as rodents, opossums and armadillos. It also catches birds, lizards, snakes and sometimes fish. It can climb and **swim** well, which is unusual for a cat.

Ocelots are **solitary animals** and have fixed territories that they mark with scent. By day they rest in hollow trees or in dense undergrowth. After a gestation of about two and a half months the female usually has only one kitten, rarely two or three. Because they have so few young, populations recover only slowly.

The ocelot belongs to the genus of **spotted cats**, scientifically Leopardus. Its closest relative is the **margay**, a smaller cat that lives almost only in trees. The spotted cats have 36 chromosomes, while most other cats have 38. Carl Linnaeus gave the ocelot its first scientific name in 1758.

In the 1960s and 1970s very many ocelots were killed for fur coats. Today international trade in ocelot skins is banned, and the species is no longer regarded as threatened worldwide. The greatest danger now is the **clearing** of the forests. Road accidents also threaten the small populations in Texas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A genus of small to medium-sized wild cats from the Americas, scientifically Leopardus.
A ring-shaped spot in the coat of some cats.
A group within a species that lives in a particular area and differs slightly.
An animal that lives alone most of the time.

gewusst: The ocelot is one of the few cats that like going into the water.
The painter Salvador Dalí is said to have gone out with an ocelot on a lead.
No ocelot has the same coat pattern as another.

teile.einleitung: A predatory fish is a fish that mainly hunts and eats other fish and larger animals. In Swiss lakes and rivers there live, for example, pike, perch, zander, wels catfish and lake trout. Predatory fish are important because they keep the balance in the water.
wichtigste: Predatory fish feed mainly on other fish.
Like all animals that hunt and eat others, they count as predators in the sense of hunters.
The lake trout helps, as a predatory fish, to keep the numbers of other fish in the lake in balance.
Typical are a large mouth, pointed teeth and good senses.
Some lie in wait in hiding, others hunt their prey by fast swimming.
The wels catfish is the largest predatory fish in Swiss waters.
Large predatory fish in the sea, such as sharks and tuna, are heavily overfished in many places.

abschnitte.text: Predatory fish are fish whose main food is other fish. Young predatory fish often still eat plankton and insect larvae and switch to fish only later. Large species also eat frogs, crayfish, mice or even young waterbirds. Like the lion or the wolf, they are **predators** and stand high up in the **food chain** of their water.

Many predatory fish have a large mouth with pointed **teeth** curved backwards, so that the prey cannot escape. They have good eyes and, with the **lateral line organ**, sense the finest movements in the water. The pike has a long body with which it can lunge forward in a flash. The wels catfish finds its prey with long barbels even in murky water and at night.

The **pike** is an ambush hunter: it stands motionless among water plants and shoots out when a fish swims past. Perch often hunt in groups and drive small fish together. Lake trout and tuna are persistent **pursuit hunters** that chase their prey. Many predatory fish hunt mainly at dusk.
