In Swiss waters there live, among others, pike, perch, zander, wels catfish, lake trout and Arctic char. The **wels catfish** can grow over 2 metres long and is the largest freshwater fish in Central Europe. The **lake trout** lives in large lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva and migrates into the inflowing rivers to spawn. Many of these fish are very popular with anglers and end up on the plate as perch or pike fillets.

Predatory fish often eat weak or sick animals and so keep the stocks of their prey fish healthy. They prevent one fish species from multiplying too strongly and upsetting the balance in the lake. At the same time, pollutants such as **mercury** build up in large predatory fish, because they eat many contaminated fish. In the sea, many large predatory fish such as sharks, swordfish and tuna have become rare because of **overfishing**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A series of living things in which each is eaten by the next.
A sense organ on the sides of fish that senses movements in the water.
An animal that waits hidden for prey and then strikes in a flash.
Thread-like feeling organs at the mouth of some fish.

gewusst: A large pike can eat prey fish that are almost half as long as itself.
Egli is the Swiss name for the perch, and in Switzerland perch fillets are a popular dish.
The great white shark, one of the best-known predatory fish in the world, is also a fish and not a mammal.

teile.einleitung: Surface tension is a force that makes the surface of water act like a thin, elastic skin. Thanks to it a pond skater can walk on water without sinking in. It also explains why drops of water are round.
wichtigste: Surface tension makes the water surface act like a thin skin.
It arises because water particles attract one another.
Surface tension stops a pond skater from sinking in.
Washing-up liquid lowers the surface tension, and then pond skaters can sink in.
The pond skater shows clearly how surface tension works in physics.
Because of surface tension, drops of water are round.

abschnitte.text: Water consists of tiny particles, the **molecules**. These attract each other, which is called cohesion. Inside the water every molecule is pulled equally strongly from all sides. At the surface the neighbours above are missing, so the molecules there pull together especially tightly and form a kind of skin.

The **pond skater** is an insect that is common on ponds and quiet streams in Switzerland too. Its long legs spread the weight over a large area. Fine, water-repellent hairs on the legs make sure that the water does not stick to them. In this way it presses only small dents into the surface and does not sink in.

Washing-up liquid and soap contain **surfactants**. These substances push between the water molecules and weaken their cohesion. As a result the surface tension falls sharply. If washing-up liquid gets into a pond, pond skaters can sink in and drown.

A paper clip can float on water if you lay it down carefully. A glass can be filled a little above the rim, because the water forms a small **dome**. Raindrops and dewdrops are round, because a sphere has the smallest surface. Soap bubbles too exist only thanks to surface tension.

The German researcher **Agnes Pockels** studied surface tension from the 1880s in her kitchen. For this she built a simple measuring device from a tin tray. In 1891 her results appeared in the famous journal Nature. Today she is regarded as one of the founders of surface research.

Many animals such as pond skaters, whirligig beetles and some spiders use surface tension for their way of life. In our lungs a special substance, the **surfactant**, lowers the surface tension so that the air sacs do not stick together. In technology it plays a role in washing, printing and painting. Without it there would be no drops and no foam bubbles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle of which substances such as water consist.
The force with which like particles attract one another.
A substance in soap and washing-up liquid that lowers the surface tension.
An insect with long legs that walks on the water surface.

gewusst: Water has one of the highest surface tensions of all liquids, and only a few substances such as mercury exceed it.
Pond skaters feel with their legs the fine ripples that an insect falling into the water causes, and so find their prey.
Warm water has a somewhat lower surface tension than cold, which is why it washes better.

teile.einleitung: Earthworms are long, red worms without legs that live in the soil. They eat dead leaves and earth and make fertile humus from them. Without earthworms our soils would be much less fertile, which is why they are also called the gardeners of nature.
wichtigste: Earthworms belong to the annelid worms and have a body made of many rings.
With small bristles they hold on in the soil.
They move forwards by alternately stretching and contracting their body.
Earthworms breathe through the skin, which is why they need moist soil.
They pull leaves into their burrows and digest them into nutrient-rich humus.
Their blood is red, as in us humans.
They are especially active in spring and autumn, when the soil is moist and mild.

abschnitte.text: The earthworm has a long, round body made of over a hundred **rings**, the segments. The common earthworm in our region often grows 20 to 30 centimetres long. Adult worms have a thickened, pale band, the **clitellum**. On every ring there are small **bristles** with which the worm holds on in its burrows.

Earthworms have no lungs, but breathe through their moist **skin**. If the soil becomes too dry, they can breathe less well and seek deeper, moister layers. After heavy rain they often come to the surface, because the air in the burrows runs short. They have no eyes, but sensory cells in the skin feel light, which is why they pull back quickly in bright light.

Although it has no legs, the earthworm makes good progress. It has two layers of muscle: **circular muscles** make it long and thin, **longitudinal muscles** make it short and thick. In alternation it stretches the front part forward and pulls the rear part after it. The bristles prevent it from slipping back.

Earthworms dig their burrows mostly vertically downwards, some to over 2 metres deep, to reach moister soil. Through these burrows air and rainwater get into the soil, and plant roots grow more easily. In autumn they pull leaves into the soil, eat them and excrete nutrient-rich **humus**. That is why the leaves in the garden disappear over time and the soil becomes loose and fertile.

Earthworms are **hermaphrodites**, so every worm is male and female at the same time. Even so, they need a partner, with whom they mate on the surface on damp nights. After that the band forms a small case, the **cocoon**, in which the eggs lie. After a few weeks, usually one or a few young worms hatch from a cocoon.

Earthworms are eaten by many animals, for example by blackbirds, moles, hedgehogs, badgers and toads. Anglers use them as **bait**, because they move on the hook and attract fish. In a good meadow, several hundred earthworms can live per square metre. The famous naturalist Charles Darwin wrote a whole book in 1881 about their importance for the soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single ring in the body of an annelid worm.
Dark, fertile soil made from decomposed plant remains.
A living thing that is male and female at the same time.
A thickened band on the earthworm that forms the cocoon during reproduction.

gewusst: When you cut an earthworm in two, you do not get two new worms, and usually at most the front part survives.
Under a well-managed meadow, the earthworms together can weigh more than the cows grazing above.
The mole builds up stores of earthworms, which it paralyses with a bite.

teile.einleitung: Placoid scales are tiny, tooth-like scales in the skin of sharks and rays. Because they all point backwards, shark skin feels smooth in one direction and rough like sandpaper in the other. They are therefore also called dermal denticles.
wichtigste: Placoid scales occur in cartilaginous fish such as sharks and rays.
They are built like little teeth.
That is why they are also called dermal denticles.
Shark skin feels rough like sandpaper against the direction of growth.
The scales help the shark to swim faster and more quietly.
The teeth of sharks developed from such scales.

abschnitte.text: A **placoid scale** is a small scale in the skin of **cartilaginous fish**, that is, sharks, rays and chimaeras. The name comes from the Greek word for plate, because each scale sits in the skin with a small base plate. Above it sticks out a tiny point, which points backwards. Many thousands of such scales cover the whole body like a coat of chain mail.

Placoid scales are built very much like our teeth. Inside lies a cavity with blood vessels, the **pulp**. Around it lies **dentine**, and on the outside a hard, enamel-like layer. Researchers believe that the teeth in a shark's mouth developed from such dermal denticles over the course of evolution.

If you stroke a shark's skin from the head to the tail, it feels fairly smooth. In the opposite direction, however, it is rough like **sandpaper**, because you are stroking against the pointed scales. In the past, dried shark skin was actually used as sandpaper for wood. Tanned ray and shark skin is called **shagreen** and was used for non-slip grips on swords.

The scales have fine grooves that run in the direction of swimming. They slow small eddies of water at the skin and so reduce **water resistance**. This allows the shark to swim faster and more quietly. Engineers have copied this model from nature for ship coatings, aircraft films and swimsuits, and this is called **biomimetics**.

The hard scales protect the skin from injuries and make it harder for small animals and algae to settle on it. Placoid scales do not grow with the animal, as the scales of many bony fish do. Instead, the shark forms new, larger ones between the old scales. Old scales also fall out and are replaced, much like the teeth in a shark's mouth.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fish with a skeleton of cartilage instead of bone, such as sharks and rays.
The hard material that teeth are largely made of.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.
Tanned skin of sharks or rays with a rough surface.

gewusst: Fossil dermal denticles of sharks are often so small that you can only see them under a microscope.
At the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney, many swimmers wore suits that were inspired by shark skin.
Hardly any bacteria settle on shark skin, which is why similar surfaces are being tested for hospitals.

teile.einleitung: Ovoviviparity is a special way of reproducing that lies between laying eggs and giving birth to live young. The eggs stay inside the mother’s body, and the young hatch shortly before or during birth. So they are born alive, although they have developed in an egg.
wichtigste: In ovoviviparity the eggs stay in the mother’s body until the young hatch.
Animals with this kind of reproduction are called ovoviviparous.
The young are fed by the yolk in the egg and not through a placenta.
Examples are the adder, the slow worm and many sharks.
The common lizard in Switzerland also usually gives birth to live young.
This kind of reproduction is an advantage especially in cold regions.

abschnitte.text: The word is put together from the Latin words ovum for egg, vivus for alive and parere for to give birth. In **ovoviviparity** the female does not lay her eggs but keeps them in her body. The embryo grows in the egg and feeds on the **yolk**. Only when it is fully developed does it hatch, usually shortly before or during birth.

In **oviparous** animals such as birds, the young hatch outside from laid eggs. In **viviparous** animals such as most mammals, the young are supplied with food inside the mother through a placenta. Ovoviviparous animals lie in between, because their young are born alive but get their food from the egg. Today many biologists also simply group this form under the term live-bearing.

In Switzerland some reptiles are ovoviviparous, for example the **adder** and the asp viper. The harmless slow worm, a legless lizard, also gives birth to live young. The **common lizard** lives high up into the Alps and in most areas is likewise live-bearing. Its young often hatch from a thin egg membrane as soon as it is laid.

Many sharks are ovoviviparous, for example the **spiny dogfish** and the great white shark. In some shark species the strongest young inside the mother even eat unfertilised eggs or siblings. Popular aquarium fish such as the **guppy** also give birth to live young. That is why such fish are often called live-bearers in pet shops.

Eggs in the ground are poorly protected in cold regions and develop only slowly in the cold. A female that carries her eggs in her body can lie in the sun and so warm the eggs. That is why ovoviviparous reptiles are often found in the mountains or in the far north. In addition, the eggs inside the mother are safe from predators.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs stay in the mother’s body and the young hatch at birth.
A store of nutrients in the egg on which the embryo feeds.
An organ that supplies an unborn mammal with food inside the mother.
A living thing in its earliest development before birth.

gewusst: The common lizard is scientifically called Zootoca vivipara, because it gives birth to live young.
A female guppy can give birth to several dozen young every few weeks.
The slow worm looks like a snake, but is a lizard and gives birth to live young.

teile.einleitung: Armoured catfish are small fish from South America whose bodies are covered with bony plates instead of scales. They root around on the bottom for food and eat scraps that other fish leave lying. That is why they are among the most popular fish in aquariums.
wichtigste: Armoured catfish come from the rivers and streams of South America.
Their body is armoured with two rows of bony plates.
They use their barbels to search for food on the bottom.
In an aquarium they eat leftover food, parts of plants and also some algae.
Armoured catfish can also swallow air and take in oxygen through the gut.
They like to live in groups and are peaceful fish.
The best known genus is called Corydoras.

abschnitte.text: Armoured catfish form the family **Callichthyidae** with over 200 species. Instead of scales they have two rows of **bony plates** on each side of the body, which protect them like armour. Around the mouth they have short threads, the **barbels**, which they use to feel and taste. Most species of the popular genus Corydoras grow to only 3 to 7 centimetres long.

Armoured catfish live in South America, for example in the **Amazon region**, in Brazil, Peru and Colombia. They inhabit calm rivers, streams and pools with a soft, sandy bottom. In the dry season the water can become warm and low in oxygen. They are well equipped for this with a special ability.

Besides gills, armoured catfish have a second way of breathing. They dart up to the surface in a flash, swallow air and take up the oxygen through the wall of their **gut**. This **gut breathing** helps them survive even in water that is low in oxygen. In an aquarium you can therefore see them dash briefly to the top now and then.

Armoured catfish root around in the sand with their barbels for small worms, insect larvae and other small animals. In an aquarium they eat leftovers that sink to the bottom, parts of plants and also some **algae**. That is why they are seen as useful helpers that keep the bottom clean. Even so, they need food of their own, for example special food tablets.

Armoured catfish are peaceful and well suited to **community tanks** with other calm fish. You should keep them in groups of at least six, because in nature they live in shoals. The bottom should be made of fine sand so that they do not hurt their sensitive barbels. Well-known species are the bronze corydoras and the panda corydoras with black patches around the eyes.

When mating, male and female often form a position that looks like a T. The female then carries a few eggs between her belly fins and sticks them to plants or to the aquarium glass. The parents do not look after the brood. After a few days tiny young fish hatch.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feeler-like threads around the mouth that fish use to feel and taste.
Taking in oxygen from swallowed air through the wall of the gut.
Hard plates made of bone that protect the body.
An aquarium in which different species of fish live together.

gewusst: Armoured catfish can wink an eye by briefly rotating it downwards.
Some armoured catfish have hard spines on their fins, which they can raise for protection.
In the Amazon, armoured catfish sometimes swim in shoals of hundreds of animals.

teile.einleitung: The oil palm is a palm from West Africa, from whose fruits palm oil is obtained. Palm oil is the most produced vegetable oil in the world and is found in many foods and cosmetics. For huge oil palm plantations, however, rainforests are cleared, which robs many animals of their habitat.
wichtigste: The African oil palm originally comes from West Africa.
Palm oil is obtained from its fruits, and palm kernel oil from the kernels.
Palm oil from plantations contributes strongly to the destruction of rainforest.
Most plantations today are in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Orangutans, tigers and many other animals lose their habitat as a result.
The oil palm yields more oil per area than other oil plants.
There are labels for more sustainably produced palm oil.

abschnitte.text: The **African oil palm** grows up to 20 metres tall, and in plantations it usually stays smaller. It bears large fruit bunches with hundreds to over a thousand reddish, plum-sized fruits. Such a fruit bunch can weigh several dozen kilograms. Originally the oil palm grew in the forests of West Africa.

From the flesh of the fruit **palm oil** is obtained by pressing, and from the kernel palm kernel oil. Palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature and keeps for a long time. That is why it is found in chocolate spread, biscuits, margarine, ready meals, soaps and candles. It is also used as a fuel.

Today most palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia. There huge areas of **rainforest** were cleared or burnt in order to plant oil palms. In the plantations only a single plant species grows, which is called a **monoculture**. When peat soils are burnt, in addition large amounts of greenhouse gases get into the air.

With the rainforest the habitat of many animals disappears. Especially threatened are the orangutans on Borneo and Sumatra, but also Sumatran tigers, elephants and rhinoceroses. The **biodiversity** in a plantation is much smaller than in natural rainforest. Some animals are killed when they look for food in plantations.

Since 2004 there has been the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO), which awards a **label**. It is meant to guarantee that no valuable forest is cleared for the plantations. Critics say the rules are still too weak. If palm oil were simply replaced by other oils, however, even more farmland would be needed, because the oil palm is especially productive.

Palm oil is also found in many products in Swiss shops. It has to be stated in the list of ingredients. In March 2021 Swiss voters narrowly approved a **free trade agreement** with Indonesia, in which tariff reductions are tied to sustainably produced palm oil. Anyone who wants to avoid palm oil can read ingredient lists and cook fresh more often.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large field on which only one crop is grown.
The cultivation of a single plant species over a large area.
Felling a forest in order to use the land in another way.
A treaty between countries that makes trade easier, for example through lower tariffs.

gewusst: Palm oil is found in a large share of all products in the supermarket, from bread to lipstick.
On one hectare of oil palms grows several times as much oil as on one hectare of rapeseed or sunflowers.
In West Africa red, unrefined palm oil has been used for cooking for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: The red kangaroo is the largest kangaroo in the world and at the same time the largest marsupial alive today. It lives in the dry, open landscapes in the interior of Australia. With its strong hind legs it can make huge leaps.
wichtigste: The red kangaroo is the largest kangaroo and marsupial in the world.
Large males can weigh up to 90 kilograms.
The coat of the males is usually reddish brown.
It lives in dry, open areas of Australia.
It eats mainly grasses and herbs.
The young one grows up for months in its mother's pouch.
With its leaps it is very fast and has great stamina.

abschnitte.text: A large male can, standing upright, be about as tall as an adult human. To this is added a thick, muscular **tail** about a metre long, which keeps its balance when leaping. The males usually have a **reddish-brown coat**, and the smaller females are often blue-grey. Typical are a white stripe on the muzzle and long, upright ears.

Red kangaroos live in the interior of Australia in semi-deserts, steppes and open **grassland**. There it is hot and dry, and it often hardly rains for months. The animals manage with little water, because they take up a lot of moisture from plants. In the midday heat they rest in the shade and become active only towards evening.

The red kangaroo is a **plant eater**. It eats mainly fresh grasses, herbs and leaves of shrubs. Much like cows, it can digest tough plants in a stomach of several parts with the help of bacteria. After rainfall, when fresh grass grows, the animals often travel long distances.

Kangaroos move by hopping on their hind legs, and a single leap can be many metres long. They briefly reach over 50 kilometres per hour. The tendons in the legs act like **springs** and save a lot of energy. Males sometimes fight one another by supporting themselves on the tail and kicking with the hind legs, which looks like boxing.

After only about a month of pregnancy, a tiny, naked young one is born, smaller than a bean. It crawls by itself into its mother's **pouch** and attaches itself to a teat. There it stays for about eight months and grows up. A female can have a young one beside her, one in the pouch and a resting embryo in her body at the same time.

The red kangaroo is an **emblem** of Australia and, together with the emu, stands in the Australian coat of arms. It is regarded as not threatened, because there are still millions of animals in Australia. Farmers sometimes see kangaroos as competition for their grazing animals. In Switzerland you can see kangaroos only in zoos and animal parks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young grow up in a pouch on the mother's belly.
An animal that feeds only on plants.
The time in which a young animal grows in its mother's belly.
A typical sign of recognition of a country or place.

gewusst: A newborn red kangaroo weighs less than a gram, and an adult male up to 90 kilograms.
Kangaroos cannot walk backwards well.
A group of kangaroos is called a “mob” in English.

teile.einleitung: Oxytocin is a hormone that is made in the brain and plays an important role for closeness and trust in humans and animals. For that reason it is sometimes also called the cuddle hormone or bonding hormone. It helps with birth, with nursing and even with the friendship between humans and dogs.
wichtigste: Oxytocin is a hormone that is made in the hypothalamus in the brain.
It is released into the blood by the pituitary gland.
Oxytocin triggers labour at birth and helps with nursing.
It strengthens the bond between mother and child.
Between humans and dogs, too, oxytocin plays a central role.
It is often called the cuddle hormone.
In medicine oxytocin is used to bring on labour.

abschnitte.text: Oxytocin is a **hormone**, that is, a messenger substance that carries messages around the body through the blood. It consists of only nine building blocks, the amino acids. It is made in the **hypothalamus**, a part of the brain, and released by the pituitary gland. The name comes from Greek and means roughly ‘quick birth’.

At birth oxytocin makes the womb contract, which is called **labour**. Later it helps with nursing, because it makes the milk flow from the breast. This works in a similar way in all mammals, for example in cows at milking too. Doctors sometimes give oxytocin as a medicine to support a birth.

Oxytocin is released when we hug or stroke someone or feel safe and secure. It strengthens **trust** and bonding, especially between mother and child. That is why it is also called the cuddle hormone. It does not work alone, however, but together with many other substances in the brain.

Researchers in Japan showed in 2015 that in dogs and their humans the oxytocin level rises when they look into each other’s eyes for a long time. This is similar to a mother and her baby. It is suspected that this **eye contact** created a special bond during the long period of domestication. When a dog is stroked, too, oxytocin is released in both.

The British researcher Henry Dale discovered in 1906 that a substance from the pituitary gland makes the womb contract. The American chemist **Vincent du Vigneaud** found out how oxytocin is built up and in 1953 made it artificially for the first time. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry in 1955. It was the first hormone made of protein building blocks that could be produced artificially.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that passes signals around the body through the blood.
A small part of the brain that controls many bodily processes.
A small gland under the brain that releases hormones into the blood, also called the hypophysis.
The contracting of the womb during birth.

gewusst: Even a friendly look between dog and human can release oxytocin in both.
Oxytocin is a very small molecule made of only nine amino acids.
Fathers, too, make oxytocin when they spend a lot of time with their baby.

teile.einleitung: The rubber duck, in German Quietscheentchen, is a small, mostly yellow toy in the shape of a duck that floats in the bathtub. When you squeeze it, it makes a squeaking sound. It is one of the best-known toys in the world and has even helped ocean research.
wichtigste: The rubber duck is a yellow toy in the shape of a duck that floats in the bath.
In the past it was made of rubber, today mostly of plastic such as PVC.
The squeak is made when air is pressed through a small hole.
The model is real ducklings, whose down is often yellowish.
In 1992 thousands of bath toys went overboard in the Pacific and helped to study ocean currents.
Researchers from Switzerland found that fungi and bacteria often grow inside bath ducks.

abschnitte.text: A rubber duck is a hollow bath toy that looks like a small **duckling**. It is mostly bright yellow and has an orange beak. Because it contains air inside, it floats upright on the water. Today there are bath ducks in many colours and costumes, for example as a pirate, a firefighter or a footballer.

On the underside of the duck there is a small hole, often with a **whistle** in it. When you squeeze the duck, the air is pressed through this hole and it whistles or squeaks. When you let go, the duck sucks air in again, sometimes bath water too. In this way water gets inside, where it stays for a long time.

Rubber toys became possible only after people learned in the 19th century to make natural rubber durable by **vulcanisation**. The first rubber ducks were often solid and did not always float straight. From the middle of the 20th century, hollow, floating bath ducks were made in large numbers. Today most are made of plastic such as **PVC** or vinyl.

In 1992 a container ship in the North Pacific lost a cargo of about 29,000 bath toys, including yellow ducks, beavers, turtles and frogs. They are now called **Friendly Floatees**. The oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer collected reports of finds from beaches all over the world. In this way people learned a lot about **ocean currents**, because some of the toys drifted through the oceans for years.

In 2018 researchers at **Eawag**, the water research institute in Dübendorf, together with ETH Zurich, cut open used bath ducks. In most of them they found a slimy coating of fungi and bacteria, a so-called **biofilm**. The reasons are warm bath water, soap residue and skin flakes, on which the germs live. Tip: buy bath toys without a hole, or squeeze them out well after bathing and let them dry.

abschnitte.titel: Bath ducks in art and everyday life
abschnitte.text: The Dutch artist Florentijn Hofman built giant inflatable rubber ducks that floated in harbours all over the world. In **duck races**, thousands of numbered plastic ducks are set into a river, often for a good cause. Programmers sometimes explain their code to a bath duck in order to find mistakes. This method is jokingly called **rubber duck debugging**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which rubber is heated and treated with sulphur so that it becomes elastic and durable.
A common plastic of which many toys are made.
A slimy layer of many tiny living things such as bacteria and fungi.
A large stream of water in the sea that carries water over long distances.

gewusst: Some of the bath toys lost in 1992 were still found on beaches in North America and Europe many years later.
Real ducklings are yellow only in some breeds such as the Pekin duck, and the chicks of the mallard have a brown and yellow pattern.
There are collectors who own several thousand different bath ducks.

teile.einleitung: The sockeye salmon, in German Rotlachs, is a salmon from the northern Pacific. It is known for its transformation at spawning time, when its body turns bright red and its head turns green. Every year, millions of sockeye migrate from the sea back into the rivers in which they were born.
wichtigste: The sockeye salmon belongs to the Pacific salmon and is also called Rotlachs in German.
It lives in the North Pacific, for example off Alaska, Canada and Russia.
To spawn it swims far upriver from the sea.
At spawning time its body turns bright red and the head green.
Young sockeye usually grow up first in a lake.
After spawning, the adult sockeye die.
Its flesh is a strong red and is gladly eaten.

abschnitte.text: In the sea the sockeye is a gleaming silver with a blue-green back. It usually grows about 60 centimetres long and weighs 2 to 3 kilograms. At spawning time it changes greatly: the body becomes **bright red**, the head green. The males also get a hump and a hooked jaw.

The sockeye lives in the northern **Pacific** between North America and Asia. Its spawning waters lie in rivers and lakes in Alaska, Canada and the east of Russia. Unlike other salmon, it almost always needs a **lake** in the river system. There the young fish spend their first one to three years before moving to the sea.

In the sea the sockeye eats mainly **plankton**, that is, tiny crustaceans such as krill. From these crustaceans it takes up red pigments that colour its flesh so strongly red. In the lake, young sockeye eat small water fleas and insect larvae. During the migration upriver, the adult fish eat nothing at all.

After usually two to three years in the sea, the sockeye return to spawn. With their sense of smell they find exactly the river in which they themselves hatched. On the way they swim against the current and leap over rapids. There **bears** often wait and fish the salmon out of the water.

The female beats a hollow in the gravel with her tail fin, the **redd**, and lays her eggs there. The male fertilises them, and then the eggs are covered with gravel. Shortly after spawning, the exhausted parents die. Their bodies fertilise rivers and forests, and many animals feed on them.

The sockeye is an important **food fish** and is caught in large numbers, above all in Alaska. Bristol Bay in Alaska is known for the largest sockeye runs in the world. In Switzerland the sockeye does not occur, but you find it as wild salmon in the shop. The native Atlantic salmon had disappeared from the Rhine and is meant today, through projects, to return to Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Laying eggs, in fish and amphibians.
Tiny living things that float in the water.
A group of salmon species from the Pacific to which the sockeye belongs.
A hollow in the gravel into which the salmon lays its eggs.

gewusst: There are also sockeye that never migrate to the sea and spend their whole life in lakes, and these are called kokanee.
For its spawning migration, a sockeye can swim over 1,000 kilometres upriver.

teile.einleitung: The red deer, in German Rothirsch, is the largest wild mammal in Switzerland. Especially impressive are the males with their mighty antlers and their loud roaring in autumn. Red deer live in forests and at forest edges and are pure plant eaters.
wichtigste: The red deer is the largest wild mammal in Switzerland.
It belongs to the deer family, like the roe deer.
Only the males carry antlers, which they shed every year.
In the rut in autumn, the stags roar loudly.
Red deer are plant eaters and active mainly at dusk.
They can run at about 60 km/h.
In winter many red deer move down into the valley.

abschnitte.text: A fully grown red deer has a shoulder height of up to about 1.5 metres. Males, the **stags**, often weigh over 150 kilograms, and females considerably less. In summer the coat is reddish brown, in winter greyish brown and denser, so it changes its coat twice a year. On the rump it has a pale patch, the mirror.

Red deer like best to live in forests and at **forest edges**, where they find cover and food. In summer many in the Alps climb up beyond the tree line. In winter, when snow lies and there is little food, they move down into the valley. Females and young live in groups called a **herd**, and the males often separately from them.

The red deer is a **plant eater** and a ruminant. It eats grasses, herbs, buds, leaves, bark and, in autumn, also acorns and beechnuts. The hunters' language calls the feeding of deer **äsen**. When too many deer live in a small area, they browse young trees and strip bark, which can harm the forest.

Only the stags carry **antlers** of bone, which fall off every year in late winter. After that a new set grows, which at first is surrounded by a soft, hairy skin, the velvet. In summer the deer rubs the velvet off on trees, which is called fraying. The antlers show other deer his strength and serve as a weapon in fights.

In September and October is the **rutting season**. The stags then roar loudly in order to scare off rivals and attract females, which can often be heard for kilometres. Stags of equal strength fight with their antlers locked together. In early summer the female usually gives birth to a single calf with white spots.

In the 19th century the red deer had been wiped out in Switzerland by heavy hunting. Towards the end of the century, animals from Austria migrated back into **Graubünden**. Today many tens of thousands of red deer live in Switzerland again, especially many in the Alps. In the Swiss National Park you can watch them roaring well in autumn.

begriffe.erklaerung: A male red deer, and the female is called a hind.
Bony head ornament that falls off every year and grows anew.
The mating season of deer in autumn.
A hunters' word for the feeding of deer and roe deer.
A plant eater that brings its food back up and chews it again.

gewusst: A deer's antlers can regrow in a few months and are among the fastest-growing tissues in mammals.
Shed antlers are gnawed by mice and other animals, because they contain valuable minerals.

teile.einleitung: Palm Sunday is the Sunday before Easter and recalls a well-known story from the Bible. Jesus rode into the city of Jerusalem on a donkey, and the people welcomed him with palm branches. With Palm Sunday Holy Week begins for Christians.
wichtigste: Palm Sunday is the Sunday before Easter.
It recalls the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem.
Jesus rode into the city on a donkey.
The people waved palm branches and cried Hosanna.
With Palm Sunday Holy Week begins.
In many churches decorated branches are blessed on this day.
In this story the donkey is a sign of peace and humility.

abschnitte.text: All four **Gospels** in the New Testament tell how Jesus came to Jerusalem shortly before the feast of Passover. He rode into the city on a young donkey. Many people laid their clothes and branches on the road and waved **palm branches**. They cried Hosanna, a shout of joy that means something like ‘Help, please’.

Powerful kings at that time often rode into a city on horses, as a sign of strength and war. The **donkey**, by contrast, was a working animal of ordinary people. That is why in this story it is a sign of peace and humility. Already in the Old Testament the prophet Zechariah announces a king who comes on a donkey.

Palm Sunday is always exactly one week before **Easter**. Because the date of Easter changes every year, Palm Sunday falls between the middle of March and the middle of April. With it begins **Holy Week**, which also includes Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. It ends with the feast of Easter, the most important feast of Christians.

In many churches on Palm Sunday branches are blessed and carried round in a **procession**. Because no palms grow here, people take branches of box, pussy willow, holly or other evergreen plants. In Catholic areas of Switzerland families tie colourful **palms** from them, decorated with ribbons, apples or pretzels. The blessed branches are afterwards often hung up at home or in the stable.

In the Middle Ages, in some places a wooden **Palmesel** (‘palm donkey’) with a figure of Jesus on wheels was pulled through the streets. Some of these figures have survived to this day. In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich one can admire a very old Palmesel from Switzerland. In some villages the custom lives on even today, sometimes even with a real donkey.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the four books in the New Testament that tell of the life of Jesus.
The week before Easter, from Palm Sunday to Holy Saturday.
A solemn parade, often with prayers and singing.
A shout of joy from the Bible with which the people greeted Jesus.

gewusst: The German word ‘Karwoche’ for Holy Week comes from the Old High German word ‘kara’, which means lament or mourning.
Some of the palms tied in Switzerland on Palm Sunday are several metres tall.
In some areas, whoever got up last on Palm Sunday used to be jokingly called ‘Palmesel’.

teile.einleitung: When duckling chicks follow their mother everywhere straight after hatching, imprinting is behind it. In this inborn form of learning, very young chicks form a firm bond with their mother in a short time. Behavioural research has been studying for over a hundred years how this astonishing process works.
wichtigste: Imprinting is the name for forming the bond with the mother in very young chicks.
Thanks to imprinting, ducklings follow their mother immediately after hatching.
Imprinting is only possible in a short window of time.
Behaviour that has once been imprinted is very stable and can hardly be reversed.
Researchers such as Oskar Heinroth and Konrad Lorenz studied imprinting.
The study of behaviour is also called ethology.

abschnitte.text: Mallard ducklings hatch almost at the same time and leave the nest with their mother after only about a day. They walk behind her in a line, often even across roads or into the water. This **following behaviour** arises through imprinting on the mother's voice and appearance. The mother calls even before the ducklings hatch, and the ducklings answer from inside the egg.

As early as the 19th century, the Briton Douglas Spalding observed that chicks follow the first moving object. The German zoologist **Oskar Heinroth** described the behaviour in geese in more detail. His pupil Konrad Lorenz gave the process the name imprinting in the 1930s. This started an important chapter of **ethology**, the science of animal behaviour.

In ducklings, imprinting is strongest in the first one to two days after hatching. Researchers tested this with decoys that moved and made sounds. Chicks that saw a decoy only later followed it much less often. This short period is called the **sensitive period** or critical period.

Imprinting shows nicely how heredity and learning work together. What is inborn is the readiness to follow a moving creature. Exactly what the chick recognises as its mother, however, it learns only through experience. Science calls this a **learning predisposition**, that is, a built-in readiness for a particular kind of learning.

In humans there is no imprinting in the narrow sense as in geese. Even so, babies too build a close **bond** with their most important carers in the first months and years of life. This bond, however, forms slowly and can also grow towards several people. Attachment research was nevertheless strongly inspired by the imprinting experiments with animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies the behaviour of animals.
When young animals walk after their mother or another creature.
A model of an animal used to test behaviour.
A close emotional relationship between a child or young animal and a carer.

gewusst: Ducklings can already hear their mother's voice in the egg and remember it.
In experiments, chicks even followed a toy train if they were imprinted on it at the right time.
The famous sculpture “Make Way for Ducklings” in Boston shows a mother duck with eight ducklings in a line.

teile.einleitung: Jellyfish are jelly-like, transparent sea animals without a brain, heart or bones. They are about 95 per cent water and mostly drift with the current through the sea. Even so, they have existed for over 500 million years.
wichtigste: Jellyfish are not fish, but cnidarians.
Their body is made up of about 95 per cent water.
Jellyfish have no brain, but a simple nerve net.
They feed mainly on plankton and small fish.
They cannot swim against strong currents.
There are over 2,000 species of jellyfish, and the smallest are only a few millimetres across.
Most jellyfish live only a few months to about a year.

abschnitte.text: Jellyfish belong to the **cnidarians**, like corals and sea anemones. Their body is shaped like a bell or an umbrella, with tentacles hanging beneath it. They have no brain, no bones and no heart, but only a simple **nerve net**. Because their body is about 95 per cent water, jellyfish dry out quickly on the beach.

Most jellyfish live in the sea, from the surface down to the deep sea. They swim by contracting their umbrella and expelling water, like a small jet propulsion. They cannot make headway against strong currents this way and mostly drift along. Sometimes huge numbers gather in a **jellyfish swarm**.

Jellyfish catch plankton, fish larvae and small fish with their tentacles. On the tentacles sit thousands of tiny **stinging capsules**, which shoot out poison on contact. Most jellyfish are harmless to humans or cause only a burning feeling, like the mauve stinger. The sea wasp off Australia, by contrast, is very dangerous, and its poison can be deadly.

Many jellyfish have an exciting life cycle. From an egg a larva develops, which settles as a **polyp**, usually on a stone or rock on the sea floor. The polyp pinches off small discs, which break free and grow into free-swimming jellyfish. The free-swimming form is called the **medusa** in technical language.

You can also see jellyfish in Switzerland, although there is no sea here. The **freshwater jellyfish** is only about two centimetres across and appears in warm summers in lakes such as Lake Zurich or Lake Maggiore. It originally comes from China and is completely harmless to humans. At the sea, for example in the Mediterranean, you often meet the moon jellyfish with its four ring-shaped markings.

The tiny jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into a polyp in old age and is therefore regarded as the immortal jellyfish. The lion's mane jellyfish is one of the largest jellyfish, and its tentacles can grow many metres long. In some countries in Asia, jellyfish are even eaten. Because seas are getting warmer and fewer fish eat jellyfish, there are more jellyfish on some coasts today than before.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with stinging capsules, which includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
The free-swimming, bell-shaped form of a jellyfish.
The fixed form of cnidarians, which often grows on the sea floor.
Tiny animals and plants that float and drift in water.

gewusst: Jellyfish existed long before the dinosaurs.
Some jellyfish in the deep sea can make light themselves.
Even a dead jellyfish washed up on the beach can still sting.

teile.einleitung: Pollen pants is the name given to the small lumps of flower dust that honeybees and bumblebees carry home on their hind legs. They sit in a special basket on the leg and look as if the bee were wearing colourful trousers. With them the bees bring protein-rich food for their young into the hive.
wichtigste: Pollen pants are lumps of pollen that bees carry on their hind legs.
They sit in the pollen basket, a hollow on the lower part of the hind leg.
The bee moistens the pollen with nectar and saliva so that it sticks together.
The colour of the pants reveals which flowers the pollen comes from.
Bumblebees also carry their pollen in baskets on their hind legs.
Many wild bees have no baskets and collect pollen in hairy brushes.
Beekeepers can harvest pollen pants with a pollen trap.

abschnitte.text: On the lower part of each hind leg, the worker has a smooth, slightly hollowed area. Long, curved hairs stand at the edge and hold the pollen in place like the rods of a basket. This spot is called the **pollen basket**. The finished ball of pollen in it is called pollen pants, because it looks a little like baggy trousers.

abschnitte.titel: How a pair of pants is made
abschnitte.text: When visiting a flower, pollen sticks in the bee's dense fur. In flight she brushes it off with her legs and moistens it with a little **nectar** and saliva. With a comb of bristles and a kind of press at the leg joint, she pushes the pollen into the basket. This teamwork takes only seconds and often happens while the bee is already flying to the next flower.

Pollen pants are not always yellow. Pollen from the **dandelion** is bright orange, pollen from the horse chestnut is dark red, and some plants even supply grey or bluish pollen. On one trip a bee usually collects from only one plant species. That is why her two pairs of pants are almost always a single colour.

Back in the hive, the collector strips her pants off into a cell of the honeycomb. Other bees pack the pollen down with their heads and make **bee bread** from it. Young nurse bees eat some of it and make food juice for the larvae in their glands. Without enough pollen a colony cannot raise new brood.

Only honeybees and bumblebees have true pollen baskets. Many **wild bees** collect the pollen dry in a hairy brush on their legs. Mason bees and leafcutter bees even carry it in a brush on the belly. In Switzerland, around 600 species of wild bee live, with very different collecting techniques.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smooth hollow with a fringe of hair on the hind leg in which the bee carries pollen.
A grid at the entrance of the beehive that strips some of the pollen pants from the bees.
A young worker bee that feeds the larvae in the hive.
A kind of bee that is not kept by people, often living as a solitary bee.

gewusst: From the mix of colours of the pollen pants at the entrance, beekeepers can tell which plants are in flower at the moment.
A single pair of pollen pants weighs only a few milligrams, but a whole colony collects many kilograms from them in a year.

teile.einleitung: Pheromones are scent substances with which animals of the same species exchange messages. Ants use them to lay scent trails to food, and butterflies use them to attract a partner. Pheromones are a kind of chemical language that you do not hear but smell.
wichtigste: Pheromones are messenger substances for communication between animals of the same species.
Ants communicate mainly with scent substances and hardly at all with sounds.
Ants walk in lines because they follow the scent trail of another ant.
When an ant finds plenty of food, it calls many helpers with scent trails.
Many butterflies find their partner by giving off scent substances.
The term “pheromone” was introduced in 1959, among others by a Swiss researcher.
In agriculture, pheromones are used to protect plants.

abschnitte.text: Pheromones are chemical **messenger substances** that an animal gives off to influence other animals of its species. They often work even in tiny amounts. They are noticed with the sense of smell, in insects mostly with the **antennae**. The word is made up of Greek words and means roughly “to carry excitement”.

In social insects such as ants, pheromones are the most important language. When an ant finds food, it lays a **scent trail** on the way back to the nest. Other ants follow this trail and strengthen it for as long as there is food, which is why ants often walk in long lines. When an ant is attacked, it gives off an **alarm pheromone**, and its nestmates rush over or flee.

Many female moths give off a **sex attractant** to attract males. The males have large, feathered antennae and can detect the scent over long distances. The first pheromone to be studied exactly was bombykol of the silk moth, which the German chemist Adolf Butenandt described in 1959. For this he had to examine the scent glands of hundreds of thousands of females.

The word **pheromone** was proposed in 1959 by the German biochemist Peter Karlson and the Swiss insect researcher Martin Lüscher. Lüscher researched termites in particular and their scent substances. In honeybees, the queen controls life in the whole colony with her **queen substance**. Mammals such as cats, dogs and horses also react to pheromones, for example when marking territories.

In agriculture, **pheromone traps** are hung up to see when pests are flying. In Swiss winegrowing, the mating disruption method is often used: many small scent dispensers spread the attractant of the grape moth. The males then no longer find the females, and there are fewer caterpillars in the grapes. In this way, insecticide can be saved and beneficial insects spared.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scent substance with which animals of the same species communicate with each other.
A path of scent substances that other animals can follow.
A pheromone with which an animal attracts a partner.
A scent substance that warns members of the same species of danger.

gewusst: A male silk moth can detect a female's attractant when only a few molecules hit its antennae.
If you wipe a finger across an ant trail, the ants briefly lose the track.
Whether humans also have pheromones has still not been proven for certain.

teile.einleitung: Big cats, in German Raubkatzen, are cats that hunt and eat prey. Usually the term means the large wild cats such as the lion, tiger, leopard and jaguar. They are among the most impressive hunters in the world, but today are threatened in many places.
wichtigste: The German word “Raubkatze” means a cat that hunts and eats prey.
Usually it refers to large wild cats such as the lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard.
All cats, including the house cat, are meat eaters.
The tiger is the largest cat in the world.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal.
In Switzerland, a larger wild cat lives again, the lynx.
Many big cats are threatened by poaching and loss of habitat.

abschnitte.text: All cats belong to the **cat** family and feed almost only on meat. The word “Raubkatze” is not a scientific term, but is used mainly for the **large cats**. These include the lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, snow leopard and the clouded leopards. Often the cheetah, the puma and the lynx are counted as well.

Big cats have strong muscles, long **canine teeth** and sharp claws, which in most species they can draw in. Their eyes see very well even at dusk, and with their whiskers they feel their surroundings. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars can **roar** loudly, because their larynx is specially built. The tiger can grow to over 3 metres long and weigh more than 250 kilograms.

Most big cats are **loners** and hunt alone, often at dusk or at night. They sneak up on their prey and overpower it with a short sprint and a bite to the throat or neck. Only the **lion** lives in groups, the prides, and the females often hunt together. The cheetah, by contrast, chases its prey at over 90 kilometres per hour.

Lions today live mainly in the savannas of Africa, with a small group also in India. Tigers are found only in Asia, from the Indian jungle to the snowy forests of eastern Russia. The **jaguar** is the largest cat of the Americas, and the snow leopard lives in the high mountains of Central Asia. In Switzerland lives the **Eurasian lynx**, which was reintroduced from 1971.

Many big cats have become rare today. Their habitats are shrinking because of farming and settlements, and they are poached for fur and bones. Of the tigers, only a few thousand are still living in the wild. Protected areas, bans on **poaching** and projects for peaceful coexistence with farmers help to preserve them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of large cats that includes the lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard.
An animal that usually lives alone and not in a group.
A group of animals that live together, for example among lions.
Illegal hunting of protected animals.

gewusst: The snow leopard cannot roar, although it belongs to the large cats.
Every tiger has its own stripe pattern, as unique as a fingerprint.
The cheetah cannot draw in its claws completely, and they serve it in the sprint like the spikes on a running shoe.

teile.einleitung: Herbivores are animals that feed only, or almost only, on plants. They include large animals such as cows and elephants, but also small ones such as caterpillars and cockchafers. Because plants are hard to digest, herbivores often have special teeth and stomachs.
wichtigste: An animal that eats only plants is called a herbivore.
The technical term for this is herbivore.
The alpaca and the cockchafer are herbivores too.
Herbivores often have broad molar teeth for chewing.
Ruminants such as cows have a stomach with four sections.
In the food chain, herbivores are the food of many predators.

abschnitte.text: A **herbivore** feeds on grass, leaves, fruit, seeds, roots or nectar. Experts also say **herbivore** for this, from the Latin word “herba” meaning herb. By contrast, carnivores eat other animals, and omnivores eat both. Many herbivores specialise in particular parts of plants, such as seed eaters or fruit eaters.

Plants contain a lot of **cellulose**, a tough substance that animals find hard to digest. That is why herbivores have broad molar teeth, with which they grind their food thoroughly. In their gut, billions of bacteria help to break down the plants. Cows, sheep and goats are **ruminants**: they bring the food back up and chew it a second time.

In Switzerland, cows, sheep, goats and horses are well-known herbivores. In the wild, roe deer, red deer, ibex, chamois, marmots and brown hares live on plants. Many insects also eat plants, such as caterpillars, grasshoppers and the **cockchafer**, whose larvae even gnaw at roots. The alpaca from South America, which is also kept on Swiss farms, eats mainly grass and hay.

The largest land animals in the world, the **elephants**, are herbivores and eat over 100 kilograms of food a day. The koala eats almost only eucalyptus leaves, and the giant panda lives mainly on bamboo. Because plants provide little energy, many herbivores spend most of the day eating. Rabbits and hares even eat part of their own droppings to get more nutrients out.

abschnitte.titel: A place in the food chain
abschnitte.text: In the **food chain**, herbivores come directly after the plants. They turn plants into meat and are therefore prey for predators such as the wolf, lynx or fox. Many herbivores have eyes at the sides of the head so that they notice enemies early. They often live in herds, because many eyes see more and the individual is safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A technical word for an animal that feeds on plants.
A herbivore that brings its food back up and chews it once more, like the cow.
The tough building material of plants, which is hard to digest.
The order of who eats whom, from the plants to the predators.

gewusst: A cow chews its cud for many hours every day, often while lying comfortably.
The giant panda belongs to the carnivores but eats almost only bamboo.
Many of the largest dinosaurs, such as the long-necked sauropods, were herbivores.

teile.einleitung: The grass snake, in German Ringelnatter, is a harmless, non-venomous snake that likes to live near water. You can often recognise it by two pale, yellowish patches behind the head. It is an excellent swimmer and one of the most common snakes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The grass snake is non-venomous to people.
It likes best to live near water and can swim very well.
In Switzerland it usually grows about 70 to 100 centimetres long, rarely more.
It is grey to olive green and often has pale patches behind the head.
It is active by day and is a meat eater.
Unlike the adder, it has round pupils.
A pond and a pile of leaves in the garden help it.

abschnitte.text: The grass snake is mostly **grey to olive green** and often has dark spots on its sides. Typical are two pale, yellowish or white patches behind the head, which are called **crescent patches**. In Switzerland it usually grows about 70 to 100 centimetres long, rarely more. The females are clearly larger than the males. Its German name probably means that it curls itself up.

The grass snake is non-venomous and harmless to people. It has many small teeth curved backwards, with which it holds its prey. You can tell it from the venomous **adder** by the round pupils, whereas the adder has vertical, slit-shaped pupils. In addition, the grass snake lacks the zigzag band on the back. It is best, however, to watch every snake from a distance and not to touch it.

The grass snake likes best to live near **water**, for example at ponds, pools, streams and lake shores. It is a good swimmer and also dives for prey. But it is also found in meadows, forests and near-natural gardens. It is active by day and likes to bask in the morning. It spends the winter in cold torpor in frost-free hiding places.

Grass snakes are **meat eaters**. They eat mainly frogs, toads, newts and tadpoles. Fish and sometimes small mammals are also on the menu. The prey is not killed with poison, but swallowed alive. After a large meal, the snake does not have to eat for days.

In summer the female lays eggs in warm places, for example in **compost heaps**, manure or rotting leaves. The warmth helps the eggs to develop. Freshly hatched grass snakes look like small versions of their parents. When in danger, the grass snake hisses, gives off a foul-smelling liquid or plays dead. In doing so it lies on its back with its mouth open and its tongue hanging out.

In Switzerland, two species are now distinguished: the **barred grass snake** in most of the country and the eastern grass snake in the east. Both are protected and are on the Red List of endangered species. Their habitats are disappearing because wetlands and ponds are being filled in. In the garden, a pond, a pile of leaves, piles of stones and a compost heap help. In this way the grass snake finds food, hiding places and places for its eggs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake family with many species that are mostly non-venomous.
Two pale patches behind the head of the grass snake.
The dark opening in the middle of the eye.
A trick in which an animal pretends to be dead in order to fool enemies.

gewusst: Freshly hatched grass snakes are only about 15 to 20 centimetres long.
In a single large compost heap, several females sometimes lay their eggs together.
A grass snake can swallow a toad that is thicker than its own head.

teile.einleitung: A carnivore, in German Raubtier, is an animal that hunts and eats other animals. In biology, “Raubtiere” is also the name of an order of mammals that includes dogs, cats, bears, martens and seals. Carnivores play an important role in nature, in Switzerland too, with the wolf, lynx and fox.
wichtigste: An animal that hunts and eats other animals is called a predator.
In biology, the carnivores (Carnivora) form an order of mammals of their own.
Typical are strong canine teeth and sharp cheek teeth, the carnassials.
Not all carnivores eat only meat, and the giant panda eats almost only bamboo.
Carnivores keep the numbers of their prey animals in balance.
In Switzerland there live, among others, the fox, badger, martens, lynx and, again, the wolf.

abschnitte.text: In everyday speech, any animal that hunts and eats other animals is called a **predator** or a hunter. By that meaning, eagles, pike or spiders would also be predators. In biology, however, the word refers to a particular group of mammals, the **order Carnivora**. This includes around 280 species, among them dogs, cats, bears, martens, hyenas and seals.

Mammal carnivores have long, pointed **canine teeth** with which they grab and kill prey. Especially typical are the **carnassials**, sharp cheek teeth that cut meat like scissors. Many have a very good sense of smell and good hearing. Cats hunt mainly with their eyes, dogs and wolves with their noses.

Although “Carnivora” means meat eaters, not all of them feed that way. The **brown bear** eats very many berries, roots and grasses, so it is an omnivore. The giant panda lives almost only on bamboo. Foxes and badgers eat earthworms, fruit and scraps as well as mice.

Carnivores often eat sick, weak or young animals and so keep the prey stocks healthy. When there are many prey animals, the predators multiply too, and then both decrease again. This up and down is called the **predator-prey relationship**. Without carnivores, roe deer and red deer, for example, can multiply so strongly that they eat young trees in the forest.

The most common carnivores in Switzerland are the **fox**, badger, stone marten and pine marten, polecat and weasel. The lynx was reintroduced from 1971, and the **wolf** came back on its own from Italy in 1995. In 2024 there were already over 30 wolf packs living in Switzerland. Now and then brown bears also wander from Italy into the Engadine, but they usually do not stay long.

Carnivores such as the wolf can kill sheep and goats, which is difficult for farmers. That is why in Switzerland there is livestock protection with fences and **livestock guardian dogs**. The rules on when wolves may be shot are often discussed in politics. At the same time, many people are glad that these animals have returned to Swiss nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The scientific name of the order of carnivores among the mammals.
Sharp cheek teeth that cut meat like scissors.
The connection between the number of hunters and the number of their prey animals.
Measures that protect farm animals such as sheep from wolves.

gewusst: In biology, seals and sea lions also count among the carnivores.
The smallest carnivore in Switzerland is the least weasel, which weighs only about 50 to 100 grams.
The polar bear is the largest carnivore living on land on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The dor beetle, in German Rosskäfer, is a large, glossy black dung beetle that lives in meadows and pastures in Europe. It probably has its German name, meaning horse beetle, because it is often found in the dung of horses. It makes sure that droppings disappear quickly and that the soil is fertilised.
wichtigste: The dor beetle is a dung beetle and grows about 2 centimetres long.
Its German name probably comes from horse dung, in which it often lives.
It digs deep tunnels into the ground under piles of droppings.
In the tunnels it stores supplies of dung for its larvae.
Its underside often shimmers blue or violet.
It helps to break down droppings and to make the soil fertile.

abschnitte.text: The dor beetle, also called the common dung beetle, is about 16 to 25 millimetres long. Its upperside is black, and the underside and the legs often gleam **metallic blue** or violet. It has strong, toothed forelegs built like shovels for digging. Its antennae end in a small club of plates.

Ross is an old word for horse. In the past there were horses everywhere on roads and pastures, and the beetle was often found in their **dung**. That is why it was called Rosskäfer. But it also uses the droppings of cows, sheep and other animals.

abschnitte.titel: Life under the pile of droppings
abschnitte.text: Unlike the dung beetle that rolls balls, the dor beetle does not roll balls. Directly beneath a pile of droppings it digs a **vertical tunnel**, which often reaches several decimetres deep into the earth. Male and female work together in doing this. At the end of the side tunnels they stuff dung in and lay an egg in each.

From the egg hatches a whitish **larva**, which feeds on the stored dung. It lives protected in the ground and grows up there. After pupation, a finished beetle comes up to the surface. Dor beetles like to fly at dusk and look for new piles of droppings.

Dor beetles are important **waste recyclers** on pastures. They bring dung into the soil, where it fertilises the plants. In addition, their tunnels loosen the earth and let air and water in. Because the droppings disappear faster, annoying flies also find less room to multiply.

In many areas, dung beetles have become rarer. One reason is that fewer animals stand outside on pastures. Another reason is worming drugs for farm animals, whose residues in the dung can harm the beetles and their larvae. In Switzerland you still find the dor beetle mainly on pastures with cows and horses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The droppings of animals, especially of horses and cows.
A beetle that feeds on animal droppings and brings them into the soil.
The young form of an insect, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
An animal that eats dead plants or droppings and so keeps nature clean.

gewusst: Dor beetles can make chirping sounds by rubbing body parts against each other.
On dor beetles there often sit tiny mites, which let themselves be carried by them to the next pile of droppings.

teile.einleitung: Puma is a large maker of sports shoes, sportswear and sports accessories from Germany. The company is named after the animal, the fast and supple big cat from the Americas. Its logo, a leaping cat, is known all over the world.
wichtigste: Puma is a company named after the animal, the puma.
It was founded in 1948 by Rudolf Dassler in Herzogenaurach in Bavaria.
His brother Adolf Dassler founded the rival firm Adidas.
Puma makes sports shoes, sportswear and accessories.
The logo shows a leaping puma.
Many famous sportswomen and sportsmen wore and still wear Puma products.

abschnitte.text: The company chose the name Puma because the big cat stands for speed, strength and suppleness. These are exactly the qualities that sportswomen and sportsmen want. The well-known **logo** shows the silhouette of a puma in mid-leap. On many shoes you also see a curved stripe, the so-called Formstrip.

From the 1920s, the brothers Rudolf and Adolf Dassler made sports shoes together in **Herzogenaurach**. After the Second World War they fell out and split in 1948. Rudolf founded Puma, and Adolf, known as Adi, founded Adidas. Both companies still have their headquarters today in the same small town in Bavaria.

Puma is especially well known in **football**. The Brazilian star Pelé wore Puma boots at the 1970 World Cup, and Diego Maradona also played in Puma boots. Later the Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt, the world record holder over 100 metres, became one of the best-known Puma athletes. The Swiss national football team has also played at several major tournaments in Puma shirts.

Puma is a **public limited company** and sells its products in over 100 countries. The company employs many thousands of people worldwide. Most of the shoes and clothes are made in factories in Asia. After Nike and Adidas, Puma is one of the largest sports goods makers in the world.

For companies such as Puma, the **brand** is very important. That is why they pay athletes and clubs a lot of money to wear their products, which is called **sponsoring**. Anyone who buys sportswear is therefore also paying for advertising and the good name. A look at the material and how it is made is therefore often worth more than just a look at the logo.

begriffe.erklaerung: A name or sign by which you recognise the products of a company.
The picture sign of a company or organisation.
When a company gives athletes or clubs money so that they advertise for it.
A company that belongs to many owners who hold shares.

gewusst: In Herzogenaurach it used to be said that the town was so divided that people first looked at the shoes of the person facing them.
At the very beginning, the company Puma was called “Ruda” for short, after Rudolf Dassler.
In 2009 Puma and Adidas staged a friendly football match in Herzogenaurach to end the old quarrel symbolically.
